contrast.en: There is a family photo hanging on the wall.
contrast.note: A photograph of the family, so 写真. 絵 would mean someone painted a portrait of them.

contrast.ja: 妹は絵が上手です。
contrast.reading: いもうとはえがじょうずです。
contrast.en: My younger sister is good at drawing.
contrast.note: This praises drawing skill. 写真が上手 is also possible, but it means she is good at photography — a different talent.

contrast.ja: この本は絵がたくさんあって読みやすいです。
contrast.reading: このほんはえがたくさんあってよみやすいです。
contrast.en: This book has lots of pictures, so it is easy to read.
contrast.note: Illustrations in a book are drawn, so 絵 — which is why a picture book is 絵本.

mistakes.wrong: 絵を撮ってください。
mistakes.right: 写真を撮ってください。
mistakes.why: 撮る is the camera verb. Asking someone to 絵を撮る sounds like you want a photograph of a painting, not a picture of you.

mistakes.wrong: 写真を描きました。
mistakes.right: 写真を撮りました。／絵を描きました。
mistakes.why: 描く means to draw, so it cannot take 写真. Pick the verb that matches the noun.

faq.q: Is a picture I made on my tablet a 絵 or a 写真?
faq.a: 絵. The distinction is drawn versus photographed, not paper versus screen.

faq.q: How do I say "picture" when I do not know which it is?
faq.a: 画像 (がぞう) is the neutral word for an image of either kind, and is what appears on websites and phone menus.

title: 市 vs 町
quickAnswer: 市 is an official administrative unit — a city as it appears in addresses and government names like 横浜市 or 市役所. 町 is the everyday word for the town or neighbourhood you actually live in and walk around. When you are talking about your life rather than paperwork, 町 is almost always the natural choice.
summary: 市 is the administrative city of addresses and city hall; 町 is the everyday town or neighbourhood you live in and walk around.

members.when: Use 市 attached to a place name (名古屋市) or in official compounds: 市内, 市役所, 市のバス, 市の図書館. It marks something as belonging to the municipal government.

examples.ja: 住所は大阪市北区です。
examples.reading: じゅうしょはおおさかしきたくです。
examples.en: My address is Kita Ward, Osaka City.

examples.ja: 市役所でパスポートの申請をしました。
examples.reading: しやくしょでパスポートのしんせいをしました。
examples.en: I applied for a passport at city hall.

members.when: Use 町 for the town or built-up area as a place you experience — quiet, lively, changing. It is also a real administrative unit smaller than a 市, as in 軽井沢町.

examples.ja: この町には駅が一つしかありません。
examples.reading: このまちにはえきがひとつしかありません。
examples.en: This town has only one station.

examples.ja: 夜の町はとてもにぎやかです。
examples.reading: よるのまちはとてもにぎやかです。
examples.en: The town is very lively at night.

contrast.ja: 週末は町を歩くのが好きです。
contrast.reading: しゅうまつはまちをあるくのがすきです。
contrast.en: I like walking around town on weekends.
contrast.note: You walk through streets, not through an administrative unit, so 町. 市を歩く is not said.

contrast.ja: 市の図書館は月曜日が休みです。
contrast.reading: しのとしょかんはげつようびがやすみです。
contrast.en: The city library is closed on Mondays.
contrast.note: The library is run by the municipal government, so 市の. 町の図書館 would suggest a small local one instead.

contrast.ja: 去年、この村は市になりました。
contrast.reading: きょねん、このむらはしになりました。
contrast.en: Last year this village became a city.
contrast.note: Here 市 is a legal status a place is granted, which 町 cannot express in this sentence.

mistakes.wrong: この市は静かです。
mistakes.right: この町は静かです。
mistakes.why: Describing the feel of where you live calls for 町. この市 sounds like you are reading off a municipal document.

mistakes.wrong: 町役所へ行きます。
mistakes.right: 市役所へ行きます。
mistakes.why: The standard word for a city office is 市役所. 町役場 exists, but only for places that really are a 町.

faq.q: My town is officially a 市. Can I still say 町?
faq.a: Yes. People in large cities routinely say この町 about their own neighbourhood; 市 is for the official framing.

faq.q: I have seen 市 read いち. Is that the same word?
faq.a: No — 市 (いち) means a market, as in 朝市, a morning market. Same kanji, different word.

title: 答える vs 返事
quickAnswer: 答える is a verb and 返事 is a noun, so they do not fit the same slot: you say 質問に答える but 返事をする. In meaning, 答える is giving the content of an answer — the information asked for — while 返事 is the act of responding at all, such as replying to an email or calling back when your name is read out.
summary: 答える is a verb for supplying an answer's content (質問に答える); 返事 is a noun for the act of responding (返事をする).

members.when: Use 答える when you supply the content of an answer. What is answered takes に: 質問に答える, 先生に答える. Never 質問を答える.

examples.ja: この質問に日本語で答えてください。
examples.reading: このしつもんににほんごでこたえてください。
examples.en: Please answer this question in Japanese.

examples.ja: だれも答えられませんでした。
examples.reading: だれもこたえられませんでした。
examples.en: Nobody could answer.

members.when: Use 返事 as a noun for a response coming back: 返事をする, 返事が来る, 返事を待つ. 返事する without を is also normal in speech. It covers letters, messages and answering when you are addressed.

examples.ja: まだ返事をもらっていません。
examples.reading: まだへんじをもらっていません。
examples.en: I still have not had a reply.

examples.ja: 呼んだらすぐに返事をしてね。
examples.reading: よんだらすぐにへんじをしてね。
examples.en: Answer right away when I call you, okay?

contrast.ja: 先生の質問に答えました。
contrast.reading: せんせいのしつもんにこたえました。
contrast.en: I answered the teacher's question.
contrast.note: You produced the information asked for, so 答える. 返事をしました would only say you responded, not that you knew the answer.

contrast.ja: メールの返事がまだ来ません。
contrast.reading: メールのへんじがまだきません。
contrast.en: The reply to my email has not come yet.
contrast.note: A reply is a thing that arrives, so a noun is needed here; 答える cannot occupy this slot.

contrast.ja: 名前を呼ばれたら返事をしてください。
contrast.reading: なまえをよばれたらへんじをしてください。
contrast.en: Please answer when your name is called.
contrast.note: Saying "here" is responding, not answering a question, so 返事. 答えてください would imply a question had been asked.

contrast.ja: その質問には答えたくありません。
contrast.reading: そのしつもんにはこたえたくありません。
contrast.en: I do not want to answer that question.
contrast.note: 答える conjugates freely as a verb; 返事 needs する before it can do the same work.

mistakes.wrong: 質問を答えます。
mistakes.right: 質問に答えます。
mistakes.why: 答える marks what is answered with に, not を. This is the most common error with this verb.

mistakes.wrong: メールに答えます。
mistakes.right: メールに返事をします。／メールに返信します。
mistakes.why: 答える supplies the content of an answer; replying to a message is 返事 or, in business writing, 返信.

mistakes.wrong: 先生に返事をしました。
mistakes.right: 先生の質問に答えました。
mistakes.why: If the point is that you gave an answer in class, 答える is correct. 先生に返事をする suggests you merely acknowledged being spoken to.

faq.q: Can I say 返事する without を?
faq.a: Yes. 返事する is normal in conversation; 返事をする is slightly more careful and is what you would write.

faq.q: What is the noun form of 答える?
faq.a: 答え (こたえ) — the answer itself, as in 答えが分かりません. That is the content; 返事 is the act of responding.

faq.q: Is 返信 different from 返事?
faq.a: 返信 is specifically a written reply to a message or letter and is the usual word in business email. 返事 is broader and more everyday.

title: 最近 vs この頃
quickAnswer: Both mean "recently", but 最近 can point at a single event in the near past (最近、引っ越しました — I moved recently), while この頃 describes an ongoing stretch of time up to now (この頃、よく眠れない — I have not been sleeping well lately). 最近 is also the neutral choice in writing; この頃 belongs mainly to conversation.
summary: 最近 covers both a one-off recent event and an ongoing trend; この頃 describes only an ongoing stretch, and is more conversational.

members.when: Use 最近 for anything in the recent past — a single event or a continuing state. It is safe in essays, email and speech, which makes it the default when you are unsure.

examples.ja: 最近、日本語の勉強を始めました。
examples.reading: さいきん、にほんごのべんきょうをはじめました。
examples.en: I started studying Japanese recently.

examples.ja: 最近の若い人はあまりテレビを見ない。
examples.reading: さいきんのわかいひとはあまりテレビをみない。
examples.en: Young people these days do not watch much television.

members.when: Use この頃 for how things have been over a recent period — habits, moods, weather, trends. It pairs naturally with ずっと and with ている forms, and sounds conversational.

examples.ja: この頃、朝晩がずいぶん涼しくなった。
examples.reading: このごろ、あさばんがずいぶんすずしくなった。
examples.en: Mornings and evenings have grown much cooler lately.

examples.ja: この頃、彼をぜんぜん見かけない。
examples.reading: このごろ、かれをぜんぜんみかけない。
examples.en: I have not seen him around at all lately.

contrast.ja: 最近、引っ越しました。
contrast.reading: さいきん、ひっこしました。
contrast.en: I moved recently.
contrast.note: A single completed event. この頃、引っ越しました is odd, because この頃 wants a continuing situation rather than one action.

contrast.ja: この頃、体の調子がよくない。
contrast.reading: このごろ、からだのちょうしがよくない。
contrast.en: I have not been feeling well lately.
contrast.note: An ongoing state, which is この頃's home ground. 最近 also works here — this is where the two genuinely overlap.

contrast.ja: 最近の調査によると、利用者は増えているそうだ。
contrast.reading: さいきんのちょうさによると、りようしゃはふえているそうだ。
contrast.en: According to a recent survey, users are increasing.
contrast.note: 最近の modifies a noun in written style. この頃の調査 is not used in this sense.

mistakes.wrong: この頃、新しい仕事を見つけました。
mistakes.right: 最近、新しい仕事を見つけました。
mistakes.why: A one-time event needs 最近. この頃 frames the sentence as how things have been going, which clashes with a single past action.

mistakes.wrong: この頃までこの会社で働いていました。
mistakes.right: 最近までこの会社で働いていました。
mistakes.why: 最近まで, meaning "until recently", is a set pattern; この頃まで is not used this way.

faq.q: Which one should I use in an essay or a report?
faq.a: 最近. この頃 is not wrong in writing, but it reads as spoken style; 最近 is the neutral choice on an exam or in a report.

faq.q: What about 近頃?
faq.a: 近頃 (ちかごろ) means much the same as この頃 but sounds older and more literary. You will meet it in reading; you rarely need to produce it.

faq.q: Is その頃 related?
faq.a: Only in form. その頃 means "back then", pointing at a past time already mentioned, not at the present period.

title: だんだん vs 徐々に
quickAnswer: They mean the same thing — gradually — and the difference is register. だんだん is the spoken, everyday word you use with friends and in class; 徐々に is the written one you use in reports, news and formal speech. Neither describes a slower change than the other; swapping them changes only how the sentence sounds.
summary: だんだん and 徐々に both mean "gradually": だんだん is spoken and everyday, 徐々に is written and formal.

members.when: Use だんだん in conversation, messages and casual writing, typically with a change you can feel: だんだん暖かくなる, だんだん上手になる. It sits most naturally with なる.

examples.ja: だんだん暖かくなってきましたね。
examples.reading: だんだんあたたかくなってきましたね。
examples.en: It has been getting warmer, hasn't it?

examples.ja: 日本語がだんだん分かるようになりました。
examples.reading: にほんごがだんだんわかるようになりました。
examples.en: I have gradually come to understand Japanese.

members.when: Use 徐々に in essays, business email, news and presentations, especially with measured or controlled change: 徐々に増える, 徐々に回復する, 徐々に進める.

examples.ja: 売り上げは徐々に回復している。
examples.reading: うりあげはじょじょにかいふくしている。
examples.en: Sales are gradually recovering.

examples.ja: 薬の量を徐々に減らしていきます。
examples.reading: くすりのりょうをじょじょにへらしていきます。
examples.en: We will reduce the dosage gradually.

contrast.ja: だんだん眠くなってきた。
contrast.reading: だんだんねむくなってきた。
contrast.en: I am gradually getting sleepy.
contrast.note: A personal, felt change in casual speech. 徐々に眠くなってきた sounds like a clinical report on yourself.

contrast.ja: 気温は徐々に上昇すると予想される。
contrast.reading: きおんはじょじょにじょうしょうするとよそうされる。
contrast.en: Temperatures are expected to rise gradually.
contrast.note: A forecast in written style, so 徐々に matches 予想される. だんだん would clash with the formality of the rest of the sentence.

contrast.ja: 少しずつでいいので続けてください。
contrast.reading: すこしずつでいいのでつづけてください。
contrast.en: Just keep at it a little at a time.
contrast.note: 少しずつ is the neutral middle ground and works in both registers when you cannot decide.

mistakes.wrong: 友だちに「徐々に上手になったね」と言われた。
mistakes.right: 友だちに「だんだん上手になったね」と言われた。
mistakes.why: 徐々に in friendly conversation is not ungrammatical, just stiff — it sounds like a news reader praising you.

mistakes.wrong: レポートに「だんだん増えています」と書いた。
mistakes.right: レポートに「徐々に増えています」と書いた。
mistakes.why: In a written report だんだん reads as casual. Graders and colleagues expect 徐々に.

faq.q: Which one should I write in a JLPT essay?
faq.a: 徐々に. In the listening and conversation material you will mostly meet だんだん.

faq.q: Does 徐々に mean more slowly than だんだん?
faq.a: Not reliably. 徐々に often feels controlled or deliberate because of the contexts it appears in, but the core meaning is the same.

faq.q: Can I use だんだん for a change for the worse?
faq.a: Yes — だんだん寒くなる and だんだん悪くなる are both normal. The word says nothing about good or bad.

title: きっと vs 必ず
quickAnswer: きっと is the speaker's own conviction about something out of their control — a confident guess, usually with でしょう or と思う. 必ず is objective inevitability or a commitment: what always happens, what a rule requires, or what you promise to do without fail. So a weather prediction is きっと晴れる, while an instruction is 必ず来てください.
summary: きっと is the speaker's confident guess (きっと晴れる); 必ず is inevitability, rules and promises (必ず来てください).

members.when: Use きっと for predictions, inferences and reassurance about things you do not control. It pairs with でしょう, だろう, はずだ and と思う, and belongs mostly to conversation.

examples.ja: 彼はきっと来ると思います。
examples.reading: かれはきっとくるとおもいます。
examples.en: I am sure he will come.

examples.ja: 心配しないで、きっと大丈夫だよ。
examples.reading: しんぱいしないで、きっとだいじょうぶだよ。
examples.en: Don't worry, it will be fine.

members.when: Use 必ず for what is guaranteed: rules, instructions, habits without exception, and promises about your own actions. It is the word in manuals, signs and business email.

examples.ja: 出かける前に必ず鍵をかけてください。
examples.reading: でかけるまえにかならずかぎをかけてください。
examples.en: Please be sure to lock up before you go out.

examples.ja: 明日までに必ず連絡します。
examples.reading: あしたまでにかならずれんらくします。
examples.en: I will contact you by tomorrow without fail.

contrast.ja: 明日はきっと晴れるでしょう。
contrast.reading: あしたはきっとはれるでしょう。
contrast.en: It will surely be sunny tomorrow.
contrast.note: Weather is a guess, however confident. 必ず晴れる would claim sunshine is guaranteed, which a speaker cannot assert.

contrast.ja: 薬は食後に必ず飲んでください。
contrast.reading: くすりはしょくごにかならずのんでください。
contrast.en: Be sure to take the medicine after meals.
contrast.note: An instruction. きっと飲んでください does not work, because きっと describes belief rather than what someone must do.

contrast.ja: 水は百度で必ず沸騰する。
contrast.reading: みずはひゃくどでかならずふっとうする。
contrast.en: Water always boils at one hundred degrees.
contrast.note: An exceptionless fact, so 必ず. きっと would turn a physical law into the speaker's hunch.

contrast.ja: 返事がないけれど、きっと忙しいんだろう。
contrast.reading: へんじがないけれど、きっといそがしいんだろう。
contrast.en: There is no reply, but he must be busy.
contrast.note: Inferring a reason from evidence is exactly きっと's job; 必ず cannot express inference at all.

mistakes.wrong: 明日は必ず雨が降るでしょう。
mistakes.right: 明日はきっと雨が降るでしょう。
mistakes.why: 必ず asserts certainty, so it fights with でしょう, which hedges. A guess takes きっと.

mistakes.wrong: きっと宿題を出してください。
mistakes.right: 必ず宿題を出してください。
mistakes.why: You cannot ask someone to be confident. Requests and rules take 必ず.

mistakes.wrong: 必ずしも来ます。
mistakes.right: 必ず来ます。
mistakes.why: 必ずしも is used only with a negative, meaning "not necessarily", as in 必ずしも安いとは限らない.

faq.q: Which do I write in an email to my boss?
faq.a: 必ず, when you are promising an action: 必ず本日中に提出します. きっと would make your own commitment sound like a guess about yourself.

faq.q: Isn't きっと来てね something people say?
faq.a: Yes, and it is fine — that is pleading rather than instructing, closer to "do come, I'm counting on it". For a real requirement, still use 必ず.

faq.q: Which one is stronger?
faq.a: 必ず, because it claims certainty about the world. きっと can sound very confident, but it stays the speaker's own belief.

title: たぶん vs おそらく
quickAnswer: Both mean "probably", with much the same level of confidence — the difference is register. たぶん is the everyday spoken word; おそらく is its formal counterpart, used in writing, news, presentations and careful speech, and it usually closes the sentence with だろう or と思われる rather than でしょう.
summary: たぶん and おそらく both mean "probably": たぶん is conversational, おそらく is the formal written equivalent.

members.when: Use たぶん in conversation, messages and anything casual. It sits comfortably with でしょう and と思う, and is the safe default when you are speaking.

examples.ja: 田中さんはたぶん来ないと思います。
examples.reading: たなかさんはたぶんこないとおもいます。
examples.en: I think Tanaka probably won't come.

examples.ja: たぶん七時ごろ着くよ。
examples.reading: たぶんしちじごろつくよ。
examples.en: I'll probably get there around seven.

members.when: Use おそらく in essays, reports, news writing and formal speech. It pairs with だろう and と思われる, and usually introduces a considered inference rather than an offhand guess.

examples.ja: おそらく原因は設定の誤りだろう。
examples.reading: おそらくげんいんはせっていのあやまりだろう。
examples.en: The cause is most likely a configuration error.

examples.ja: この方法ではおそらく間に合わないと思われる。
examples.reading: このほうほうではおそらくまにあわないとおもわれる。
examples.en: This approach will probably not make the deadline.

contrast.ja: ごめん、たぶん遅れる。
contrast.reading: ごめん、たぶんおくれる。
contrast.en: Sorry, I'll probably be late.
contrast.note: A short message to a friend. おそらく遅れる here reads like a press statement.

contrast.ja: おそらく今後も同じ傾向が続くだろう。
contrast.reading: おそらくこんごもおなじけいこうがつづくだろう。
contrast.en: The same trend will most likely continue from here on.
contrast.note: Written analysis with だろう — おそらく's natural home. たぶん would undercut the tone of the sentence.

contrast.ja: 会議はおそらく二時間ほどかかる見込みです。
contrast.reading: かいぎはおそらくにじかんほどかかるみこみです。
contrast.en: The meeting is expected to take about two hours.
contrast.note: Formal spoken Japanese at work. 見込みです and おそらく match each other in register.

mistakes.wrong: 友だちに「おそらく行けない」と送った。
mistakes.right: 友だちに「たぶん行けない」と送った。
mistakes.why: おそらく to a friend is not wrong, but it is markedly stiff — the effect is like writing "it is likely that I shall be unable to attend" in a text message.

mistakes.wrong: レポートに「たぶん原因は…」と書いた。
mistakes.right: レポートに「おそらく原因は…」と書いた。
mistakes.why: たぶん in a written report sounds like a shrug. Formal writing expects おそらく.

mistakes.wrong: おそらく行きます。
mistakes.right: おそらく行くだろう。／たぶん行きます。
mistakes.why: おそらく normally wants a tentative ending such as だろう or と思われる; a bare ます form with おそらく sounds mismatched.

faq.q: Is おそらく more certain than たぶん?
faq.a: Not really. Both sit around "probably". おそらく can feel better reasoned because it appears in analytical writing, but it is not a stronger claim.

faq.q: Which should I use in a JLPT essay?
faq.a: おそらく, and the kanji form 恐らく is equally fine. Keep たぶん for the conversational material.

faq.q: What about もしかしたら?
faq.a: That is weaker — "maybe, possibly" — and points at an outside chance rather than the likely outcome.

title: とても vs 非常に
quickAnswer: Both intensify an adjective, and the difference is register: とても is the everyday spoken word for "very", while 非常に is the formal written one found in reports, news and business email. 非常に also leans towards objective, weighty descriptions such as 非常に重要な問題, and sounds comical applied to your lunch.
summary: とても is everyday spoken "very"; 非常に is the formal intensifier for reports, news and business Japanese.

members.when: Use とても in conversation and ordinary writing, with any adjective: とても暑い, とてもおいしい, とても好き. It is never out of place in polite speech.

examples.ja: この料理はとてもおいしいです。
examples.reading: このりょうりはとてもおいしいです。
examples.en: This dish is very good.

examples.ja: 昨日の試験はとても難しかった。
examples.reading: きのうのしけんはとてもむずかしかった。
examples.en: Yesterday's exam was very hard.

members.when: Use 非常に in formal writing and formal speech — reports, academic essays, business email, announcements. It fits objective evaluations rather than personal taste.

examples.ja: これは非常に重要な問題です。
examples.reading: これはひじょうにじゅうようなもんだいです。
examples.en: This is an extremely important issue.

examples.ja: 今回の結果は非常に残念です。
examples.reading: こんかいのけっかはひじょうにざんねんです。
examples.en: This result is deeply regrettable.

contrast.ja: 母の作るカレーはとてもおいしい。
contrast.reading: ははのつくるカレーはとてもおいしい。
contrast.en: My mother's curry is really good.
contrast.note: Personal taste in casual speech. 非常においしい here sounds like a food inspector filing a report.

contrast.ja: 本件は非常に緊急性が高いと判断いたしました。
contrast.reading: ほんけんはひじょうにきんきゅうせいがたかいとはんだんいたしました。
contrast.en: We have judged this matter to be extremely urgent.
contrast.note: Business writing throughout, so 非常に matches 判断いたしました. とても would sit oddly in this register.

contrast.ja: こんなにたくさん、とても食べられません。
contrast.reading: こんなにたくさん、とてもたべられません。
contrast.en: There is no way I can eat this much.
contrast.note: With a negative, とても means "cannot possibly" rather than "very". 非常に has no such use.

mistakes.wrong: 友だちに「このケーキは非常においしいね」と言った。
mistakes.right: 友だちに「このケーキはとてもおいしいね」と言った。
mistakes.why: 非常に about a cake among friends is grammatical but funny — the register is several steps above the situation.

mistakes.wrong: この荷物はとても持てます。
mistakes.right: この荷物はとても持てません。／この荷物は軽いので持てます。
mistakes.why: とても before a potential verb belongs to the とても〜ない pattern and needs a negative. In the affirmative it does not work as a plain intensifier.

faq.q: Can I use とても in a business email?
faq.a: Yes — とても is polite and neutral. 非常に simply raises the formality a level, which suits reports and serious announcements.

faq.q: Where does すごく fit?
faq.a: すごく is a step more casual than とても and belongs in conversation with friends rather than in writing.

faq.q: Is 非常に related to 非常口?
faq.a: They share the kanji, but 非常口, an emergency exit, uses 非常 in its "emergency" sense. Treat 非常に as its own adverb.

title: 見る vs 観る
quickAnswer: 見る and 観る are the same word, みる — only the kanji differs. 見る is the default for seeing or looking at anything, while 観る is an optional spelling used when you are watching something you chose and are giving your attention to, such as a film, a play or a match. Writing 見る everywhere is still correct.
summary: 見る and 観る are both みる: 見る is the default for seeing, 観る an optional spelling for watching a film, play or match you chose.

members.when: The default spelling for anything your eyes do: noticing, looking at, checking, and watching too. If you are unsure, 見る is safe — it is never wrong, and it is the spelling used in textbooks and newspapers.

examples.ja: 毎晩テレビでニュースを見ます。
examples.reading: まいばんテレビでニュースをみます。
examples.en: I watch the news on TV every evening.

examples.ja: この漢字をよく見てください。
examples.reading: このかんじをよくみてください。
examples.en: Please look carefully at this kanji.

members.when: Chosen when the watching is deliberate and the thing is something put on to be watched — a film, a play, a match, a concert. 観 carries the sense of viewing and observing, as in 観察 and 観光. It is a writer's choice, not a grammar rule.

examples.ja: 週末に映画館で映画を観ました。
examples.reading: しゅうまつにえいがかんでえいがをみました。
examples.en: I watched a film at the cinema at the weekend.

examples.ja: 日曜日にサッカーの試合を観に行きます。
examples.reading: にちようびにサッカーのしあいをみにいきます。
examples.en: I'm going to watch a football match on Sunday.

contrast.ja: 空を見てください。星がきれいです。
contrast.reading: そらをみてください。ほしがきれいです。
contrast.en: Look at the sky. The stars are beautiful.
contrast.note: Nothing was staged for you and nothing was chosen — this is plain looking, so 観る would read as a mistake.

contrast.ja: 道で友だちの顔を見ました。
contrast.reading: みちでともだちのかおをみました。
contrast.en: I saw my friend's face in the street.
contrast.note: Seeing something by chance is always 見る; 観る is never used for noticing.

contrast.ja: 昨日、歌舞伎を観ました。
contrast.reading: きのう、かぶきをみました。
contrast.en: I watched kabuki yesterday.
contrast.note: A performance you bought a ticket for and sat through — the classic place for 観る, though 見ました here is equally correct.

contrast.ja: 説明書をよく見て組み立てます。
contrast.reading: せつめいしょをよくみてくみたてます。
contrast.en: I read the instructions carefully and assemble it.
contrast.note: Careful, attentive looking is not enough for 観る: it wants a performance or an event, not a document.

mistakes.wrong: きれいな空を観ました。
mistakes.right: きれいな空を見ました。
mistakes.why: Learners take 観る to mean "look at properly" and use it for scenery. 観る needs something presented to an audience; for the sky it sounds as if the sky were a show you attended.

mistakes.wrong: 食べて観る
mistakes.right: 食べてみる
mistakes.why: The auxiliary ～てみる ("try doing") is written in kana, never with 見 or 観. It has nothing to do with watching.

mistakes.wrong: 目が悪いので、よく観ることができません。
mistakes.right: 目が悪いので、よく見ることができません。
mistakes.why: Being able to see at all is 見る / 見える. 観る never covers eyesight.

faq.q: Is 観る a different word from 見る?
faq.a: No. Both are read みる and they are the same verb, conjugated the same way. The writer just picks a kanji that suits what the verb is doing in that sentence.

faq.q: Do I have to write 映画を観る?
faq.a: No. 観 is not among the everyday jōyō readings the way 見 is, so newspapers, textbooks and plenty of ordinary writers use 見る for films too. 映画を見る is completely normal Japanese.

faq.q: Which one do I need for the JLPT?
faq.a: 見る. It is the N5 word you have to read and write; 観る appears in the wild but you are never required to produce it.

title: 聞く vs 聴く
quickAnswer: 聞く and 聴く are the same word, きく — only the kanji differs. 聞く is the default: it covers hearing, listening, and also "to ask". 聴く is an optional spelling for listening attentively and on purpose — music, a lecture, someone's story taken seriously — and it can never mean "to ask". Writing 聞く everywhere is still correct.
summary: 聞く and 聴く are both きく: 聞く is the default and the only spelling for "to ask", 聴く an optional one for deliberate, attentive listening.

members.when: The default spelling for every sense of きく: sound reaching your ears, listening in general, and asking a question. If you are unsure, use 聞く — it is the textbook spelling and is never wrong.

examples.ja: 毎朝ラジオを聞きながら朝ごはんを食べます。
examples.reading: まいあさラジオをききながらあさごはんをたべます。
examples.en: Every morning I eat breakfast while listening to the radio.

examples.ja: すみません、駅への道を聞いてもいいですか。
examples.reading: すみません、えきへのみちをきいてもいいですか。
examples.en: Excuse me, may I ask you the way to the station?

members.when: Chosen when the listening is deliberate and focused — putting on music to listen to it, sitting through a lecture, hearing someone out. 聴 is the kanji of 聴講 and 傾聴; it is never used for sound that simply reaches you, and never for asking.

examples.ja: 家で静かにクラシックを聴きます。
examples.reading: いえでしずかにクラシックをききます。
examples.en: I listen to classical music quietly at home.

examples.ja: 先生の講義を最後まで聴きました。
examples.reading: せんせいのこうぎをさいごまでききました。
examples.en: I listened to the professor's lecture right to the end.

contrast.ja: 交番で道を聞きました。
contrast.reading: こうばんでみちをききました。
contrast.en: I asked the way at the police box.
contrast.note: "To ask" is only ever 聞く. This is the one clean rule here: 聴く can never replace it.

contrast.ja: 隣の部屋から音が聞こえます。
contrast.reading: となりのへやからおとがきこえます。
contrast.en: I can hear a sound from the next room.
contrast.note: Sound arriving on its own, with no intention behind it — 聞こえる is always written with 聞.

contrast.ja: ヘッドホンでゆっくり音楽を聴きます。
contrast.reading: ヘッドホンでゆっくりおんがくをききます。
contrast.en: I listen to music slowly on headphones.
contrast.note: Sitting down to listen on purpose is where 聴く fits best, though 聞きます would also be fine.

contrast.ja: 彼女の悩みを最後まで聴きました。
contrast.reading: かのじょのなやみをさいごまでききました。
contrast.en: I heard out her worries to the end.
contrast.note: Taking someone's story seriously; the 聴 spelling signals the attention. 聞きました is still correct and more common.

mistakes.wrong: 先生に宿題について聴きました。
mistakes.right: 先生に宿題について聞きました。
mistakes.why: This sentence means "I asked the teacher", and asking is never 聴く. Learners who have decided 聴く is the polite or serious spelling put it here too — it simply does not exist in that meaning.

mistakes.wrong: 外で大きな音が聴こえました。
mistakes.right: 外で大きな音が聞こえました。
mistakes.why: 聞こえる is sound reaching you without your choosing it, which is the opposite of what 聴 means. It is always written 聞こえる.

mistakes.wrong: 音楽を聞くのは間違いだ。
mistakes.right: 音楽を聞くのも聴くのも正しい。
mistakes.why: Learners are often told 聴く is "the correct one for music" and start treating 聞く as an error. 聴 is not among the everyday jōyō readings, so many writers use 聞く for everything, including music.

faq.q: Is 聴く a different word from 聞く?
faq.a: No. Both are read きく and conjugate identically (聞きます / 聴きます). It is one word with two kanji a writer can choose between.

faq.q: Can 聴く mean "to ask"?
faq.a: Never. 道を聞く, 先生に聞く, 名前を聞く — all of these take 聞く only. If the sentence means asking, the spelling is decided for you.

faq.q: Should I write 音楽を聴く or 音楽を聞く?
faq.a: Either. 聴く suits listening you sat down to do, but 聞く is standard everywhere and is what textbooks and the JLPT use. You never have to write 聴く.

title: 入る vs 入れる
quickAnswer: 入る (はいる) means someone or something goes in by itself — the thing that enters takes が: 水が入る. 入れる (いれる) means you put something in, and that thing takes を: 水を入れる. This is the standard Japanese intransitive/transitive pair: the intransitive verb describes the event with no doer, the transitive verb adds a doer and marks the affected thing with を.
summary: 入る is to go in by itself (が); 入れる is to put something in (を). The same が/を rule as 開く/開ける.

members.when: Use 入る when the subject itself moves into a place, or when something ends up inside with nobody named as doing it. The place takes に, and the thing entering takes が (or は as topic) — never を.

examples.ja: 子どもが部屋に入りました。
examples.reading: こどもがへやにはいりました。
examples.en: The child went into the room.

examples.ja: かばんに水が入っています。
examples.reading: かばんにみずがはいっています。
examples.en: Water has gotten into my bag.

members.when: Use 入れる when a person puts something into somewhere. The thing put in takes を and the destination takes に. If you can say "put X in" in English, it is 入れる.

examples.ja: かばんに本を入れました。
examples.reading: かばんにほんをいれました。
examples.en: I put the book in my bag.

examples.ja: コーヒーに砂糖を入れますか。
examples.reading: コーヒーにさとうをいれますか。
examples.en: Do you take sugar in your coffee?

contrast.ja: かばんに水が入りました。
contrast.reading: かばんにみずがはいりました。
contrast.en: Water got into my bag.
contrast.note: 水 takes が, so this is an accident — nobody put it there. 入る is the only choice.

contrast.ja: かばんに水を入れました。
contrast.reading: かばんにみずをいれました。
contrast.en: I put water in the bag.
contrast.note: Same bag, same water, but 水 takes を, so there is a doer. Swapping が for を is what forces 入れる.

contrast.ja: お風呂に入ります。
contrast.reading: おふろにはいります。
contrast.en: I take a bath.
contrast.note: You go into the bath yourself, so it is 入る. お風呂を入れる would mean running a bath for someone else.

contrast.ja: 先生が教室に入ってきました。
contrast.reading: せんせいがきょうしつにはいってきました。
contrast.en: The teacher came into the classroom.
contrast.note: The teacher moves herself, so even with a person as subject it is 入る, not 入れる.

mistakes.wrong: 部屋を入ります。
mistakes.right: 部屋に入ります。
mistakes.why: 入る takes に for the place you enter, not を. を here sounds like you are inserting the room somewhere.

mistakes.wrong: かばんに本が入りました。 (meaning "I put the book in my bag")
mistakes.right: かばんに本を入れました。
mistakes.why: With が the sentence says the book got in by itself. If you did it, the book must take を and the verb must be 入れる.

mistakes.wrong: お茶を入りました。
mistakes.right: お茶を入れました。
mistakes.why: お茶を入れる (to make tea) has a doer and an を object, so only the transitive 入れる works.

faq.q: How do I remember which one is which?
faq.a: Look at the particle in front of the verb, not the English. が before the verb means the intransitive one (入る); を means the transitive one (入れる). The same test works for 開く/開ける, 閉まる/閉める and every other pair like this.

faq.q: Why is はいる written with the same kanji as いれる?
faq.a: 入 just means "in". Japanese builds a pair on one kanji: 入る for something going in and 入れる for someone putting it in. You have to learn the two readings separately — はいる and いれる.

faq.q: Is お茶を入れる really the same verb?
faq.a: Yes. Making tea is literally putting tea into a pot or cup, so it uses 入れる with を, like every other transitive use.

title: 出る vs 出す
quickAnswer: 出る (でる) means something goes out or appears by itself, with no doer named: 月が出る, 学生が出る. 出す (だす) means a person takes something out or sends it out, and that thing takes を: 手紙を出す. It is the usual intransitive/transitive pair — 出る describes the event, 出す adds the person doing it.
summary: 出る is something coming out on its own; 出す is taking or sending something out. Watch the particle, not the English.

members.when: Use 出る when the subject itself goes out, comes out or appears. Nothing separate is being moved. It also covers attending or appearing in something: 会議に出る, テレビに出る.

examples.ja: 七時にうちを出ました。
examples.reading: しちじにうちをでました。
examples.en: I left home at seven.

examples.ja: 空に月が出ています。
examples.reading: そらにつきがでています。
examples.en: The moon is out in the sky.

members.when: Use 出す when someone moves something out of somewhere, or sends it off — mailing, handing in, serving, taking out. The thing moved takes を and the source takes から.

examples.ja: かばんから本を出しました。
examples.reading: かばんからほんをだしました。
examples.en: I took a book out of my bag.

examples.ja: 明日までに宿題を出してください。
examples.reading: あしたまでにしゅくだいをだしてください。
examples.en: Please hand in your homework by tomorrow.

contrast.ja: かばんから本が出ました。
contrast.reading: かばんからほんがでました。
contrast.en: A book came out of the bag.
contrast.note: 本 takes が — it just came out. No one is said to have taken it.

contrast.ja: かばんから本を出しました。
contrast.reading: かばんからほんをだしました。
contrast.en: I took the book out of the bag.
contrast.note: Same book, but を means a doer is acting on it, so the verb must be 出す.

contrast.ja: このお店はおいしい料理を出します。
contrast.reading: このおみせはおいしいりょうりをだします。
contrast.en: This restaurant serves delicious food.
contrast.note: The shop sends the food out to customers, so 料理 takes を and only 出す works.

contrast.ja: 会議に出ます。
contrast.reading: かいぎにでます。
contrast.en: I will attend the meeting.
contrast.note: You yourself appear at the meeting, so 出る with に. 会議を出す is not Japanese.

mistakes.wrong: 手紙を出ました。
mistakes.right: 手紙を出しました。
mistakes.why: 手紙 takes を, so the verb has to be the transitive 出す. 出る cannot take an object like this.

mistakes.wrong: ゴミが出してください。
mistakes.right: ゴミを出してください。
mistakes.why: Asking someone to put the rubbish out is a transitive action, so it is ゴミを出す. が would mean the rubbish comes out by itself.

mistakes.wrong: 電車から出します。 (meaning "I get off the train")
mistakes.right: 電車から出ます。
mistakes.why: You are the one leaving and nothing is being taken out, so it is 出る. More natural still is 電車を降ります。

faq.q: Why is it 家を出る with を if 出る is intransitive?
faq.a: This を marks the place you move away from, not an object — the same を as 公園を歩く or 電車を降りる. 出る still has no object; nothing is being acted on. It is the one を you will meet with an intransitive verb, so learn it as a set pattern.

faq.q: How is this the same rule as 入る/入れる?
faq.a: Exactly the same shape: 出る and 入る describe something going out or in by itself and take が, while 出す and 入れる have a person doing it and take を. Once you see the が/を flip, the whole family works the same way.

faq.q: Does 出す mean "to submit"?
faq.a: Yes — handing in homework, mailing a letter and putting in an application are all 出す, because you are sending something out to somewhere. They all take を.

title: 開く vs 開ける
quickAnswer: 開く (あく) means something opens by itself and takes が: ドアが開きます. 開ける (あける) means a person opens something, and that thing takes を: ドアを開けます. Both are "open" in English, so let the particle decide — が goes with the intransitive 開く, を with the transitive 開ける.
summary: ドアが開く is the door opening; ドアを開ける is you opening it. が means 開く, を means 開ける.

members.when: Use 開く when the thing simply opens — an automatic door, a shop opening for business, a window that stands open. The thing that opens takes が, and no person is mentioned.

examples.ja: ドアが開きました。
examples.reading: ドアがあきました。
examples.en: The door opened.

examples.ja: この店は九時に開きます。
examples.reading: このみせはくじにあきます。
examples.en: This shop opens at nine.

members.when: Use 開ける when someone opens something on purpose. The thing opened takes を. Requests such as "please open the window" are always 開ける.

examples.ja: 窓を開けてください。
examples.reading: まどをあけてください。
examples.en: Please open the window.

examples.ja: 暑いですから、ドアを開けました。
examples.reading: あついですから、ドアをあけました。
examples.en: It was hot, so I opened the door.

contrast.ja: ドアが開きます。
contrast.reading: ドアがあきます。
contrast.en: The door opens.
contrast.note: The door is the が subject and opens on its own — an automatic door, or the wind.

contrast.ja: ドアを開けます。
contrast.reading: ドアをあけます。
contrast.en: I open the door.
contrast.note: Identical event, but を means someone is doing it, which forces 開ける.

contrast.ja: 窓が開いています。
contrast.reading: まどがあいています。
contrast.en: The window is open.
contrast.note: 〜が開いている describes the resulting state. Use this when you just mean the window is open now.

contrast.ja: 窓を開けてあります。
contrast.reading: まどをあけてあります。
contrast.en: The window has been left open on purpose.
contrast.note: Transitive 開ける plus てある says someone opened it and left it that way, which 開いています does not imply.

mistakes.wrong: 窓を開きます。 (meaning "I open the window")
mistakes.right: 窓を開けます。
mistakes.why: あく never takes an を object, so with を you must use 開ける. The same kanji read ひらく is a different verb that can take an object, as in 本を開く.

mistakes.wrong: ドアが開けました。
mistakes.right: ドアが開きました。
mistakes.why: With が the door opened by itself, so the verb must be 開く. If you opened it, change the particle too: ドアを開けました。

mistakes.wrong: 店は九時に開けます。 (meaning "the shop opens at nine")
mistakes.right: 店は九時に開きます。
mistakes.why: Opening hours describe the shop opening, with no doer — that is 開く. 店を開ける means the owner unlocks the shop.

faq.q: Can I say 窓が開けています?
faq.a: No. Mixing が with the transitive 開ける is ungrammatical. Say 窓が開いています for "the window is open", or 窓を開けています for "I am opening the window".

faq.q: Isn't 開く sometimes read ひらく?
faq.a: Yes, and that is a separate verb which can be transitive: 本を開く, 会を開く. At N5 level, learn あく as the intransitive partner of 開ける and treat ひらく as its own word.

faq.q: Does the same rule cover 閉まる and 閉める?
faq.a: Yes, and 入る/入れる and 集まる/集める too. The intransitive one takes が, the transitive one takes を. Learning one pair properly teaches you all of them.

title: 閉まる vs 閉める
quickAnswer: 閉まる (しまる) means something closes by itself and takes が: ドアが閉まります. 閉める (しめる) means a person closes something, and that thing takes を: ドアを閉めます. Choose by the particle rather than the English — が goes with 閉まる, を goes with 閉める.
summary: ドアが閉まる is the door closing; ドアを閉める is you closing it. The が/を test decides it every time.

members.when: Use 閉まる when the thing closes on its own or is simply closed — train doors, a shop shutting for the day, a window that is already shut. The thing takes が.

examples.ja: ドアが閉まります。ご注意ください。
examples.reading: ドアがしまります。ごちゅういください。
examples.en: The doors are closing. Please be careful.

examples.ja: その店は九時に閉まります。
examples.reading: そのみせはくじにしまります。
examples.en: That shop closes at nine.

members.when: Use 閉める when someone closes something. The thing closed takes を. Any request or report of a person shutting a door, window or lid uses 閉める.

examples.ja: 寒いので窓を閉めてください。
examples.reading: さむいのでまどをしめてください。
examples.en: It's cold, so please close the window.

examples.ja: 私が最後にドアを閉めました。
examples.reading: わたしがさいごにドアをしめました。
examples.en: I was the one who closed the door last.

contrast.ja: ドアが閉まりました。
contrast.reading: ドアがしまりました。
contrast.en: The door closed.
contrast.note: が — the door closed by itself, perhaps automatically or in the wind.

contrast.ja: ドアを閉めました。
contrast.reading: ドアをしめました。
contrast.en: I closed the door.
contrast.note: Same door, but を puts a person behind the action, so the verb becomes 閉める.

contrast.ja: 窓が閉まっています。
contrast.reading: まどがしまっています。
contrast.en: The window is closed.
contrast.note: The plain state of the window now, saying nothing about who shut it.

contrast.ja: 窓を閉めてあります。
contrast.reading: まどをしめてあります。
contrast.en: The window has been closed deliberately.
contrast.note: The transitive 閉める with てある says someone closed it on purpose and left it so.

mistakes.wrong: ドアを閉まってください。
mistakes.right: ドアを閉めてください。
mistakes.why: A request to a person is transitive and ドア takes を, so it must be 閉める. 閉まる cannot take an を object.

mistakes.wrong: 店が八時に閉めます。
mistakes.right: 店は八時に閉まります。
mistakes.why: Opening hours describe the shop closing, with no doer, so 閉まる. 店を閉める means the owner shuts up shop.

mistakes.wrong: 窓が閉めています。
mistakes.right: 窓が閉まっています。
mistakes.why: To say a window is currently closed, use the intransitive 閉まっている. が with 閉める is ungrammatical.

faq.q: What is the difference between 閉まる and 閉じる?
faq.a: 閉まる is the everyday word for doors, windows and shops closing. 閉じる is a little more formal or written and is often transitive (本を閉じる, 目を閉じる). For N5 sentences, stick with 閉まる and 閉める.

faq.q: How is this the same as 開く/開ける?
faq.a: It is the mirror image: 閉まる and 開く take が and describe the event, 閉める and 開ける take を and add a person doing it. 入る/入れる and 集まる/集める follow the same rule.

faq.q: Can I use 閉める for a shop going out of business?
faq.a: Yes — 店を閉める is closing a shop down, since the owner is doing it. For the shop simply being shut for the night, use 閉まる.

title: 集まる vs 集める
quickAnswer: 集まる (あつまる) means people or things come together by themselves and takes が: 人が集まる. 集める (あつめる) means someone brings them together or collects them, and they take を: 切手を集める. It is the standard intransitive/transitive pair — が for the event on its own, を when there is a doer.
summary: 人が集まる is a crowd forming; 人を集める is someone gathering them. が for 集まる, を for 集める.

members.when: Use 集まる when people or things come together on their own — a crowd forming, donations coming in, friends meeting up. The ones gathering take が and the place takes に.

examples.ja: 駅前に人がたくさん集まっています。
examples.reading: えきまえにひとがたくさんあつまっています。
examples.en: A lot of people are gathered in front of the station.

examples.ja: 土曜日の十時に公園に集まりましょう。
examples.reading: どようびのじゅうじにこうえんにあつまりましょう。
examples.en: Let's meet up at the park at ten on Saturday.

members.when: Use 集める when a person gathers or collects things or people. What is collected takes を. This is the verb for hobbies like collecting stamps and for calling people together.

examples.ja: 子どものときから切手を集めています。
examples.reading: こどものときからきってをあつめています。
examples.en: I have collected stamps since I was a child.

examples.ja: 先生が学生を教室に集めました。
examples.reading: せんせいががくせいをきょうしつにあつめました。
examples.en: The teacher gathered the students in the classroom.

contrast.ja: 教室に学生が集まりました。
contrast.reading: きょうしつにがくせいがあつまりました。
contrast.en: The students gathered in the classroom.
contrast.note: 学生 takes が — they came of their own accord.

contrast.ja: 先生が学生を教室に集めました。
contrast.reading: せんせいががくせいをきょうしつにあつめました。
contrast.en: The teacher gathered the students in the classroom.
contrast.note: Same event from the teacher's side: 学生 now takes を and 先生 is the が subject, so the verb is 集める.

contrast.ja: お金がたくさん集まりました。
contrast.reading: おかねがたくさんあつまりました。
contrast.en: A lot of money came in.
contrast.note: Reporting the result without naming who ran the collection — が forces 集まる.

contrast.ja: みんなでお金を集めましょう。
contrast.reading: みんなでおかねをあつめましょう。
contrast.en: Let's collect money together.
contrast.note: Here we are the collectors, so お金 takes を and only 集める works.

mistakes.wrong: 切手を集まっています。
mistakes.right: 切手を集めています。
mistakes.why: 切手 takes を, so the verb must be the transitive 集める. Collecting is something you do to the stamps.

mistakes.wrong: 人を集まりました。
mistakes.right: 人が集まりました。 / 人を集めました。
mistakes.why: 集まる cannot take を. Decide whether the people came on their own (が集まる) or you called them together (を集める).

mistakes.wrong: 三時に集めましょう。 (meaning "let's meet at three")
mistakes.right: 三時に集まりましょう。
mistakes.why: When you and your friends come together, nobody is being collected, so it is 集まる. 集めましょう would mean "let's gather some things up".

faq.q: Which one do I use to tell friends where to meet?
faq.a: 集まる: 駅に集まりましょう。You are all coming together yourselves, so nobody takes を. Only an organiser gathering other people would say 集める.

faq.q: How do I say "my collection"?
faq.a: Use 集めている plus the thing: 集めている切手 for the stamps you collect, or 切手集め for stamp collecting. The noun 集まり, from 集まる, means a get-together.

faq.q: Is this the same pattern as 決まる/決める?
faq.a: Yes. 集まる, 決まる and 閉まる all take が and describe things happening; 集める, 決める and 閉める all take を and have a doer. The 〜まる / 〜める shape is a very common pairing.

title: 決まる vs 決める
quickAnswer: Both translate as "decide", so ignore the English and look at the particle: 決まる (きまる) means something gets settled with no decider named and takes が — 日が決まりました, the date has been decided. 決める (きめる) means a person decides something, and that takes を — 私が日を決めます, I'll decide the date. This が/を split is the general rule for every Japanese intransitive/transitive pair.
summary: 決まる is something being settled (が); 決める is a person deciding it (を). Same English word, different particle.

members.when: Use 決まる to report that something is now fixed, without saying who fixed it. The thing settled takes が. English renders it as "has been decided" or "is set", which is why it feels passive.

examples.ja: 旅行の日が決まりました。
examples.reading: りょこうのひがきまりました。
examples.en: The date of the trip has been decided.

examples.ja: 会議は三時に決まりましたよ。
examples.reading: かいぎはさんじにきまりましたよ。
examples.en: The meeting has been set for three.

members.when: Use 決める when a person makes the decision. What is decided takes を, and the decider is the が subject. Asking someone to choose is always 決める.

examples.ja: 何を食べるか決めてください。
examples.reading: なにをたべるかきめてください。
examples.en: Please decide what you want to eat.

examples.ja: 出発の日は私が決めます。
examples.reading: しゅっぱつのひはわたしがきめます。
examples.en: I'll be the one to decide the departure date.

contrast.ja: 予定が決まりました。
contrast.reading: よていがきまりました。
contrast.en: The schedule has been decided.
contrast.note: 予定 takes が, so you are reporting the outcome. Nobody is credited or blamed.

contrast.ja: 予定を決めました。
contrast.reading: よていをきめました。
contrast.en: I decided the schedule.
contrast.note: Same schedule, but を means you did it. The particle alone changes who is responsible.

contrast.ja: 新しい社長が決まりました。
contrast.reading: あたらしいしゃちょうがきまりました。
contrast.en: The new president has been chosen.
contrast.note: Announcing a result. 決めました here would sound like you personally appointed them.

contrast.ja: 毎週月曜日に掃除をすることに決まっています。
contrast.reading: まいしゅうげつようびにそうじをすることにきまっています。
contrast.en: It's the rule that we clean every Monday.
contrast.note: 〜ことに決まっている is the standing-rule use of the intransitive verb: the rule stands, nobody is deciding it now.

mistakes.wrong: 私は明日の予定が決まります。
mistakes.right: 私は明日の予定を決めます。
mistakes.why: If you are the one deciding, the thing decided takes を and the verb is 決める. With が you are only saying the schedule is getting settled.

mistakes.wrong: 日にちを決まりました。
mistakes.right: 日にちが決まりました。 / 日にちを決めました。
mistakes.why: 決まる cannot take an を object. Use が決まる to report the result, or を決める to say you decided it.

mistakes.wrong: もう決めましたか。 (asked about a schedule someone else controls)
mistakes.right: もう決まりましたか。
mistakes.why: Asking whether something has been settled — not whether the listener personally chose — takes 決まる. 決めましたか puts the decision on them and can sound pushy.

faq.q: Both mean "decide", so how do I pick?
faq.a: Ask whether a person is doing the deciding in your sentence. If yes, the thing decided takes を and you use 決める. If you are only reporting that it is now fixed, it takes が and you use 決まる. The particle test is far more reliable than the English.

faq.q: Why does 決まりました sound passive in English?
faq.a: Because English has no plain intransitive "decide". 決まる is not a passive form — it is its own verb, like 開く beside 開ける. You meet the same mismatch with 続く/続ける.

faq.q: What does 決まっている mean?
faq.a: It means something is already settled or is the standing rule: 会議は三時に決まっています, the meeting is set for three. It describes the state that 決まる leaves behind.

title: 続く vs 続ける
quickAnswer: English uses "continue" for both, so go by the particle: 続く (つづく) means something goes on by itself and takes が — 雨が続いています, the rain keeps on. 続ける (つづける) means a person keeps something going and it takes を — 勉強を続けます, I keep studying. That が/を split is the general rule for Japanese intransitive/transitive pairs.
summary: 続く is something going on by itself (が); 続ける is a person keeping it up (を). Use the particle, not the English.

members.when: Use 続く when a situation, a spell of weather, a road or a story goes on without anyone driving it. The thing continuing takes が, and durations are often marked with も for emphasis.

examples.ja: 暑い日が続いています。
examples.reading: あついひがつづいています。
examples.en: Hot days have been going on.

examples.ja: 会議は三時間も続きました。
examples.reading: かいぎはさんじかんもつづきました。
examples.en: The meeting went on for three whole hours.

members.when: Use 続ける when a person keeps an activity up. The activity takes を. It also attaches to a verb stem — 走り続ける, 話し続ける — to mean "keep on doing".

examples.ja: 毎日日本語の勉強を続けています。
examples.reading: まいにちにほんごのべんきょうをつづけています。
examples.en: I keep studying Japanese every day.

examples.ja: 疲れても最後まで続けたいです。
examples.reading: つかれてもさいごまでつづけたいです。
examples.en: Even if I get tired, I want to keep going to the end.

contrast.ja: 雨が続いています。
contrast.reading: あめがつづいています。
contrast.en: The rain has been going on.
contrast.note: Nobody makes rain continue, so it can only be 続く with が.

contrast.ja: 練習を続けています。
contrast.reading: れんしゅうをつづけています。
contrast.en: I'm keeping up my practice.
contrast.note: 練習 takes を because you are the one keeping it going, which forces 続ける.

contrast.ja: 話が続きませんでした。
contrast.reading: はなしがつづきませんでした。
contrast.en: The conversation didn't keep going.
contrast.note: The conversation died on its own, so が続く. Compare 話を続けました, "I carried on talking".

contrast.ja: この道はずっと海まで続いています。
contrast.reading: このみちはずっとうみまでつづいています。
contrast.en: This road goes all the way to the sea.
contrast.note: 続く also covers things extending in space. There is no doer, so 続ける is impossible here.

mistakes.wrong: 勉強が続けます。
mistakes.right: 勉強を続けます。
mistakes.why: If you are keeping the studying up, it takes を. が with 続ける is ungrammatical; 勉強が続く would mean the studying carries on by itself.

mistakes.wrong: 雨を続けています。
mistakes.right: 雨が続いています。
mistakes.why: Nobody can act on the rain, so it takes が with 続く.

mistakes.wrong: 仕事を続いています。
mistakes.right: 仕事を続けています。 / 仕事が続いています。
mistakes.why: 続く never takes an を object. Use を続ける if you are staying in the job, が続く if the work simply keeps coming.

faq.q: They both mean "continue" — how do I choose?
faq.a: Check whether a person keeps it going. If someone is doing it, the activity takes を and you use 続ける. If it just carries on, it takes が and you use 続く. The English cannot tell you; the particle can.

faq.q: What is the difference between 走り続ける and 走っている?
faq.a: 走り続ける stresses that you keep going without stopping, often against some difficulty. 走っている just says you are running now. Verb stem plus 続ける is very common: 食べ続ける, 待ち続ける.

faq.q: Which one goes at the end of a story instalment?
faq.a: 続く. You see 続く on a screen or page for "to be continued" — the story goes on by itself, with no doer involved.

title: 落ちる vs 落とす
quickAnswer: 落ちる (おちる) means something falls by itself and takes が: 鍵が落ちました, the key fell. 落とす (おとす) means a person drops it — and in everyday speech, loses it — and it takes を: 財布を落としました, I lost my wallet. Same intransitive/transitive rule as 開く/開ける: が for the event, を when there is a doer.
summary: 落ちる is something falling (が); 落とす is you dropping or losing it (を) — 財布を落とした means you lost your wallet.

members.when: Use 落ちる when something falls, comes off or drops on its own. The thing falling takes が. It also covers failing an exam (試験に落ちる) and a stain coming out (汚れが落ちる).

examples.ja: 木から葉が落ちました。
examples.reading: きからはがおちました。
examples.en: A leaf fell from the tree.

examples.ja: かばんから鍵が落ちましたよ。
examples.reading: かばんからかぎがおちましたよ。
examples.en: Your key just fell out of your bag.

members.when: Use 落とす when a person lets something fall — and, just as commonly, when they lose it. 財布を落とした normally means "I lost my wallet", not that you watched it hit the floor. The thing takes を.

examples.ja: 財布を落としてしまいました。
examples.reading: さいふをおとしてしまいました。
examples.en: I lost my wallet.

examples.ja: スマホを落として、画面が割れました。
examples.reading: スマホをおとして、がめんがわれました。
examples.en: I dropped my phone and the screen cracked.

contrast.ja: 鍵が落ちました。
contrast.reading: かぎがおちました。
contrast.en: The key fell.
contrast.note: が — you are describing the key falling, perhaps pointing it out on the ground.

contrast.ja: 鍵を落としました。
contrast.reading: かぎをおとしました。
contrast.en: I dropped my key.
contrast.note: Same key, but を makes you the one who let it go — and in everyday speech this is how you say you lost it.

contrast.ja: シャツの汚れが落ちません。
contrast.reading: シャツのよごれがおちません。
contrast.en: The stain on the shirt won't come out.
contrast.note: The stain behaves on its own, so が落ちる. Compare 汚れを落とす, to get the stain out.

contrast.ja: 車のスピードを落としてください。
contrast.reading: くるまのスピードをおとしてください。
contrast.en: Please slow the car down.
contrast.note: スピード takes を and the driver acts, so only 落とす works. 落ちる would merely say the speed dropped.

mistakes.wrong: 財布が落としました。
mistakes.right: 財布を落としました。
mistakes.why: With 落とす the thing lost takes を. 財布が落ちました is also good Japanese, but it means the wallet fell, not that you lost it.

mistakes.wrong: 試験を落ちました。
mistakes.right: 試験に落ちました。
mistakes.why: 落ちる is intransitive and takes に for the exam you failed. 試験を落とす exists but means an examiner failing a candidate.

mistakes.wrong: スマホが落として、画面が割れました。
mistakes.right: スマホを落として、画面が割れました。
mistakes.why: You dropped it, so it takes を with 落とす. Note the second half correctly uses が割れる — the screen cracked by itself.

faq.q: How do I say "I lost my wallet"?
faq.a: 財布を落としました is the usual way. 落とす covers losing something by dropping it somewhere, which is how most things get lost. なくす is the broader word for losing something, including mislaying it at home.

faq.q: Why is 汚れが落ちる "the stain comes out"?
faq.a: 落ちる means something comes off or away, not only downward. The stain leaves the fabric by itself, so it takes が. When you scrub it out yourself it is 汚れを落とす.

faq.q: Is this the same pattern as 届く/届ける?
faq.a: Yes, though the endings differ. 落ちる and 届く take が and describe what happens; 落とす and 届ける take を and add a doer. The 〜る/〜す shape, as in 落ちる/落とす and 出る/出す, is one of several pairings that follow the same rule.

title: 届く vs 届ける
quickAnswer: 届く (とどく) means something arrives at its destination by itself and takes が: 荷物が届きました, the package arrived. 届ける (とどける) means a person takes something to someone, and it takes を: 荷物を届けます, I'll deliver the package. The English "be delivered" sounds passive, but 届く is simply the intransitive partner — が for the arrival, を when someone carries it.
summary: 届く is mail arriving (が); 届ける is delivering or taking something to someone (を). 届く is not a passive form.

members.when: Use 届く when a letter, parcel or message arrives. The thing arriving takes が and the recipient takes に. It also means "to reach" physically, as in 手が届く.

examples.ja: 昨日、手紙が届きました。
examples.reading: きのう、てがみがとどきました。
examples.en: A letter arrived yesterday.

examples.ja: 注文した本がまだ届いていません。
examples.reading: ちゅうもんしたほんがまだとどいていません。
examples.en: The book I ordered hasn't arrived yet.

members.when: Use 届ける when a person takes something to where it should go — a courier delivering, you dropping something round to a friend, or handing in something you found. The thing takes を and the destination takes に or まで.

examples.ja: この荷物を家まで届けてください。
examples.reading: このにもつをいえまでとどけてください。
examples.en: Please deliver this package to the house.

examples.ja: 駅で拾った財布を交番に届けました。
examples.reading: えきでひろったさいふをこうばんにとどけました。
examples.en: I turned in the wallet I found at the station to the police box.

contrast.ja: 荷物が届きました。
contrast.reading: にもつがとどきました。
contrast.en: The package arrived.
contrast.note: が — you are reporting that it got here. Who carried it is not part of the sentence.

contrast.ja: 荷物を届けました。
contrast.reading: にもつをとどけました。
contrast.en: I delivered the package.
contrast.note: Same package, but を means you took it there, so the verb becomes 届ける.

contrast.ja: 友だちにケーキを届けます。
contrast.reading: ともだちにケーキをとどけます。
contrast.en: I'll take the cake round to my friend.
contrast.note: ケーキ takes を and you do the carrying, so 届ける. 届きます would mean the cake arrives on its own.

contrast.ja: 上の棚に手が届きません。
contrast.reading: うえのたなにてがとどきません。
contrast.en: I can't reach the top shelf.
contrast.note: 手が届く, "one's hand reaches", is a common idiom built on the intransitive verb. 手を届ける is not said.

mistakes.wrong: 手紙を届きました。 (meaning "a letter arrived")
mistakes.right: 手紙が届きました。
mistakes.why: 届く cannot take an を object. The letter is the subject that arrived, so it takes が.

mistakes.wrong: 荷物が届けました。 (meaning "I delivered the package")
mistakes.right: 荷物を届けました。
mistakes.why: With a doer, the package takes を and the verb is 届ける. が with 届ける is ungrammatical.

mistakes.wrong: メールを届けました。 (meaning "I sent you an email")
mistakes.right: メールを送りました。
mistakes.why: 届ける is about taking something to a place. For sending mail or email use 送る, though メールが届く is fine for the mail arriving.

faq.q: Why does 届く translate as "be delivered" if it isn't passive?
faq.a: Japanese simply has a separate verb for the arriving event. 届く is intransitive, like 開く or 落ちる, and takes が. The passive 届けられる exists, but you rarely need it — 届きました is the natural way to say something arrived.

faq.q: Which one do I use for a parcel I'm waiting on?
faq.a: 届く: 荷物はいつ届きますか, when will the package arrive? You would only use 届ける if you were asking about someone delivering it, as in いつ届けてくれますか.

faq.q: What does 交番に届ける mean?
faq.a: It means handing something you found in to a police box. 届ける covers taking a lost item to where it belongs, not just courier deliveries.

title: もう vs まだ
quickAnswer: These are not synonyms — they mark aspect, and each one flips meaning with negation. もう means "already" in a positive sentence and "no longer" in a negative one; まだ means "still" in a positive sentence and "not yet" in a negative one. So もう食べました is "I already ate", まだ食べていません is "I haven't eaten yet", まだあります is "there's still some", もうありません is "there's none left".
summary: もう = already / no longer, まだ = still / not yet. The meaning flips with negation — the four-way table is the whole answer.

members.when: Use もう when a change has already happened: positive means "already", negative means "no longer". It always points at a state that has arrived or run out.

examples.ja: もう昼ご飯を食べました。
examples.reading: もうひるごはんをたべました。
examples.en: I've already eaten lunch.

examples.ja: お金はもうありません。
examples.reading: おかねはもうありません。
examples.en: I don't have any money left.

members.when: Use まだ when the change has not happened yet: positive means "still", negative means "not yet". The negative almost always takes 〜ていません, not 〜ませんでした.

examples.ja: 雨はまだ降っています。
examples.reading: あめはまだふっています。
examples.en: It's still raining.

examples.ja: その映画はまだ見ていません。
examples.reading: そのえいがはまだみていません。
examples.en: I haven't seen that movie yet.

contrast.ja: もう宿題をしましたか。いいえ、まだしていません。
contrast.reading: もうしゅくだいをしましたか。いいえ、まだしていません。
contrast.en: Have you done your homework yet? No, not yet.
contrast.note: The question asks with もう (already?) and the "not yet" answer must use まだ plus 〜ていません. Swapping the two words is impossible here.

contrast.ja: ビールはまだありますか。いいえ、もうありません。
contrast.reading: ビールはまだありますか。いいえ、もうありません。
contrast.en: Is there still beer? No, it's all gone.
contrast.note: まだあります means some is left; the negative of that idea is もうありません, not まだありません.

contrast.ja: もう子どもじゃありません。
contrast.reading: もうこどもじゃありません。
contrast.en: I'm not a child any more.
contrast.note: With a negative, もう means "no longer" — a change that has happened. まだ子どもじゃありません would mean "not a child yet", which makes no sense for someone growing up.

contrast.ja: 彼はまだ来ていません。
contrast.reading: かれはまだきていません。
contrast.en: He hasn't arrived yet.
contrast.note: まだ implies he is still expected. もう来ていません would mean he no longer comes at all — a completely different statement.

mistakes.wrong: まだ食べませんでした。
mistakes.right: まだ食べていません。
mistakes.why: This is the single most common まだ error. 〜ませんでした is a closed past — "I didn't eat, and that is the end of it". "Not yet" is an open present state, so Japanese uses まだ plus 〜ていません. To a native speaker まだ食べませんでした sounds self-contradictory.

mistakes.wrong: まだお金がありません。 (said when your wallet has run empty)
mistakes.right: もうお金がありません。
mistakes.why: If the money has run out, the state has changed, so you need もう meaning "no longer". まだありません would mean the money has not arrived yet, for example while you are waiting to be paid.

mistakes.wrong: もう終わっていません。
mistakes.right: まだ終わっていません。
mistakes.why: Learners reach for もう because the question used もう. But "not finished" is an unrealised change, which is always まだ. Answer a もう question with まだ whenever the answer is no.

faq.q: Is まだ just the negative form of もう?
faq.a: No. Both work in positive and negative sentences; it is the meaning that flips. もう plus positive is already, もう plus negative is no longer, まだ plus positive is still, まだ plus negative is not yet. Learn the four boxes together and the pair stops being confusing.

faq.q: Why can't I say まだ食べませんでした for "I haven't eaten yet"?
faq.a: Because 〜ませんでした reports a finished past event, while "not yet" describes your situation right now. Japanese expresses that with まだ〜ていません. The same goes for まだ来ていません, まだ読んでいません and まだ決めていません.

faq.q: Can I just answer a question with まだです?
faq.a: Yes. まだです is a complete, natural answer meaning "not yet", and it is the usual reply to もう食べましたか. The matching positive answer is もう食べました, or simply はい. Note that もう has a second sense of "more" in the fixed patterns もう少し, もう一度 and もう一つ, where まだ never works.

title: 大切 vs 大事
quickAnswer: These two genuinely overlap, and in most sentences about people or possessions either one is fine — 家族は大切です and 家族は大事です are both natural. The tendency is that 大切 leans toward what you cherish and want to protect, while 大事 leans toward what matters practically or is serious: 大事な話 (an important talk), 大事な試験 (a crucial exam), お大事に (take care of yourself).
summary: 大切 and 大事 really do overlap. 大切 leans toward what you cherish; 大事 toward what matters practically or is serious, as in 大事な話.

members.when: Use 大切 for things and people you value and want to look after — family, friends, a keepsake, your health, your time. It carries a warmer feeling and is the safer choice in careful writing.

examples.ja: 家族は私にとって大切です。
examples.reading: かぞくはわたしにとってたいせつです。
examples.en: My family is precious to me.

examples.ja: この指輪を大切にしています。
examples.reading: このゆびわをたいせつにしています。
examples.en: I take good care of this ring.

members.when: Use 大事 when something matters, is serious, or must not go wrong — 大事な話, 大事な会議, 大事な試験. It is also the word in the set phrases 体を大事にする and お大事に.

examples.ja: 大事な話があるので、少し時間をください。
examples.reading: だいじなはなしがあるので、すこしじかんをください。
examples.en: I have something important to discuss, so please give me a moment.

examples.ja: 体を大事にしてください。
examples.reading: からだをだいじにしてください。
examples.en: Please take care of your health.

contrast.ja: お大事に。
contrast.reading: おだいじに。
contrast.en: Take care. (to someone who is unwell)
contrast.note: A fixed phrase. お大切に does not exist, so 大切 can never be substituted here.

contrast.ja: 明日は大事な試験があります。
contrast.reading: あしたはだいじなしけんがあります。
contrast.en: I have a crucial exam tomorrow.
contrast.note: The exam matters; it is not something you cherish, so 大事 is the natural choice. 大切な試験 is not wrong but sounds slightly off.

contrast.ja: 友だちを大切にしてください。
contrast.reading: ともだちをたいせつにしてください。
contrast.en: Treasure your friends.
contrast.note: Cherishing a person is 大切's home ground. 大事にする also works here, but 大切 sounds warmer.

contrast.ja: 水は生活にとって大切です。
contrast.reading: みずはせいかつにとってたいせつです。
contrast.en: Water is vital to daily life.
contrast.note: A general, slightly formal statement of value — 大切 is the default in this kind of written sentence, while 大事 would sound more conversational.

mistakes.wrong: お大切に。
mistakes.right: お大事に。
mistakes.why: The parting phrase for someone who is ill is fixed as お大事に. Learners generalise from 大切にする and produce a phrase nobody says.

mistakes.wrong: 大切な話があります。 (when you mean an urgent, serious talk)
mistakes.right: 大事な話があります。
mistakes.why: Not ungrammatical — 大切な話 does exist — but when you mean "we need to talk, this is serious", native speakers reach for 大事な話. 大切な話 sounds more like a treasured story.

faq.q: Is there a rule that tells me which one to use?
faq.a: Not a reliable one, and you should be suspicious of any page that gives you a clean rule. For people and possessions both words are used constantly and either is fine. What does hold: お大事に and 大事な話 are fixed with 大事, and 大切 is a little more common in careful writing.

faq.q: Which one is more polite?
faq.a: Neither is more polite. 大切 sounds a touch softer and more formal in writing, while 大事 is very common in everyday speech. Politeness comes from です and ます, not from the choice between these two.

faq.q: Are 大切にする and 大事にする the same thing?
faq.a: Almost. Both mean to treasure something or take good care of it. 大切にする is preferred for people and precious objects; 大事にする is the usual one for looking after your body or health, as in 体を大事にする.

title: うれしい vs 楽しい
quickAnswer: うれしい is how you feel at a moment because something good happened; 楽しい is how an activity or stretch of time feels while you are enjoying it. A present makes you うれしい, but a party is 楽しい. 楽しい describes the thing you are doing; うれしい describes you.
summary: うれしい is a momentary reaction to something good; 楽しい is enjoyment over a period. Presents are うれしい, parties are 楽しい.

members.when: Use うれしい for your own glad reaction to an event: passing a test, getting a gift, hearing good news. It is a feeling at a point in time, and it usually has its cause attached with 〜て or 〜ので.

examples.ja: 合格したので、とてもうれしいです。
examples.reading: ごうかくしたので、とてもうれしいです。
examples.en: I'm really glad because I passed.

examples.ja: 手紙をもらって、うれしかったです。
examples.reading: てがみをもらって、うれしかったです。
examples.en: I was happy to get your letter.

members.when: Use 楽しい to describe an activity, event or period that is enjoyable — a party, a trip, a class, everyday life. The subject is typically the thing, not you.

examples.ja: 昨日のパーティーは楽しかったです。
examples.reading: きのうのパーティーはたのしかったです。
examples.en: Yesterday's party was fun.

examples.ja: 友だちと話すのは楽しいです。
examples.reading: ともだちとはなすのはたのしいです。
examples.en: Talking with friends is enjoyable.

contrast.ja: 旅行は楽しかったです。
contrast.reading: りょこうはたのしかったです。
contrast.en: The trip was fun.
contrast.note: A trip is a stretch of time you enjoy, so 楽しい. 旅行はうれしかった would sound as if the trip itself were a piece of good news.

contrast.ja: そう言ってもらえて、うれしいです。
contrast.reading: そういってもらえて、うれしいです。
contrast.en: I'm glad you said that.
contrast.note: A reaction at one moment to something someone did, so only うれしい works. 楽しい would suggest their words were entertaining.

contrast.ja: 日本語の勉強は楽しいです。
contrast.reading: にほんごのべんきょうはたのしいです。
contrast.en: Studying Japanese is fun.
contrast.note: An ongoing activity takes 楽しい. Use うれしい here and it sounds as if studying had just delivered you a surprise.

contrast.ja: 誕生日にプレゼントをもらって、うれしかったです。
contrast.reading: たんじょうびにプレゼントをもらって、うれしかったです。
contrast.en: I was happy to get a present for my birthday.
contrast.note: Receiving something is a moment, so うれしい. The party around it, though, would be 楽しかった.

mistakes.wrong: パーティーはうれしかったです。
mistakes.right: パーティーは楽しかったです。
mistakes.why: An event you spent time enjoying is 楽しい. うれしい makes the party sound like good news you received rather than something you were at.

mistakes.wrong: 合格して楽しいです。
mistakes.right: 合格してうれしいです。
mistakes.why: Passing an exam is a single piece of good fortune, not an enjoyable activity. 楽しい makes it sound as if the act of passing were entertaining.

mistakes.wrong: 田中さんはうれしいです。
mistakes.right: 田中さんはうれしそうです。
mistakes.why: Plain emotion adjectives describe your own feelings. To say how someone else feels, use 〜そうです or a quoted statement. The same applies to 楽しい: 楽しそうですね.

faq.q: Can I say 楽しい about a person?
faq.a: Not to mean that the person is happy. 楽しい人 means someone who is fun to be around. To say a person looks happy, use うれしそうです or 楽しそうです, depending on whether you mean a moment or an activity.

faq.q: How do I say "I had a good time, thank you"?
faq.a: 楽しかったです、ありがとうございました. This is the standard thing to say when leaving a party or a dinner. うれしかったです fits better when someone did something kind specifically for you.

faq.q: Is 楽しみ related to 楽しい?
faq.a: Yes. 楽しみです means you are looking forward to something, as in 明日が楽しみです. It is used about the future and cannot be replaced by うれしい.

title: 上手 vs 得意
quickAnswer: The real difference is who you may say it about. 上手 praises someone else's skill and sounds boastful about yourself, so 私は日本語が上手です is best avoided. 得意 means "this is one of my strengths" and is completely normal in the first person: 料理が得意です.
summary: 上手 praises other people and is odd about yourself; 得意 is what you are good at and is natural in the first person.

members.when: Use 上手 to praise another person's skill, judged from the outside, as in 日本語がお上手ですね. Avoid it about yourself; about your own family it is fine, because you are describing them rather than you.

examples.ja: 日本語がお上手ですね。
examples.reading: にほんごがおじょうずですね。
examples.en: Your Japanese is really good.

examples.ja: 母は料理が上手です。
examples.reading: はははりょうりがじょうずです。
examples.en: My mother is a good cook.

members.when: Use 得意 for something that is one of your strong points — a subject, a skill, a signature dish. It is the natural word for your own abilities, and it works about other people too.

examples.ja: 私は料理が得意です。
examples.reading: わたしはりょうりがとくいです。
examples.en: Cooking is one of my strengths.

examples.ja: 数学は得意ですが、英語は苦手です。
examples.reading: すうがくはとくいですが、えいごはにがてです。
examples.en: I'm good at maths, but weak at English.

contrast.ja: 田中さんは歌が上手ですね。
contrast.reading: たなかさんはうたがじょうずですね。
contrast.en: You're a good singer, Tanaka.
contrast.note: Praising the person in front of you is exactly what 上手 is for. 得意ですね would sound like a comment on their own self-assessment.

contrast.ja: スポーツが得意です。
contrast.reading: スポーツがとくいです。
contrast.en: Sports are one of my strong points.
contrast.note: About yourself, 得意 is the safe word. スポーツが上手です strikes listeners as self-praise.

contrast.ja: 得意な料理はカレーです。
contrast.reading: とくいなりょうりはカレーです。
contrast.en: My signature dish is curry.
contrast.note: 得意な plus a noun means the thing you are good at. 上手な料理 would describe a dish that is skilfully made, not your specialty.

contrast.ja: 字が上手ですね。
contrast.reading: じがじょうずですね。
contrast.en: You have lovely handwriting.
contrast.note: A compliment on a visible result, which is 上手's core use and one of the first compliments learners hear.

mistakes.wrong: 私は日本語が上手です。
mistakes.right: 私は日本語が得意です。
mistakes.why: 上手 is an outside judgement, so applying it to yourself sounds boastful. Say 得意です instead, or deflect a compliment with まだまだです.

mistakes.wrong: 日本語がお上手ですね。 はい、上手です。
mistakes.right: 日本語がお上手ですね。 いいえ、まだまだです。
mistakes.why: Agreeing with a compliment about your own skill is socially awkward in Japanese. The expected replies are いいえ、まだまだです or ありがとうございます.

mistakes.wrong: 私は料理を上手です。
mistakes.right: 私は料理が上手です。
mistakes.why: Both 上手 and 得意 take が for the skill, not を, because they are adjectives rather than verbs. The pattern is 〜が上手だ and 〜が得意だ.

faq.q: Can I ever use 上手 about myself?
faq.a: In practice, treat it as off limits in the first person. The exception is the negative, as in まだ上手じゃありません, where there is no boasting. About your own mother or child, 上手 is perfectly fine.

faq.q: Is 得意 modest enough for a job interview?
faq.a: Yes. 得意 is the standard way to state a strength in Japanese, and 得意なことは〜です is expected in interviews and self-introductions. It states a fact rather than claiming praise.

faq.q: What is the opposite of each one?
faq.a: 上手's opposite is 下手, and 得意's is 苦手. They follow the same social pattern: 下手 is blunt about ability, while 苦手 is the gentler word most people use about themselves.

title: 下手 vs 苦手
quickAnswer: 下手 means your skill is poor, and that is all it means. 苦手 covers both being weak at something and simply not liking or not coping with it, which is why 私は虫が苦手です (I can't deal with insects) and ピーマンが苦手です (I don't like green peppers) work — 下手 could never be used for either. 苦手 is also softer, so it is the normal choice about yourself.
summary: 下手 is purely poor skill; 苦手 covers dislike and discomfort too, and is the softer word to use about yourself.

members.when: Use 下手 only for a genuine lack of skill at something you do — cooking, singing, handwriting, a sport. It is blunt, so it is fine about yourself but rude about the person you are speaking to.

examples.ja: 私は絵が下手です。
examples.reading: わたしはえがへたです。
examples.en: I'm bad at drawing.

examples.ja: 歌は下手ですが、大好きです。
examples.reading: うたはへたですが、だいすきです。
examples.en: I'm a terrible singer, but I love it.

members.when: Use 苦手 for anything you are weak at, uncomfortable with, or would rather avoid — a school subject, a food, insects, a certain person. It says nothing about skill on its own and is far gentler than 下手.

examples.ja: 私は虫が苦手です。
examples.reading: わたしはむしがにがてです。
examples.en: I really can't deal with insects.

examples.ja: ピーマンが苦手なので、残してもいいですか。
examples.reading: ピーマンがにがてなので、のこしてもいいですか。
examples.en: I'm not keen on green peppers, so may I leave them?

contrast.ja: 納豆が苦手です。
contrast.reading: なっとうがにがてです。
contrast.en: I'm not a fan of natto.
contrast.note: Food is about taste, not skill, so only 苦手 is possible. 納豆が下手です is meaningless.

contrast.ja: 字が下手ですみません。
contrast.reading: じがへたですみません。
contrast.en: Sorry about my bad handwriting.
contrast.note: A concrete skill you perform badly, which is 下手's home ground. 字が苦手 would suggest you avoid writing rather than that the result looks bad.

contrast.ja: あの人はちょっと苦手です。
contrast.reading: あのひとはちょっとにがてです。
contrast.en: I find that person a bit hard to get on with.
contrast.note: 苦手 is the polite way to say you dislike someone. 下手 cannot describe a relationship at all.

contrast.ja: 英語は苦手ですが、少しずつ勉強しています。
contrast.reading: えいごはにがてですが、すこしずつべんきょうしています。
contrast.en: English is a weak point for me, but I'm studying bit by bit.
contrast.note: For a subject you struggle with, 苦手 is the natural and modest choice; 下手 sounds harshly self-critical and is odd with school subjects.

mistakes.wrong: ピーマンが下手です。
mistakes.right: ピーマンが苦手です。
mistakes.why: 下手 only describes how well you do something. Disliking a food has nothing to do with skill, so 下手 produces a sentence that makes no sense to a native speaker.

mistakes.wrong: 日本語が下手ですね。
mistakes.right: 日本語はまだ難しいですよね。
mistakes.why: Telling someone their Japanese is 下手 is genuinely rude. Keep 下手 for yourself; about another person, avoid it entirely.

mistakes.wrong: 私は数学が下手です。
mistakes.right: 私は数学が苦手です。
mistakes.why: Not ungrammatical, but school subjects normally take 苦手. 下手 fits physical or performed skills such as playing, drawing and cooking rather than academic ones.

faq.q: Can I use 苦手 about a person I dislike?
faq.a: Yes, and it is the standard polite way to do it. あの人は苦手です means you find them hard to deal with, without the harshness of 嫌いです. This use is impossible with 下手.

faq.q: Which should I use about myself?
faq.a: 苦手 in most cases, because it is softer and covers more ground. Keep 下手 for when you specifically mean your skill is poor, where it is a normal, modest thing to say about your own cooking or singing.

faq.q: Does 苦手 mean I'm actually bad at it?
faq.a: Not necessarily. 苦手 says you find something hard or unpleasant; you may still be perfectly competent. That gap is exactly why people say 苦手 about subjects, foods and people alike.

title: ちょっと vs 少し
quickAnswer: For quantity they mean the same thing — ちょっと待って and 少し待って are both "wait a bit" — with ちょっと the casual spoken form and 少し the neutral or written one. The difference that matters is that ちょっと also softens and refuses: 今日はちょっと… is a complete, polite no, and 少し has no such use.
summary: Same meaning for quantity; ちょっと is casual and 少し neutral. Only ちょっと works as a softener and as a polite refusal.

members.when: Everyday spoken Japanese, and the only choice when softening a request, getting someone's attention, or declining. Trailing off with ちょっと… is understood as a polite refusal.

examples.ja: ちょっとすみません、駅はどこですか。
examples.reading: ちょっとすみません、えきはどこですか。
examples.en: Excuse me, where is the station?

examples.ja: 今日はちょっと…。また今度お願いします。
examples.reading: きょうはちょっと…。またこんどおねがいします。
examples.en: Today is a bit... Could we do it another time?

members.when: Neutral register: writing, polite or formal speech, and anywhere you are simply stating a small amount. It is the safer word in business email and on tests.

examples.ja: 少し疲れましたので、休みましょう。
examples.reading: すこしつかれましたので、やすみましょう。
examples.en: I'm a little tired, so let's take a break.

examples.ja: 日本語が少し分かります。
examples.reading: にほんごがすこしわかります。
examples.en: I understand a little Japanese.

contrast.ja: 今晩、飲みに行きませんか。 今日はちょっと…。
contrast.reading: こんばん、のみにいきませんか。 きょうはちょっと…。
contrast.en: Want to go for a drink tonight? Tonight is a bit...
contrast.note: This is ちょっと's most important use and it has no 少し equivalent. 今日は少し… is not a refusal and merely sounds unfinished.

contrast.ja: 少しお待ちください。
contrast.reading: すこしおまちください。
contrast.en: Please wait a moment.
contrast.note: In an announcement or to a customer, 少し fits the register. ちょっとお待ちください is possible but noticeably more casual.

contrast.ja: ちょっと、聞いてる？
contrast.reading: ちょっと、きいてる？
contrast.en: Hey, are you even listening?
contrast.note: Used on its own, ちょっと calls someone out or gets their attention. 少し cannot be used this way at all.

contrast.ja: この問題は少し難しいです。
contrast.reading: このもんだいはすこしむずかしいです。
contrast.en: This question is a little difficult.
contrast.note: A plain statement of degree, where both work: 少し is the neutral pick for writing and ちょっと for conversation.

mistakes.wrong: 手伝ってくれませんか。 はい、少しです。
mistakes.right: 手伝ってくれませんか。 すみません、今日はちょっと…。
mistakes.why: Learners look for a word meaning no and miss that ちょっと… is the refusal itself. 少し in that slot does not communicate a decline, and a flat いいえ sounds abrupt.

mistakes.wrong: レポートをちょっと直しました。 (in an email to your boss)
mistakes.right: レポートを少し直しました。
mistakes.why: ちょっと belongs to casual speech. In a business email or a written report, 少し or 少々 is the appropriate register; ちょっと reads as too chatty.

faq.q: Are they interchangeable for amounts?
faq.a: Essentially yes. ちょっと高い and 少し高い both mean "a bit expensive". Choose by register: ちょっと when speaking casually, 少し in writing or polite speech.

faq.q: Why does ちょっと mean no?
faq.a: Because trailing off is how Japanese declines politely. The full sentence is something like ちょっと都合が悪いです, and speakers cut it short at ちょっと…. Everyone understands it as a refusal, so you do not need to finish it.

faq.q: What about 少々?
faq.a: 少々 is the formal version of 少し, used in service and business language, as in 少々お待ちください. Recognise it when you hear it, and use 少し in your own sentences at first.

title: でも vs しかし
quickAnswer: Both mean "but" at the start of a sentence, and the difference is register: でも is what you say out loud and write to friends, しかし belongs to essays, news and formal speeches. If you want "but" in the middle of one sentence, neither is right — use が or けど.
summary: でも is the spoken, casual "but"; しかし is the written, formal one. Mid-sentence, use が or けど instead.
