mistakes.why: If you are the one walking or driving past, it is 通る. 通す needs something else that you are sending through.

faq.q: この道は駅まで通っている — why 通る for a road that isn't moving?
faq.a: 通る also describes a route existing and running somewhere: 駅まで道が通っている, "a road runs as far as the station." The same idea covers lines and utilities: 電気が通っている, "there is electricity connected."

faq.q: Is 試験に通る the same as 試験に合格する?
faq.a: Same meaning. 合格する is the formal one you would see on a notice, 通る is the everyday spoken version, and 受かる sits in between and is very common in conversation.

faq.q: What is 目を通す?
faq.a: To look something over, to skim it. 資料に目を通しておいてください means "please have a look through the materials beforehand" — you send your eyes through it.

title: 見つかる vs 見つける
quickAnswer: 見つける is you actively finding something (いい店を見つけた, "I found a nice shop"); 見つかる is something turning up, with the thing found marked by が (鍵が見つかった). 見つかる is not a passive form — it is an ordinary intransitive verb, and Japanese uses it constantly where English says "I found it".
summary: 見つける = you find it (を); 見つかる = it turns up (が). 見つかった is normal Japanese for "I found it", not a passive.

members.when: Use 見つかる when the focus is on the thing appearing rather than on who searched — including when you were the searcher. It also means to get caught or spotted, with the catcher marked by に.

examples.ja: なくした鍵がやっと見つかりました。
examples.reading: なくしたかぎがやっとみつかりました。
examples.en: The key I lost finally turned up.

examples.ja: いい仕事が見つかるといいですね。
examples.reading: いいしごとがみつかるといいですね。
examples.en: I hope you find a good job.

members.when: Use 見つける when you want to name the finder and their action — you searched, you spotted it. The thing found takes を.

examples.ja: 駅の近くでいい店を見つけました。
examples.reading: えきのちかくでいいみせをみつけました。
examples.en: I found a nice shop near the station.

examples.ja: 先生がレポートの間違いを見つけた。
examples.reading: せんせいがレポートのまちがいをみつけた。
examples.en: The teacher spotted a mistake in the report.

contrast.ja: 探していた資料が見つかりました。
contrast.reading: さがしていたしりょうがみつかりました。
contrast.en: I found the documents I was looking for.
contrast.note: English says "I found", but Japanese naturally reports the result with 見つかる and が.

contrast.ja: 弟が私の日記を見つけた。
contrast.reading: おとうとがわたしのにっきをみつけた。
contrast.en: My little brother found my diary.
contrast.note: The finder matters here — he did it — so 見つける with を.

contrast.ja: 教室でお菓子を食べていて、先生に見つかった。
contrast.reading: きょうしつでおかしをたべていて、せんせいにみつかった。
contrast.en: I was eating sweets in class and got caught by the teacher.
contrast.note: "Get caught" is 見つかる, with に for the person who caught you.

contrast.ja: アパートはまだ見つかっていません。
contrast.reading: アパートはまだみつかっていません。
contrast.en: I still haven't found an apartment.
contrast.note: An ongoing search reported as a state — 見つかっていない is far more common here than 見つけていない.

mistakes.wrong: 鍵が見つけられました。
mistakes.right: 鍵が見つかりました。
mistakes.why: Because English says "was found", learners reach for the passive. Japanese already has 見つかる for this, and 見つけられる sounds off here — it mostly suggests someone unwelcome found it.

mistakes.wrong: 私は鍵を見つかりました。
mistakes.right: 私は鍵を見つけました。／鍵が見つかりました。
mistakes.why: 見つかる cannot take を. Either name yourself as the finder with 見つける, or drop the doer and use が.

mistakes.wrong: いい仕事を見つかるといいですね。
mistakes.right: いい仕事が見つかるといいですね。
mistakes.why: The same particle slip in the commonest well-wishing phrase. This one is fixed with が.

faq.q: If 見つかる means "be found", isn't it a passive verb?
faq.a: No. It is an intransitive verb paired with 見つける, exactly like 開く and 開ける. It has no doer built in — which is why 先生に見つかった needs に to add one.

faq.q: When do I have to use 見つける then?
faq.a: When the finder is part of the point: someone else found your diary, the teacher spotted the mistake, you deliberately hunted something down. If you only care that the thing turned up, use 見つかる.

faq.q: Which do I use for finding a job?
faq.a: Both exist. 仕事を見つける emphasises your effort; 仕事が見つかる is the everyday way to say a job came through, and is what you use in wishes and reports: 仕事が見つかりました.

title: 治る vs 治す
quickAnswer: 治る is intransitive: an illness, cold or wound gets better, marked with が (風邪が治った). 治す is transitive: someone cures or heals it, marked with を (医者が病気を治す, 早く風邪を治したい).
summary: 治る = it heals (が); 治す = someone cures it (を). Note the separate 直る/直す, same reading, for fixing things.

members.when: Use 治る when the condition itself improves and no one is named as curing it. The illness, cold, wound or pain takes が, and the patient, if mentioned, takes は.

examples.ja: 風邪はもうすっかり治りました。
examples.reading: かぜはもうすっかりなおりました。
examples.en: My cold has completely cleared up.

examples.ja: この傷は一週間で治ると思います。
examples.reading: このきずはいっしゅうかんでなおるとおもいます。
examples.en: I think this wound will heal in a week.

members.when: Use 治す when someone acts to cure it — a doctor treating a patient, or you deliberately getting yourself over something. The illness takes を.

examples.ja: その病院で病気を治してもらいました。
examples.reading: そのびょういんでびょうきをなおしてもらいました。
examples.en: I had my illness treated at that hospital.

examples.ja: 今日はよく寝て、風邪を治します。
examples.reading: きょうはよくねて、かぜをなおします。
examples.en: I'll sleep well today and get over this cold.

contrast.ja: 薬を飲んだら、頭痛が治りました。
contrast.reading: くすりをのんだら、ずつうがなおりました。
contrast.en: I took medicine and my headache went away.
contrast.note: The headache improved; the medicine is not the grammatical doer, so 治る with が.

contrast.ja: 医者が母の病気を治してくれました。
contrast.reading: いしゃがははのびょうきをなおしてくれました。
contrast.en: The doctor cured my mother's illness.
contrast.note: A named curer acting on the illness — 治す with を.

contrast.ja: 早く治るといいですね。
contrast.reading: はやくなおるといいですね。
contrast.en: I hope you get better soon.
contrast.note: The standard get-well phrase, always 治る. お大事に often follows it.

mistakes.wrong: 風邪を治りました。
mistakes.right: 風邪が治りました。／風邪を治しました。
mistakes.why: 治る never takes を. Use が if it cleared up on its own, を治す if you actively worked at getting over it.

mistakes.wrong: エアコンが治りました。
mistakes.right: エアコンが直りました。
mistakes.why: Machines, cars and broken things use 直る and 直す. 治る is for bodies. Both are read なおる, which is why this slips through.

faq.q: 治る and 直る sound identical — how do I choose?
faq.a: 治 is for health: illness, colds, wounds, pain. 直 is for things and states: a broken appliance, a typo, a bad habit. The same split applies to the transitive 治す and 直す. We have a separate page comparing 直す and 治す if you want the details.

faq.q: Can a person be the subject of 治る?
faq.a: It is more natural to make the illness the subject: 彼は風邪が治った, "his cold got better." You do hear 彼はもう治った about a person, but the illness-as-subject version is the safe pattern.

faq.q: Is 怪我を治す correct, since I can't cure my own injury?
faq.a: Yes — it means treating it or getting it healed through your own effort, e.g. 怪我を治してから練習に戻ります. If you just mean it healed, use 怪我が治る.

title: 並ぶ vs 並べる
quickAnswer: 並ぶ is intransitive: people or things are lined up, and the ones lining up are marked with が (人が並んでいる, 店の前に並ぶ). 並べる is transitive: you arrange or set things out, marked with を (皿を並べる).
summary: 並ぶ = they line up, or you queue (が); 並べる = you set things out in a row (を).

members.when: Use 並ぶ when you or others stand in a queue, or when things happen to be in a row. The place you queue takes に. In ～ている it describes the resulting state: 人が並んでいる.

examples.ja: みんな店の前に並んでいます。
examples.reading: みんなみせのまえにならんでいます。
examples.en: Everyone is queueing in front of the shop.

examples.ja: 駅前には店がたくさん並んでいる。
examples.reading: えきまえにはみせがたくさんならんでいる。
examples.en: There are lots of shops lined up in front of the station.

members.when: Use 並べる when a person arranges things into a row or sets them out. What you arrange takes を, and where you put it takes に.

examples.ja: テーブルに皿を並べてください。
examples.reading: テーブルにさらをならべてください。
examples.en: Please set the plates out on the table.

examples.ja: 机の上に本をきれいに並べました。
examples.reading: つくえのうえにほんをきれいにならべました。
examples.en: I arranged the books neatly on the desk.

contrast.ja: 一時間並んで、やっとラーメンを食べた。
contrast.reading: いちじかんならんで、やっとラーメンをたべた。
contrast.en: I queued for an hour and finally got my ramen.
contrast.note: You yourself are in the line — 並ぶ, with no object at all.

contrast.ja: いすを並べて、席を作りましょう。
contrast.reading: いすをならべて、せきをつくりましょう。
contrast.en: Let's line up the chairs and make some seating.
contrast.note: You are moving the chairs, so 並べる with を.

contrast.ja: 棚にきれいに並んでいる本を一冊取った。
contrast.reading: たなにきれいにならんでいるほんをいっさつとった。
contrast.en: I took one of the books lined up neatly on the shelf.
contrast.note: Describing how the books sit, not who put them there — 並んでいる.

mistakes.wrong: レストランの前に並べました。
mistakes.right: レストランの前に並びました。
mistakes.why: If you queued, it is 並びました. 並べました says you arranged something in front of the restaurant.

mistakes.wrong: 人がたくさん並べています。
mistakes.right: 人がたくさん並んでいます。
mistakes.why: People in a queue line themselves up, so 並ぶ. 並べる needs an object being arranged.

faq.q: Is there a difference between 並んでいる and 並べてある?
faq.a: 並んでいる just says things are in a row. 並べてある says someone arranged them and left them that way, hinting at intention: 料理が並べてある, "the dishes have been laid out."

faq.q: How do I say "stand in line here"?
faq.a: ここに並んでください. The に marks the place a line forms. ここで並んでください is understood too, but に is the standard particle here.

faq.q: Can 並ぶ mean "match" or "rival"?
faq.a: Yes, in the pattern 〜に並ぶ: 彼に並ぶ選手はいない, "there is no player who matches him." It is a step above N5 usage, but you will meet it in reading.

title: 揃う vs 揃える
quickAnswer: 揃う is what things do by themselves — a set becomes complete, everyone shows up — and takes が. 揃える is what you do to things: you gather the full set, or line them up evenly, and it takes を. If a person is doing it on purpose, use 揃える.
summary: 揃う means a set becomes complete on its own (が); 揃える means someone completes or lines up that set (を).

members.when: The thing that becomes complete is the subject with が. Use it when the full set is now there, or when all the people have turned up. Very often in the ～ている form, describing the resulting state.

examples.ja: メンバーが全員揃いました。
examples.reading: めんばーがぜんいんそろいました。
examples.en: All the members are here now.

examples.ja: サイズが揃っていないので、売れません。
examples.reading: さいずがそろっていないので、うれません。
examples.en: We can't sell them because the sizes don't match up.

members.when: Someone acts on the things, marked with を. Two jobs: gathering a complete set (道具を揃える), and making things even or aligned (靴を揃える, 髪の長さを揃える).

examples.ja: 面接に必要な書類を揃えました。
examples.reading: めんせつにひつようなしょるいをそろえました。
examples.en: I got together all the documents I need for the interview.

examples.ja: 玄関で靴を揃えてください。
examples.reading: げんかんでくつをそろえてください。
examples.en: Please line your shoes up neatly at the entrance.

contrast.ja: 道具が揃いました。
contrast.reading: どうぐがそろいました。
contrast.en: The tools are all here.
contrast.note: The speaker reports the state of the set. Nobody is credited with the work, so 揃う with が.

contrast.ja: 道具を揃えました。
contrast.reading: どうぐをそろえました。
contrast.en: I got all the tools together.
contrast.note: Same set, but now the speaker went out and assembled it. An actor plus を forces 揃える.

contrast.ja: みんなで声を揃えて歌いましょう。
contrast.reading: みんなでこえをそろえてうたいましょう。
contrast.en: Let's all sing in unison.
contrast.note: 声を揃える is fixed with を: the singers deliberately match their voices. 声が揃う exists, but it describes the result rather than the instruction.

contrast.ja: 全員揃ってから出発します。
contrast.reading: ぜんいんそろってからしゅっぱつします。
contrast.en: We'll leave once everyone is here.
contrast.note: People arriving of their own accord is 揃う. 全員を揃える would sound like lining bodies up.

mistakes.wrong: 書類を揃いました。
mistakes.right: 書類を揃えました。／書類が揃いました。
mistakes.why: 揃う cannot take を. Pick the form that matches the particle: を with 揃えました if you did it, が with 揃いました if you are just reporting that the set is complete.

mistakes.wrong: 靴を揃った。
mistakes.right: 靴を揃えた。
mistakes.why: Straightening shoes is a deliberate act on the shoes, so it is always 揃える.

faq.q: Does 揃う only mean 'to be complete'?
faq.a: It also covers matching or being even — サイズが揃う means the sizes all match. The common thread is that a group has become uniform or full without anyone being named as the doer.

faq.q: Is 揃える the same as 集める?
faq.a: Close but not identical. 集める is just gathering things; 揃える implies gathering everything that was needed, or making the items even. 切手を集める is a hobby, while 切手を揃える sounds like completing a set.

faq.q: Why is 揃っている so common?
faq.a: Because the useful information is usually the current state — whether the set is complete right now. 揃った alone can sound like a one-off event, so ～ている is the everyday choice.

title: 片付く vs 片付ける
quickAnswer: 片付ける is the tidying you do, with を: 部屋を片付ける. 片付く is the room ending up tidy, with が: 部屋が片付く. Beyond cleaning, both also mean getting a task or problem settled — 仕事が片付く, 仕事を片付ける.
summary: 片付ける is to tidy or deal with something (を); 片付く is for it to end up tidy or settled (が).

members.when: The room, desk, or job is the subject with が, and you are reporting the finished state. Often with やっと or ようやく, because it is the relief of something finally being done.

examples.ja: やっと部屋が片付いた。
examples.reading: やっとへやがかたづいた。
examples.en: The room is finally tidy.

examples.ja: 今日中に仕事が片付きそうです。
examples.reading: きょうじゅうにしごとがかたづきそうです。
examples.en: It looks like the work will be wrapped up today.

members.when: You are the one tidying, and the mess takes を. Also used for disposing of a task: 宿題を片付ける means to get the homework out of the way. Requests and orders are nearly always 片付ける.

examples.ja: 使った皿を片付けてください。
examples.reading: つかったさらをかたづけてください。
examples.en: Please clear away the dishes you used.

examples.ja: 面倒な仕事を先に片付けます。
examples.reading: めんどうなしごとをさきにかたづけます。
examples.en: I'll get the annoying job out of the way first.

contrast.ja: 部屋を片付けなさい。
contrast.reading: へやをかたづけなさい。
contrast.en: Tidy your room.
contrast.note: An order aimed at a person. Only the transitive 片付ける can be commanded.

contrast.ja: 部屋が片付いていて気持ちいい。
contrast.reading: へやがかたづいていてきもちいい。
contrast.en: The room is tidy and it feels good.
contrast.note: No doer in view, just the pleasant state, so 片付いている.

contrast.ja: その問題はもう片付きました。
contrast.reading: そのもんだいはもうかたづきました。
contrast.en: That problem has already been settled.
contrast.note: Reporting that the matter is closed, without pointing at who closed it.

contrast.ja: その問題は私が片付けます。
contrast.reading: そのもんだいはわたしがかたづけます。
contrast.en: I'll take care of that problem.
contrast.note: Naming yourself as the one who will handle it forces 片付ける.

mistakes.wrong: 部屋を片付きました。
mistakes.right: 部屋を片付けました。
mistakes.why: 片付く never takes を. If you did the tidying, it has to be 片付けました.

mistakes.wrong: 机の上が片付けています。
mistakes.right: 机の上が片付いています。
mistakes.why: With が describing a state, use 片付いている. 片付けている with を means someone is in the middle of tidying.

faq.q: Can 片付ける mean throwing things away?
faq.a: Not exactly — it is putting things where they belong. If you mean discarding, 捨てる is the word. 片付ける often involves some throwing away, but it does not say so.

faq.q: Why do I hear 仕事を片付ける when nothing is being cleaned?
faq.a: Both verbs extend naturally from clearing a space to clearing a workload. 仕事を片付ける is everyday office Japanese for getting a task finished and off your plate.

faq.q: Is 片付けておく different?
faq.a: It adds the sense of doing it in advance for later. 客が来る前に片付けておく means tidying ahead of time so things are ready when the guests arrive.

title: 混ざる vs 混ぜる
quickAnswer: 混ぜる is stirring things together yourself, with を: 卵を混ぜる. 混ざる is things ending up mixed, with が: 色が混ざる. If there is a spoon or a cook involved, it is 混ぜる.
summary: 混ぜる is to stir or blend something (を); 混ざる is for things to end up blended together (が).

members.when: The things that blend are the subject with が. Use it for colours running together, a smell in the air, or something unwanted finding its way in. Frequently ～ている for the resulting state.

examples.ja: 青と黄色が混ざると緑になる。
examples.reading: あおときいろがまざるとみどりになる。
examples.en: Blue and yellow make green when they mix.

examples.ja: この米には古い米が混ざっている。
examples.reading: このこめにはふるいこめがまざっている。
examples.en: There's old rice mixed in with this rice.

members.when: You do the mixing and the ingredients take を. This is the verb of recipes and instructions: よく混ぜる, かき混ぜる. Use ～に混ぜる for what you mix something into.

examples.ja: 卵と砂糖をよく混ぜてください。
examples.reading: たまごとさとうをよくまぜてください。
examples.en: Please mix the eggs and sugar well.

examples.ja: 牛乳を少しずつ混ぜながら温めます。
examples.reading: ぎゅうにゅうをすこしずつまぜながらあたためます。
examples.en: Heat it while stirring in the milk a little at a time.

contrast.ja: よく混ぜてから飲んでください。
contrast.reading: よくまぜてからのんでください。
contrast.en: Please stir it well before drinking.
contrast.note: An instruction to the listener, so the transitive 混ぜる.

contrast.ja: 絵の具が混ざって、汚い色になった。
contrast.reading: えのぐがまざって、きたないいろになった。
contrast.en: The paints ran together and turned an ugly colour.
contrast.note: Nobody meant it to happen; the paints did it, so 混ざる with が.

contrast.ja: 水に薬を混ぜます。
contrast.reading: みずにくすりをまぜます。
contrast.en: I mix the medicine into the water.
contrast.note: Two things marked differently — を for what you add, に for what it goes into. Only 混ぜる takes this pattern.

contrast.ja: ごみに紙が混ざっていました。
contrast.reading: ごみにかみがまざっていました。
contrast.en: There was paper mixed in with the rubbish.
contrast.note: Something got in by accident, and 混ざっている reports the state you discovered.

mistakes.wrong: 砂糖を混ざってください。
mistakes.right: 砂糖を混ぜてください。
mistakes.why: 混ざる cannot take を, and a request to the listener always needs the transitive 混ぜる.

mistakes.wrong: 色を混ざりました。
mistakes.right: 色を混ぜました。／色が混ざりました。
mistakes.why: Choose by particle: を with 混ぜました if you did it, が with 混ざりました if the colours ran together on their own.

faq.q: What about 交ざる — is it the same word?
faq.a: Same reading, different nuance. 混 is used when things blend into one whole, like liquids or colours; 交 is used when the parts stay distinguishable, such as one foreign word among Japanese ones. For cooking, 混 is the safe choice.

faq.q: Is 混じる different from 混ざる?
faq.a: They overlap heavily and are often interchangeable. 混じる leans slightly toward a small amount present in a larger whole, while 混ざる is the more general everyday choice, and using 混ざる is rarely wrong.

faq.q: Which one do I use for joining a group of people?
faq.a: 混ざる: 私も混ざっていい？ means 'can I join in too?'. 混ぜて also works as a casual 'let me in', where you are asking someone to include you.

title: 立つ vs 立てる
quickAnswer: 立つ is you standing up, with が: 人が立つ. 立てる is standing something else up, with を: 本を立てる. 立てる also carries a set of everyday idioms that 立つ does not — 計画を立てる (make a plan) and 音を立てる (make a noise).
summary: 立つ is to stand yourself (が); 立てる is to stand something up (を), and also to make a plan or a sound.

members.when: The one standing is the subject with が. It covers a person rising to their feet or being on their feet, and also things that are upright — 木が立っている, ビルが立っている.

examples.ja: みなさん、立ってください。
examples.reading: みなさん、たってください。
examples.en: Everyone, please stand up.

examples.ja: 駅の前に大きなビルが立っています。
examples.reading: えきのまえにおおきなびるがたっています。
examples.en: There's a big building standing in front of the station.

members.when: You put something into an upright position, marked with を. Learn the idioms as set phrases too: 計画を立てる, 予定を立てる, 音を立てる, 役に立てる.

examples.ja: 夏休みの計画を立てました。
examples.reading: なつやすみのけいかくをたてました。
examples.en: I made plans for the summer holiday.

examples.ja: 本を棚に立てて並べます。
examples.reading: ほんをたなにたててならべます。
examples.en: I stand the books upright on the shelf.

contrast.ja: 彼は教室の前に立っています。
contrast.reading: かれはきょうしつのまえにたっています。
contrast.en: He is standing at the front of the classroom.
contrast.note: He is on his own feet and nothing is being acted on, so 立つ.

contrast.ja: 傘を壁に立てておきました。
contrast.reading: かさをかべにたてておきました。
contrast.en: I stood the umbrella against the wall.
contrast.note: The umbrella cannot stand itself; someone put it there, so を立てる.

contrast.ja: 旅行の予定を立てましょう。
contrast.reading: りょこうのよていをたてましょう。
contrast.en: Let's make a plan for the trip.
contrast.note: A fixed idiom. 予定が立つ exists and means the plan has firmed up, but proposing to make one is always 立てる.

contrast.ja: 音を立てないでください。
contrast.reading: おとをたてないでください。
contrast.en: Please don't make any noise.
contrast.note: You cause the sound, so を立てる. 音がする is the natural way to say a sound simply occurs.

mistakes.wrong: 計画を立ちました。
mistakes.right: 計画を立てました。
mistakes.why: 計画 is something you construct, so it needs the transitive 立てる. 計画が立つ is possible, but it means the plan has come together.

mistakes.wrong: 私は立てました。
mistakes.right: 私は立ちました。
mistakes.why: Standing up yourself is 立つ. 立てました leaves the listener waiting for an object — what did you stand up?

mistakes.wrong: この本は役に立てます。
mistakes.right: この本は役に立ちます。
mistakes.why: 役に立つ, 'to be useful', is the intransitive idiom. 役に立てる means to put something to use and needs an object.

faq.q: Isn't 立てる also the potential form of 立つ?
faq.a: Yes, and the forms look identical. Context sorts it out: 一時間も立てない means 'I can't stand for even an hour', while 本を立てる is standing a book up. The particle helps, since the potential takes が or は and the transitive takes を.

faq.q: Do I use 立つ or 建つ for a building?
faq.a: For buildings, 建つ is the usual kanji, and 建てる for constructing one. 立つ can appear for something merely being upright, but 家を建てる is the standard way to say building a house.

faq.q: What does 腹が立つ mean?
faq.a: It means to get angry, literally 'the stomach stands up'. It is intransitive and takes が; 腹を立てる also exists with the same meaning but a slightly more deliberate feel.

title: 着く vs 届く
quickAnswer: 着く is for someone who travels arriving somewhere — a person, a train, a plane: 駅に着く. 届く is for something that was sent arriving at its destination: 荷物が届く. The parcel you ordered 届く, and you 着く at home.
summary: 着く is a person or vehicle arriving somewhere; 届く is a sent thing — a parcel, letter or email — being delivered.

members.when: The subject is something that moved under its own power or carried people: you, a friend, a bus, a flight. The destination takes に. Ask whether the subject travelled there — if so, 着く.

examples.ja: 六時に東京駅に着きます。
examples.reading: ろくじにとうきょうえきにつきます。
examples.en: I'll arrive at Tokyo Station at six.

examples.ja: 飛行機が予定より早く着きました。
examples.reading: ひこうきがよていよりはやくつきました。
examples.en: The plane arrived earlier than scheduled.

members.when: The subject is something someone sent: a parcel, a letter, an email, flowers. It always implies a sender. It also has a second everyday meaning — reaching far enough, as in 手が届く.

examples.ja: 注文した本がまだ届いていません。
examples.reading: ちゅうもんしたほんがまだとどいていません。
examples.en: The book I ordered still hasn't arrived.

examples.ja: 背が低くて棚の上に手が届かない。
examples.reading: せがひくくてたなのうえにてがとどかない。
examples.en: I'm too short to reach the top of the shelf.

contrast.ja: 荷物が届きました。
contrast.reading: にもつがとどきました。
contrast.en: The package arrived.
contrast.note: Someone sent it and it was delivered here. 荷物が着きました is not how this is said.

contrast.ja: 友達が駅に着きました。
contrast.reading: ともだちがえきにつきました。
contrast.en: My friend arrived at the station.
contrast.note: A person who travelled there, so 着く.

contrast.ja: メールが届いていませんか。
contrast.reading: めーるがとどいていませんか。
contrast.en: Did my email not reach you?
contrast.note: Email is sent rather than travelling on its own, so 届く. This is the standard business phrasing.

contrast.ja: 私は昨日ホテルに着きました。
contrast.reading: わたしはきのうほてるにつきました。
contrast.en: I arrived at the hotel yesterday.
contrast.note: You are the traveller. 届く would make it sound as though you had been mailed there.

mistakes.wrong: 荷物が着きました。
mistakes.right: 荷物が届きました。
mistakes.why: This is the most common slip with this pair. A parcel does not travel of its own accord — it is delivered, so it 届く. 着く with luggage sounds as though the suitcase walked in by itself.

mistakes.wrong: 手紙を届きました。
mistakes.right: 手紙が届きました。／手紙を届けました。
mistakes.why: 届く is intransitive and takes が. If you were the one who delivered it, use the transitive 届ける with を.

mistakes.wrong: 電車が届きました。
mistakes.right: 電車が着きました。
mistakes.why: A train carries itself and its passengers to the platform, so it 着く.

faq.q: Which one do I use for luggage arriving at the airport?
faq.a: If it was handled by the airline and came out on the belt, 荷物が届く is natural. When your bags simply travelled with you, people usually talk about themselves instead: 荷物と一緒に着きました.

faq.q: Can I say 家に届く?
faq.a: Yes — 家に荷物が届く means the parcel was delivered to your house. Here 家 is the delivery address, not somewhere the parcel travelled to under its own power.

faq.q: What is the difference between 着く and 到着する?
faq.a: Same meaning, different register. 到着する is the stiffer word used in announcements and timetables, while 着く is what you say in conversation.

title: 住む vs 暮らす
quickAnswer: 住む is where your home is — the address, the city, the building: 大阪に住んでいます. 暮らす is how you live your daily life: alone, with family, comfortably, on a small income — 一人で暮らしています. If a place name follows, you almost always want 住む.
summary: 住む says where you reside (大阪に住む); 暮らす says how you live your daily life (一人で暮らす).

members.when: Pairs with a location and に: 東京に住む, アパートに住む. Say it in the ～ている form — 住んでいます — because it describes an ongoing state rather than an action.

examples.ja: 去年から大阪に住んでいます。
examples.reading: きょねんからおおさかにすんでいます。
examples.en: I've been living in Osaka since last year.

examples.ja: 駅に近いアパートに住みたいです。
examples.reading: えきにちかいあぱーとにすみたいです。
examples.en: I want to live in an apartment near the station.

members.when: Pairs with how, not where: 一人で, 家族と, 幸せに, 楽しく. It takes in your whole daily life — money, routine, mood. A place can appear with で (田舎で暮らす), which frames it as a lifestyle rather than an address.

examples.ja: 田舎で静かに暮らしたいです。
examples.reading: いなかでしずかにくらしたいです。
examples.en: I want to live quietly in the countryside.

examples.ja: 少ない給料で暮らすのは大変です。
examples.reading: すくないきゅうりょうでくらすのはたいへんです。
examples.en: Living on a small salary is hard.

contrast.ja: どこに住んでいますか。
contrast.reading: どこにすんでいますか。
contrast.en: Where do you live?
contrast.note: Asking for an address or area. This is the fixed question; どこで暮らしていますか sounds like an enquiry into someone's circumstances.

contrast.ja: 家族と一緒に楽しく暮らしています。
contrast.reading: かぞくといっしょにたのしくくらしています。
contrast.en: I live happily together with my family.
contrast.note: 楽しく describes the manner of living, not a location, so 暮らす.

contrast.ja: 一人で暮らすのは寂しいです。
contrast.reading: ひとりでくらすのはさびしいです。
contrast.en: Living alone is lonely.
contrast.note: The topic is the experience of daily life rather than the flat, so 暮らす.

contrast.ja: この町には十万人が住んでいます。
contrast.reading: このまちにはじゅうまんにんがすんでいます。
contrast.en: A hundred thousand people live in this town.
contrast.note: A count of residents — pure location, so 住む.

mistakes.wrong: 私は東京に住みます。
mistakes.right: 私は東京に住んでいます。
mistakes.why: Plain 住みます sounds like a future move, 'I will live in Tokyo'. Where you live now is an ongoing state, so it needs 住んでいます. This is the most frequent error with this verb.

mistakes.wrong: 大阪に暮らしています。
mistakes.right: 大阪に住んでいます。／大阪で暮らしています。
mistakes.why: 暮らす does not take に for a place. Use 住む with に for an address, or 暮らす with で when you mean life there.

mistakes.wrong: 一人で住んでいて、お金がありません。
mistakes.right: 一人で暮らしていて、お金がありません。
mistakes.why: Once the sentence is about getting by day to day, 暮らす is the fitting verb; 住む only reports where you are.

faq.q: Can I say 住んでいる for a short stay?
faq.a: Not really. 住む implies a settled base. For a hotel or a few weeks somewhere, use 泊まる or 滞在する instead.

faq.q: Is 暮らす more formal than 住む?
faq.a: Not formal so much as broader and a little warmer. It appears constantly in ordinary speech about family life, money and retirement, while 住む is the neutral, factual word.

faq.q: Which do I use for animals?
faq.a: 住む. 森にくまが住んでいます is natural. 暮らす is about a way of life and fits people much better.

title: 働く vs 勤める
quickAnswer: 働く is the activity of working — putting in labour — and marks the place with で: 会社で働く. 勤める is being employed by an organisation and marks it with に: 会社に勤める. Only 働く can describe work with no employer at all, such as housework or a one-day job.
summary: 働く is the act of working (会社で働く, with で); 勤める is being on an organisation's payroll (会社に勤める, with に).

members.when: Focuses on the activity. The workplace takes で, because it is where the action happens. Use it with adverbs about effort or hours: よく働く, 朝から晩まで働く. It needs no employer, so it covers part-time jobs, farming and work at home.

examples.ja: 父は銀行で働いています。
examples.reading: ちちはぎんこうではたらいています。
examples.en: My father works at a bank.

examples.ja: 今日は朝から晩まで働きました。
examples.reading: きょうはあさからばんまではたらきました。
examples.en: I worked from morning until night today.

members.when: States that you belong to an organisation as an employee, and that organisation takes に. Normally in the ～ている form, because it describes standing employment rather than today's labour. It is the word for saying which company you are with.

examples.ja: 兄は自動車会社に勤めています。
examples.reading: あにはじどうしゃがいしゃにつとめています。
examples.en: My older brother works for a car company.

examples.ja: その病院に十年勤めました。
examples.reading: そのびょういんにじゅうねんつとめました。
examples.en: I worked at that hospital for ten years.

contrast.ja: 今日は日曜日ですが、働きます。
contrast.reading: きょうはにちようびですが、はたらきます。
contrast.en: It's Sunday, but I'm working.
contrast.note: Today's labour, not your employment status, so 働く. 勤めます cannot describe one day's work.

contrast.ja: どちらの会社に勤めていますか。
contrast.reading: どちらのかいしゃにつとめていますか。
contrast.en: Which company do you work for?
contrast.note: Asking who employs you, with に marking the organisation you belong to.

contrast.ja: 母は家でよく働きます。
contrast.reading: はははいえでよくはたらきます。
contrast.en: My mother works hard at home.
contrast.note: No employer exists here, so only 働く is possible.

contrast.ja: コンビニで働いています。
contrast.reading: こんびにではたらいています。
contrast.en: I work at a convenience store.
contrast.note: Natural for a part-time job. コンビニに勤めている sounds oddly weighty, as if it were a career post.

mistakes.wrong: 会社に働いています。
mistakes.right: 会社で働いています。
mistakes.why: 働く marks the workplace with で, because it is where the activity takes place. Borrowing 勤める's に is the commonest slip with this pair.

mistakes.wrong: 会社で勤めています。
mistakes.right: 会社に勤めています。
mistakes.why: 勤める points at the organisation you belong to, and that relationship is marked with に.

mistakes.wrong: 昨日は十時間勤めました。
mistakes.right: 昨日は十時間働きました。
mistakes.why: Hours put in are labour, not employment. 勤める with a length of time means years of service, as in 十年勤めた.

faq.q: Which one should I use to introduce my job?
faq.a: Either works. 銀行に勤めています is slightly more formal and stresses that the bank employs you; 銀行で働いています is the everyday version and is never wrong.

faq.q: Can I use 勤める for a part-time job?
faq.a: It is unusual. 勤める suggests a regular post with an organisation, so part-time and casual work is normally 働く or アルバイトをする.

faq.q: Does 働く always mean paid work?
faq.a: No. It can mean any exertion, including unpaid work such as ボランティアで働く. That breadth is exactly what 勤める lacks.

title: 終わる vs 済む
quickAnswer: 終わる simply means something reaches its end — 授業が終わる. 済む means a matter has been dealt with and is off your hands, usually with a note of relief: 手続きが済んだ. 済む also has a second use 終わる cannot copy — getting by with only something, as in 千円で済む.
summary: 終わる is for something reaching its end; 済む is for a matter being dealt with, or getting by with just something.

members.when: Neutral: a class, a film, a year or a task reaches its endpoint. Pairs happily with clock times — 五時に終わる. Use it whenever you simply mean 'finish', with no sense of a burden lifted.

examples.ja: 映画は九時に終わります。
examples.reading: えいがはくじにおわります。
examples.en: The film ends at nine.

examples.ja: 長い冬がやっと終わった。
examples.reading: ながいふゆがやっとおわった。
examples.en: The long winter is finally over.

members.when: Something you had to get through is now dealt with — paperwork, an errand, an exam — and it carries relief. Also the patterns ～で済む, 'it only takes that much', and ～ないで済む, 'to get away without doing it'.

examples.ja: 用事が済んだら電話します。
examples.reading: ようじがすんだらでんわします。
examples.en: I'll call once I'm done with my errands.

examples.ja: 修理は五千円で済みました。
examples.reading: しゅうりはごせんえんですみました。
examples.en: The repair only came to five thousand yen.

contrast.ja: 授業は三時に終わります。
contrast.reading: じゅぎょうはさんじにおわります。
contrast.en: Class ends at three.
contrast.note: A scheduled endpoint. 済む would oddly suggest class was an obligation you got through.

contrast.ja: 引っ越しの手続きがやっと済みました。
contrast.reading: ひっこしのてつづきがやっとすみました。
contrast.en: The moving paperwork is finally taken care of.
contrast.note: A troublesome duty now off your hands — the core use of 済む.

contrast.ja: 電話一本で済む話です。
contrast.reading: でんわいっぽんですむはなしです。
contrast.en: It's something a single phone call would settle.
contrast.note: The ～で済む pattern. 終わる cannot be used this way at all.

contrast.ja: 傘があったので、濡れないで済んだ。
contrast.reading: かさがあったので、ぬれないですんだ。
contrast.en: I had an umbrella, so I got away without getting wet.
contrast.note: ～ないで済む means avoiding something unpleasant, and is again exclusive to 済む.

mistakes.wrong: 映画が済みました。
mistakes.right: 映画が終わりました。
mistakes.why: A film is not a chore you dispatch. For something simply reaching its end, use 終わる.

mistakes.wrong: 千円で終わりました。
mistakes.right: 千円で済みました。
mistakes.why: 'Getting by with just this much' is the ～で済む pattern, and 終わる has no such meaning.

mistakes.wrong: 済むは何時ですか。
mistakes.right: 終わるのは何時ですか。
mistakes.why: Asking what time something ends is 終わる. 済む rarely attaches to a clock time, because it is about the matter being settled rather than the moment it stops.

faq.q: Are 仕事が終わる and 仕事が済む both fine?
faq.a: Yes, and here they genuinely overlap. 終わる says the workday is over, while 済む adds a small note of relief that the job is off your plate. Either sounds natural.

faq.q: Is this 済む the same word as 住む?
faq.a: Same reading, different kanji and different meaning. Context keeps them apart — 東京に住む is residing, 用事が済む is finishing. There is also 澄む, 'to become clear'.

faq.q: What does すみません really come from?
faq.a: It is the negative of 済む: literally 'this is not settled', meaning what I did cannot be put right. That is why it serves both as an apology and as a thank-you, and it is usually written in kana.

title: 選ぶ vs 決める
quickAnswer: 選ぶ is picking one item out of a set that is in front of you; 決める is settling a matter, and it does not need a set of options at all. You 選ぶ a colour from the colours on the menu, but you 決める the date of the trip, the rules, or your mind.
summary: 選ぶ means picking from options you can see; 決める means settling something, with or without options.

members.when: Use 選ぶ when there is a set of candidates and you take one of them. If you can naturally add 〜の中から (from among ~), 選ぶ is the word.

examples.ja: この三つの中から一つ選んでください。
examples.reading: このみっつのなかからひとつえらんでください。
examples.en: Please choose one from these three.

examples.ja: 彼はクラスの代表に選ばれました。
examples.reading: かれはクラスのだいひょうにえらばれました。
examples.en: He was chosen as the class representative.

members.when: Use 決める when you fix or settle something — a date, a rule, a plan, an intention. There may be options behind the scenes, but 決める looks at the result, not at the choosing.

examples.ja: 出発の日を決めましょう。
examples.reading: しゅっぱつのひをきめましょう。
examples.en: Let's decide the departure date.

examples.ja: 留学すると心に決めました。
examples.reading: りゅうがくするとこころにきめました。
examples.en: I made up my mind to study abroad.

contrast.ja: メニューから好きなものを選んでください。
contrast.reading: メニューからすきなものをえらんでください。
contrast.en: Please choose whatever you like from the menu.
contrast.note: The menu is the set of candidates, so 選ぶ. 決める would sound like you are being asked to settle the restaurant's policy.

contrast.ja: 会議の時間を決めてください。
contrast.reading: かいぎのじかんをきめてください。
contrast.en: Please decide the time of the meeting.
contrast.note: No list of times is given; you are fixing one. 時間を選ぶ would only work if someone had already offered you two or three slots.

contrast.ja: クラスのルールを決めます。
contrast.reading: クラスのルールをきめます。
contrast.en: We will set the class rules.
contrast.note: Rules are created, not picked off a list, so 決める is the only option.

contrast.ja: どの大学にするか、まだ決めていません。
contrast.reading: どのだいがくにするか、まだきめていません。
contrast.en: I haven't decided which university yet.
contrast.note: Options do exist here, but the speaker is talking about not having settled it. 選んでいません would stress the act of picking and sounds odd as a general answer.

mistakes.wrong: 明日の予定を選びます。
mistakes.right: 明日の予定を決めます。
mistakes.why: A schedule is not a row of items you pick from; you fix it. 選ぶ needs candidates.

mistakes.wrong: この二つの中から決めてください。
mistakes.right: この二つの中から選んでください。
mistakes.why: 〜の中から names a set, so the verb has to be 選ぶ. Saying どちらにするか決めてください is fine, because the set is no longer stated as 〜の中から.

faq.q: Can both work in the same sentence?
faq.a: Often yes, with a shift in focus. 大学を選びました means you picked one of several; 大学を決めました means it is now settled. Neither is wrong, but 決める is the natural answer to "have you decided yet?"

faq.q: Which one do I use for ordering food?
faq.a: Both are common. 何にするか決めた is the usual casual way to ask whether someone has decided, while 選ぶ shows up when the menu itself is the topic: メニューから選ぶ.

faq.q: Is 選ぶ only for physical things?
faq.a: No. You can 選ぶ a job, a word or a path, as long as the sentence implies there were alternatives.

title: 返す vs 戻す
quickAnswer: 返す is giving something back to the person or place it came from — its owner or lender. 戻す is putting something back into the position it was in. Returning a borrowed book to the library is 返す; putting a book back on the shelf you took it from is 戻す.
summary: 返す gives something back to its owner; 戻す puts something back where it was. Books to the library: 返す.

members.when: Use 返す when something was borrowed, lent or received and now goes back to whoever it belongs to. There is another party involved.

examples.ja: 図書館に本を返しました。
examples.reading: としょかんにほんをかえしました。
examples.en: I returned the book to the library.

examples.ja: 借りたお金は来週返します。
examples.reading: かりたおかねはらいしゅうかえします。
examples.en: I'll pay back the money I borrowed next week.

members.when: Use 戻す when something moves back to its original place or original state. No owner is involved — only a position.

examples.ja: 読んだ本は棚に戻してください。
examples.reading: よんだほんはたなにもどしてください。
examples.en: Please put the books you've read back on the shelf.

examples.ja: いすを元の場所に戻しました。
examples.reading: いすをもとのばしょにもどしました。
examples.en: I put the chair back where it was.

contrast.ja: 友達にペンを返しました。
contrast.reading: ともだちにペンをかえしました。
contrast.en: I gave my friend's pen back to her.
contrast.note: The pen has an owner, so 返す. 戻す would sound like you merely moved it back to a spot.

contrast.ja: 使ったはさみを引き出しに戻してください。
contrast.reading: つかったはさみをひきだしにもどしてください。
contrast.en: Please put the scissors back in the drawer.
contrast.note: The drawer is a place, not an owner, so 戻す.

contrast.ja: 話を元に戻しますね。
contrast.reading: はなしをもとにもどしますね。
contrast.en: Let me get back to the topic.
contrast.note: Returning to an earlier state — only 戻す works here, and 元に返す is not Japanese.

contrast.ja: この店では買った物を返すことができます。
contrast.reading: このみせではかったものをかえすことができます。
contrast.en: You can return purchased items at this shop.
contrast.note: The goods go back to the shop they came from, so 返す.

mistakes.wrong: 本を棚に返してください。
mistakes.right: 本を棚に戻してください。
mistakes.why: A shelf does not own the book. 返す needs a person or institution that lent it; for a position, use 戻す. This is the most common slip with this pair.

mistakes.wrong: 図書館に本を戻しました。
mistakes.right: 図書館に本を返しました。
mistakes.why: The library lent the book, so it is 返す. 戻す would suggest you merely carried the book back into the building.

faq.q: What about returning a library book to its shelf inside the library?
faq.a: Then 戻す is right: 本を棚に戻す. The test is whether you are settling a loan (返す) or restoring a position (戻す).

faq.q: Can I say 元に返す?
faq.a: No — the set phrase is 元に戻す. 返す does not take 元に.

faq.q: Which one for replying to an email?
faq.a: 返す. メールを返す and 返事を返す are natural; 戻す would not be used here.

title: 持つ vs 取る
quickAnswer: 持つ is having something in your hand or owning it — and in practice you will meet it most often as 持っている, meaning "to have". 取る is the movement of reaching out and picking something up. You 取る the salt off the table, and then you 持つ it.
summary: 持つ is holding or owning something, usually as 持っている; 取る is reaching out and picking it up.

members.when: Use 持つ for having something with you, in your hand, or as a possession. For possession the form is almost always 持っている, not plain 持つ.

examples.ja: 傘を持っていますか。
examples.reading: かさをもっていますか。
examples.en: Do you have an umbrella with you?

examples.ja: 重そうですね。かばんを持ちましょうか。
examples.reading: おもそうですね。かばんをもちましょうか。
examples.en: That looks heavy. Shall I carry your bag?

members.when: Use 取る for the one-off action of taking something into your hand — reaching, picking up, passing. It also covers fixed uses such as 休みを取る and ノートを取る.

examples.ja: すみません、塩を取ってください。
examples.reading: すみません、しおをとってください。
examples.en: Excuse me, could you pass the salt?

examples.ja: 棚の上の箱を取ってもらえますか。
examples.reading: たなのうえのはこをとってもらえますか。
examples.en: Could you get the box down off the shelf for me?

contrast.ja: お金を持っていません。
contrast.reading: おかねをもっていません。
contrast.en: I don't have any money.
contrast.note: Possession, so 持っている. 取っていません would mean you did not pick any up.

contrast.ja: 机の上のペンを取って、書き始めました。
contrast.reading: つくえのうえのペンをとって、かきはじめました。
contrast.en: I picked up the pen on the desk and started writing.
contrast.note: The moment of reaching and grasping is 取る.

contrast.ja: 来週、三日休みを取ります。
contrast.reading: らいしゅう、みっかやすみをとります。
contrast.en: I'm taking three days off next week.
contrast.note: A fixed collocation: 休みを取る. 持つ is impossible here.

contrast.ja: 彼女は車を持っています。
contrast.reading: かのじょはくるまをもっています。
contrast.en: She has a car.
contrast.note: Ownership over time — only 持っている.

mistakes.wrong: 傘を取っていますか。
mistakes.right: 傘を持っていますか。
mistakes.why: To ask whether someone has something with them, use 持っている. 取っている sounds like they are in the middle of grabbing one.

mistakes.wrong: 塩を持ってください。
mistakes.right: 塩を取ってください。
mistakes.why: At the table you want the salt passed to you, which is 取る. 持ってください asks the listener to hold it, which is not what you mean.

mistakes.wrong: 私は車を持つ。
mistakes.right: 私は車を持っています。
mistakes.why: Plain 持つ is not used for stating what you own. Japanese marks a continuing state with the 〜ている form.

faq.q: Why is it always 持っている and not 持つ?
faq.a: Because possession is a state, and Japanese marks states with 〜ている. Plain 持つ appears mostly in future or general statements, like 将来、家を持ちたい.

faq.q: Which one means "to bring"?
faq.a: Neither on its own — use 持っていく to take something there and 持ってくる to bring it here.

faq.q: Can 取る mean steal?
faq.a: It can, in context: 人の物を取る sounds like taking what isn't yours. For a clear "steal", the word is 盗む.

title: 乗る vs 乗せる
quickAnswer: 乗る is you getting on or into a vehicle; 乗せる is putting someone or something else on it — giving a person a lift, or loading luggage. バスに乗る means you board the bus; 友達を車に乗せる means you give your friend a ride.
summary: 乗る is you getting on a vehicle; 乗せる is putting someone or something else on it — a lift, or loading.

members.when: Use 乗る when the subject is the one boarding. The vehicle is marked with に: バスに乗る, 車に乗る.

examples.ja: 毎朝、七時のバスに乗ります。
examples.reading: まいあさ、しちじのバスにのります。
examples.en: I take the seven o'clock bus every morning.

examples.ja: 駅で電車に乗りました。
examples.reading: えきででんしゃにのりました。
examples.en: I got on the train at the station.

members.when: Use 乗せる when you put someone or something onto a vehicle or a surface. What is put on takes を and the place takes に: 友達を車に乗せる.

examples.ja: 駅まで友達を車に乗せました。
examples.reading: えきまでともだちをくるまにのせました。
examples.en: I gave my friend a lift as far as the station.

examples.ja: 荷物をトラックに乗せてください。
examples.reading: にもつをトラックにのせてください。
examples.en: Please load the luggage onto the truck.

contrast.ja: 子どもを自転車の後ろに乗せます。
contrast.reading: こどもをじてんしゃのうしろにのせます。
contrast.en: I put my child on the back of the bicycle.
contrast.note: Someone else is being put on, so 乗せる with を.

contrast.ja: 私も自転車に乗れます。
contrast.reading: わたしもじてんしゃにのれます。
contrast.en: I can ride a bicycle too.
contrast.note: The subject is the rider, so 乗る with に.

contrast.ja: 駅まで乗せていってくれませんか。
contrast.reading: えきまでのせていってくれませんか。
contrast.en: Could you give me a lift to the station?
contrast.note: Asking to be carried by someone else — 乗せる, here in the 〜ていく form.

contrast.ja: ケーキを皿に乗せました。
contrast.reading: ケーキをさらにのせました。
contrast.en: I put the cake on the plate.
contrast.note: 乗せる is not limited to vehicles; it is also placing something on top of a surface.

mistakes.wrong: 友達を車に乗りました。
mistakes.right: 友達を車に乗せました。
mistakes.why: 乗る cannot take a を object like this. If the person boarding is not the subject, you need 乗せる.

mistakes.wrong: 私はバスを乗ります。
mistakes.right: 私はバスに乗ります。
mistakes.why: 乗る marks the vehicle with に, not を.

faq.q: How do I say that someone gave me a ride?
faq.a: 乗せてくれました, or from your own side 乗せてもらいました: 駅まで乗せてもらいました.

faq.q: Does 乗せる only work for vehicles?
faq.a: No. Putting anything on top of a surface is のせる: 皿に乗せる, テーブルに乗せる. In that sense it is also written 載せる, especially for putting something on a list or in a publication.

faq.q: What about 乗る for a chair?
faq.a: For sitting on furniture, use 座る. 乗る means getting on top of something, so いすに乗る means standing on the chair.

title: 走る vs 駆ける
quickAnswer: 走る is the everyday word for running and covers essentially every situation a learner needs. 駆ける is literary — it suggests dashing or galloping, and in speech it appears mainly inside compounds like 駆け出す or 駆け寄る. If you are unsure, use 走る.
summary: 走る is the ordinary word for run; 駆ける is literary or means dashing, and learners rarely need it.

members.when: Use 走る for running in any ordinary sense: exercise, hurrying, and also vehicles moving along a road or a road running somewhere.

examples.ja: 毎朝、公園を走っています。
examples.reading: まいあさ、こうえんをはしっています。
examples.en: I run in the park every morning.

examples.ja: 遅れそうだったので、駅まで走りました。
examples.reading: おくれそうだったので、えきまではしりました。
examples.en: I was about to be late, so I ran to the station.

members.when: 駆ける belongs to written and literary Japanese — a horse galloping, a character dashing across a field. In speech you will almost only meet it inside compounds: 駆け出す for breaking into a run, 駆け寄る for rushing up to someone, 駆けつける for rushing to the scene.

examples.ja: 馬が野原を駆けていた。
examples.reading: うまがのはらをかけていた。
examples.en: A horse was galloping across the field.

examples.ja: 子どもが母親のもとへ駆け寄った。
examples.reading: こどもがははおやのもとへかけよった。
examples.en: The child rushed over to his mother.

contrast.ja: 健康のために毎日走ります。
contrast.reading: けんこうのためにまいにちはしります。
contrast.en: I run every day for my health.
contrast.note: Ordinary exercise. 駆ける here would sound like a line out of a novel.

contrast.ja: 知らせを聞いて病院に駆けつけた。
contrast.reading: しらせをきいてびょういんにかけつけた。
contrast.en: Hearing the news, he rushed to the hospital.
contrast.note: 駆けつける is the fixed word for rushing to where something has happened; there is no 走りつける.

contrast.ja: 電車が線路を走っています。
contrast.reading: でんしゃがせんろをはしっています。
contrast.en: A train is running along the track.
contrast.note: Vehicles only take 走る.

mistakes.wrong: 毎朝、駆けています。
mistakes.right: 毎朝、走っています。
mistakes.why: 駆ける is too literary for describing your daily jog; it sounds like narration rather than conversation.

mistakes.wrong: 車が道を駆けています。
mistakes.right: 車が道を走っています。
mistakes.why: 駆ける is for living things moving on their own legs. Vehicles take 走る.

faq.q: Do I need to learn 駆ける at all?
faq.a: Not for speaking — a learner rarely needs it. It is worth knowing passively for reading, and for the compounds 駆け出す, 駆け寄る and 駆けつける, which do turn up in ordinary conversation.

faq.q: Aren't there other words read かける?
faq.a: Yes — 掛ける, 賭ける, 欠ける and others share the reading. The kanji and the context tell them apart, and 駆ける is the rarest of them in speech.

faq.q: Is 駆ける faster than 走る?
faq.a: It carries a sense of dashing, but the difference is mostly register rather than measured speed. 速く走る is the normal way to say that someone runs fast.

title: 笑う vs 微笑む
quickAnswer: 笑う covers both laughing and smiling — it is the everyday word for either, and an adverb tells you which is meant. 微笑む is only a quiet, soundless smile, and it belongs to written or descriptive Japanese. In conversation a smile is usually にこにこ笑う or 笑顔, not 微笑む.
summary: 笑う covers both laughing and smiling; 微笑む is only a quiet, soundless smile and sounds literary.

members.when: Use 笑う for any laughing or smiling in ordinary speech. Adverbs show which is meant: 大きな声で笑う is laughing out loud, にこにこ笑う is smiling. It also covers being laughed at: 人に笑われる.

examples.ja: みんな大きな声で笑いました。
examples.reading: みんなおおきなこえでわらいました。
examples.en: Everyone laughed out loud.

examples.ja: 彼女はいつもにこにこ笑っています。
examples.reading: かのじょはいつもにこにこわらっています。
examples.en: She is always smiling.

members.when: Use 微笑む only for a soft, silent smile, and mainly in writing or narration. It never means laughing, and it is not used for laughing at someone.

examples.ja: 彼女は静かに微笑んだ。
examples.reading: かのじょはしずかにほほえんだ。
examples.en: She smiled quietly.

examples.ja: 赤ちゃんが私に微笑んだ。
examples.reading: あかちゃんがわたしにほほえんだ。
examples.en: The baby smiled at me.

contrast.ja: その話を聞いて、みんなが笑った。
contrast.reading: そのはなしをきいて、みんながわらった。
contrast.en: Everyone laughed when they heard that story.
contrast.note: Audible laughter, so 笑う only. 微笑む has no sound.

contrast.ja: 母は何も言わずに微笑んでいた。
contrast.reading: はははなにもいわずにほほえんでいた。
contrast.en: My mother was smiling without saying anything.
contrast.note: A still, quiet smile in narration is the home ground of 微笑む. 笑っていた is also correct here, just plainer.

contrast.ja: 失敗して、みんなに笑われました。
contrast.reading: しっぱいして、みんなにわらわれました。
contrast.en: I messed up and everyone laughed at me.
contrast.note: Being laughed at uses the passive of 笑う; 微笑む cannot be used this way.

mistakes.wrong: 友達と話しながら微笑みました。
mistakes.right: 友達と話しながら笑いました。
mistakes.why: In everyday conversation about yourself, 微笑む sounds like a novel describing you from the outside. Use 笑う.

mistakes.wrong: おもしろくて微笑んでしまった。
mistakes.right: おもしろくて笑ってしまった。
mistakes.why: Something funny produces laughter, and 微笑む excludes sound entirely.

faq.q: How do I make clear I mean smiling, not laughing?
faq.a: Add an adverb or use the noun: にこにこ笑う, 笑顔で, or 笑顔になる. Native speakers rely on adverbs and context far more than on switching to 微笑む.

faq.q: Is 微笑む wrong, then?
faq.a: No — it is correct, just a different register. It is common in fiction, lyrics and descriptive writing, and the noun 微笑み is used more often than the verb.

faq.q: What about ほほえましい?
faq.a: That is a related but separate adjective meaning heartwarming, used of a scene rather than of a person's face.

title: 休む vs 眠る
quickAnswer: 休む is resting, and above all taking a day off work or school: 今日は会社を休みます. 眠る is actually being asleep. You can 休む all day without sleeping at all, and taking a day off never uses 眠る.
summary: 休む means to rest or take a day off work or school; 眠る means to be asleep.

members.when: Use 休む for taking time off — school, work, a lesson — with を marking what you are absent from, and for pausing to rest. It says nothing about whether you sleep.

examples.ja: かぜをひいたので、今日は会社を休みます。
examples.reading: かぜをひいたので、きょうはかいしゃをやすみます。
examples.en: I caught a cold, so I'm taking today off work.

examples.ja: 疲れたので、少し休みましょう。
examples.reading: つかれたので、すこしやすみましょう。
examples.en: I'm tired, so let's rest a little.

members.when: Use 眠る for the state of being asleep and for how well you slept. It never takes を for a place you are absent from.

examples.ja: 赤ちゃんはもう眠っています。
examples.reading: あかちゃんはもうねむっています。
examples.en: The baby is already asleep.

examples.ja: 昨日はよく眠れませんでした。
examples.reading: きのうはよくねむれませんでした。
examples.en: I couldn't sleep well last night.

contrast.ja: 熱があるので学校を休みました。
contrast.reading: ねつがあるのでがっこうをやすみました。
contrast.en: I had a fever, so I was absent from school.
contrast.note: Absence from an institution — only 休む, and the institution takes を.

contrast.ja: 薬を飲んだら、よく眠れました。
contrast.reading: くすりをのんだら、よくねむれました。
contrast.en: After taking the medicine I slept well.
contrast.note: The quality of sleep is 眠る. 休めました would mean you got some rest, not that you slept.

contrast.ja: 一日中家で休んでいましたが、あまり眠っていません。
contrast.reading: いちにちじゅういえでやすんでいましたが、あまりねむっていません。
contrast.en: I rested at home all day, but I didn't sleep much.
contrast.note: The two come apart cleanly here: resting without sleeping is perfectly ordinary.

contrast.ja: お先に休みます。
contrast.reading: おさきにやすみます。
contrast.en: I'll turn in now.
contrast.note: 休む does have a polite sense of retiring to bed, which is why the pair feels close — but it is a set, slightly formal expression.

mistakes.wrong: 今日は会社を眠ります。
mistakes.right: 今日は会社を休みます。
mistakes.why: 眠る is about being asleep and cannot take a workplace or school with を. Taking a day off is always 休む.

mistakes.wrong: 少し眠りましょう。
mistakes.right: 少し休みましょう。
mistakes.why: If you only mean a break — sitting down, stopping work — 眠る commits you to actually falling asleep.

faq.q: Can 休む mean sleep?
faq.a: Only in the polite お休みなさい and in 休む used for retiring to bed, which is formal. For a plain statement that you sleep, use 寝る or 眠る.

faq.q: How do I say I am taking a day off?
faq.a: 会社を休みます, or 休みを取ります with 取る. For paid leave the usual phrase is 有給を取る.

faq.q: Is 休む used for a shop being closed?
faq.a: Yes: 店は月曜日に休みます, and the noun 定休日 names the regular closing day.

title: 寝る vs 眠る
quickAnswer: 寝る is the act — going to bed or lying down — while 眠る is the state of being asleep. That is why 寝られない means you cannot get to bed and 眠れない means you are in bed but sleep will not come. For saying you go to bed at eleven, it is always 寝る.
summary: 寝る is going to bed or lying down; 眠る is being asleep. 寝られない and 眠れない are different complaints.

members.when: Use 寝る for going to bed, lying down, and sleeping as a daily routine. It is the everyday word and the one you want in almost all conversation.

examples.ja: いつも十一時に寝ます。
examples.reading: いつもじゅういちじにねます。
examples.en: I always go to bed at eleven.

examples.ja: ソファに寝ていました。
examples.reading: ソファにねていました。
examples.en: I was lying on the sofa.

members.when: Use 眠る for being asleep and for the quality of sleep. Because it describes a condition, it pairs with ぐっすり and よく, and with the potential form 眠れる.

examples.ja: 子どもはぐっすり眠っています。
examples.reading: こどもはぐっすりねむっています。
examples.en: The child is sleeping soundly.

examples.ja: 暑くてなかなか眠れませんでした。
examples.reading: あつくてなかなかねむれませんでした。
examples.en: It was hot and I could hardly get to sleep.

contrast.ja: 昨日は早く寝ましたが、眠れませんでした。
contrast.reading: きのうははやくねましたが、ねむれませんでした。
contrast.en: I went to bed early yesterday, but I couldn't get to sleep.
contrast.note: The clearest sentence for this pair: the act happened, the state did not.

contrast.ja: 隣がうるさくて眠れない。
contrast.reading: となりがうるさくてねむれない。
contrast.en: The neighbours are noisy and I can't get to sleep.
contrast.note: You are already in bed and sleep will not come, so 眠れない.

contrast.ja: 仕事が終わらなくて、まだ寝られない。
contrast.reading: しごとがおわらなくて、まだねられない。
contrast.en: My work isn't finished, so I can't go to bed yet.
contrast.note: Here the obstacle is to the act of going to bed, so 寝られない is right.

contrast.ja: 授業中に寝てしまいました。
contrast.reading: じゅぎょうちゅうにねてしまいました。
contrast.en: I fell asleep during class.
contrast.note: Everyday dozing off is 寝る. 眠ってしまいました is possible but describes the state from the outside.

mistakes.wrong: 毎日十一時に眠ります。
mistakes.right: 毎日十一時に寝ます。
mistakes.why: A bedtime is an action at a clock time, which is 寝る. 眠る would claim you fall asleep on the dot every night.

mistakes.wrong: 昨日はよく寝られませんでした。
mistakes.right: 昨日はよく眠れませんでした。
mistakes.why: If you mean that sleep would not come, 眠れない is the natural complaint. 寝られない is heard too, but it literally points at not being able to get to bed.

faq.q: Which one should I use by default?
faq.a: 寝る. It is N5, far more frequent, and covers going to bed, sleeping and lying down. Reach for 眠る when you are talking about being asleep or about how well you slept.

faq.q: Is 寝られない just wrong for insomnia?
faq.a: Not wrong — many speakers say 寝られない for it, and 寝つけない is common too. But 眠れない is the precise word, and the one in 眠れない夜.

faq.q: Can 寝る mean lying down without sleeping?
faq.a: Yes, that is a genuine use: ソファに寝る means lying on the sofa, sleep or no sleep. 眠る cannot mean that.

title: 食べる vs 飲む
quickAnswer: 食べる is for things you chew, 飲む for things that go down without chewing — and Japanese counts more things as 飲む than English does: medicine is 薬を飲む, never 薬を食べる. Soup is 飲む when you drink it from a bowl or cup and 食べる when you eat it with a spoon and it has solid pieces in it.
summary: 食べる is for what you chew, 飲む for what you swallow. Medicine is always 飲む; soup and jelly depend on how you take them.

members.when: Use 食べる when the thing is chewed, bitten or spooned up as solid food. Anything with pieces in it, and anything you eat with chopsticks or a fork, is 食べる.

examples.ja: ゼリーを食べます。
examples.reading: ぜりーをたべます。
examples.en: I eat jelly.

examples.ja: 具がたくさん入ったスープを食べました。
examples.reading: ぐがたくさんはいったすーぷをたべました。
examples.en: I ate a soup with a lot of ingredients in it.

members.when: Use 飲む when the thing passes down the throat without chewing: liquids, and also pills, capsules and powdered medicine. If you tip it from a cup or swallow it whole, it is 飲む.

examples.ja: 頭が痛いので薬を飲みました。
examples.reading: あたまがいたいのでくすりをのみました。
examples.en: I had a headache, so I took some medicine.

examples.ja: カップのスープを飲みます。
examples.reading: かっぷのすーぷをのみます。
examples.en: I drink the soup from the cup.

contrast.ja: 薬を飲む時間です。
contrast.reading: くすりをのむじかんです。
contrast.en: It's time to take your medicine.
contrast.note: Medicine is 飲む in Japanese even when it is a tablet you swallow dry. 薬を食べる is not said.

contrast.ja: スープをスプーンで食べます。
contrast.reading: すーぷをすぷーんでたべます。
contrast.en: I eat the soup with a spoon.
contrast.note: With a spoon and solid pieces, the same soup takes 食べる. Served in a mug and sipped, it takes 飲む.

contrast.ja: ゼリーを食べながら、ジュースを飲みます。
contrast.reading: ぜりーをたべながら、じゅーすをのみます。
contrast.en: I eat jelly while drinking juice.
contrast.note: Jelly is soft but has shape and is spooned, so it is 食べる; the juice beside it is 飲む.

contrast.ja: ヨーグルトを食べますか、飲みますか。
contrast.reading: よーぐるとをたべますか、のみますか。
contrast.en: Do you eat your yogurt or drink it?
contrast.note: Both are natural, because the verb follows the form: cup yogurt is 食べる, drinking yogurt is 飲む.

mistakes.wrong: 薬を食べます。
mistakes.right: 薬を飲みます。
mistakes.why: English says 'take medicine', so learners reach for 食べる for pills. Japanese fixes 薬 to 飲む whatever the shape of the medicine, and 薬を食べる sounds like you are chewing it as a snack.

mistakes.wrong: スープは必ず飲むと覚える。
mistakes.right: スープは飲むことも食べることもある。
mistakes.why: Learners who memorise 'soup is 飲む' over-apply it. A thick soup eaten with a spoon really is 食べる; the verb tracks how it is taken, not the word スープ.

mistakes.wrong: たばこを食べます。
mistakes.right: たばこを吸います。
mistakes.why: Neither verb works here. Smoking takes 吸う, and beginners sometimes guess 食べる or 飲む because the cigarette goes to the mouth.

faq.q: Why is medicine 飲む even when it's a tablet?
faq.a: Because 飲む covers swallowing without chewing, not just liquids. A tablet, a capsule and powdered medicine all go down whole, so all of them are 薬を飲む.

faq.q: Is soup 食べる or 飲む?
faq.a: Both, depending on how it is served. Miso soup sipped from the bowl or a soup drunk from a mug is 飲む; a thick soup with vegetables that you spoon up is 食べる.

faq.q: What about jelly and pudding?
faq.a: ゼリー and プリン are normally 食べる because you spoon them. A drinkable jelly in a pouch, though, is 飲む — again the form decides.

title: 置く vs 入れる
quickAnswer: 置く means to set something down on top of a surface, and 入れる means to put something inside a container or space. 机の上に置く is on the desk; かばんに入れる is in the bag — if the thing ends up enclosed by something, use 入れる.
summary: 置く puts something down on a surface; 入れる puts it inside something. On the desk is 置く, in the bag is 入れる.

members.when: Use 置く when the object comes to rest on a surface and stays visible: a table, the floor, a shelf. The place is marked with 〜に, often with 上 or ここ.

examples.ja: かぎをテーブルの上に置きました。
examples.reading: かぎをてーぶるのうえにおきました。
examples.en: I put the keys on the table.

examples.ja: 重いので、荷物をここに置きます。
examples.reading: おもいので、にもつをここにおきます。
examples.en: It's heavy, so I'll set the luggage down here.

members.when: Use 入れる when the object goes inside something — a bag, a box, a pocket, a fridge, a cup. It also covers adding an ingredient into food or drink.

examples.ja: 牛乳を冷蔵庫に入れてください。
examples.reading: ぎゅうにゅうをれいぞうこにいれてください。
examples.en: Please put the milk in the fridge.

examples.ja: コーヒーに砂糖を入れますか。
examples.reading: こーひーにさとうをいれますか。
examples.en: Would you like sugar in your coffee?

contrast.ja: 本を机の上に置きます。
contrast.reading: ほんをつくえのうえにおきます。
contrast.en: I put the book on the desk.
contrast.note: The book rests on the surface and nothing encloses it, so 置く.

contrast.ja: 本をかばんに入れます。
contrast.reading: ほんをかばんにいれます。
contrast.en: I put the book in the bag.
contrast.note: Same book, but now it goes inside a container, so 入れる. 本をかばんに置く would sound like you balanced it on top of the bag.

contrast.ja: 財布をポケットに入れた。
contrast.reading: さいふをぽけっとにいれた。
contrast.en: I put my wallet in my pocket.
contrast.note: A pocket is an enclosed space; 置く is impossible here.

contrast.ja: お茶を入れましょうか。
contrast.reading: おちゃをいれましょうか。
contrast.en: Shall I make some tea?
contrast.note: A set phrase: pouring tea into a cup is 入れる, and it is the ordinary way to say 'make tea'.

mistakes.wrong: かばんに本を置きます。
mistakes.right: かばんに本を入れます。
mistakes.why: English 'put' covers both, so learners default to 置く. Using 置く with a container makes it sound like the book is sitting on top of the bag rather than inside it.

mistakes.wrong: コーヒーに砂糖を置きます。
mistakes.right: コーヒーに砂糖を入れます。
mistakes.why: Adding anything into a food or drink is 入れる. 置く would mean you set a sugar cube down beside the cup.

faq.q: How do I decide when the place could be either?
faq.a: Ask whether the thing ends up surrounded. On a shelf, on a desk, on the floor: 置く. In a drawer, in a box, in a bag: 入れる. 棚に置く and 棚に入れる are both possible and mean different things — on the shelf versus inside the cupboard.

faq.q: Why is making tea お茶を入れる?
faq.a: Because the tea goes into the cup. It is a fixed expression for preparing and serving tea, and お茶を置く would only mean setting the cup down.

faq.q: Is 置く also used for leaving something somewhere?
faq.a: Yes. 荷物を置いていく means to leave your luggage behind, and 置いておく means to leave something as it is. That sense never transfers to 入れる.

title: 渡す vs 与える
quickAnswer: 渡す is the everyday verb for handing something over — you physically pass it to someone. 与える is formal and often abstract, used for bestowing something from a higher position (影響を与える, チャンスを与える) or for feeding animals. Handing a friend a pen is ペンを渡す; ペンを与える sounds like you are granting them a favour.
summary: 渡す is handing something over in daily life; 与える is formal, often abstract giving from above, as in 影響を与える.

members.when: Use 渡す for the physical act of passing an object to another person, whoever they are. It is neutral and normal in conversation.

examples.ja: この書類を部長に渡してください。
examples.reading: このしょるいをぶちょうにわたしてください。
examples.en: Please hand these documents to the manager.

examples.ja: 友だちにペンを渡しました。
examples.reading: ともだちにぺんをわたしました。
examples.en: I handed my friend a pen.

members.when: Use 与える in writing and formal speech, for giving something the other side cannot simply take — an opportunity, an influence, damage — or for giving food to animals. It carries a sense of the giver being above the receiver.

examples.ja: この事件は社会に大きな影響を与えた。
examples.reading: このじけんはしゃかいにおおきなえいきょうをあたえた。
examples.en: This incident had a big influence on society.

examples.ja: 動物にえさを与えないでください。
examples.reading: どうぶつにえさをあたえないでください。
examples.en: Please do not feed the animals.

contrast.ja: 先生にレポートを渡しました。
contrast.reading: せんせいにれぽーとをわたしました。
contrast.en: I handed my report to the teacher.
contrast.note: A physical object passed hand to hand, so 渡す, even though the teacher is senior to you.

contrast.ja: 台風は町に大きな被害を与えた。
contrast.reading: たいふうはまちにおおきなひがいをあたえた。
contrast.en: The typhoon caused great damage to the town.
contrast.note: Nothing is handed over; 被害 and 影響 are abstract, and 与える is the fixed choice.

contrast.ja: 若い社員にチャンスを与えたい。
contrast.reading: わかいしゃいんにちゃんすをあたえたい。
contrast.en: I want to give the young staff a chance.
contrast.note: An opportunity is granted from a position of authority, which is exactly 与える territory.

contrast.ja: 受付でパンフレットを渡されました。
contrast.reading: うけつけでぱんふれっとをわたされました。
contrast.en: I was handed a pamphlet at the reception desk.
contrast.note: Ordinary handing over in daily life — 与えられました here would sound oddly grand.

mistakes.wrong: 友だちにペンを与えました。
mistakes.right: 友だちにペンを渡しました。
mistakes.why: 与える puts the speaker above the receiver, so using it with a friend and an everyday object sounds pompous, as if you were bestowing the pen on them.

mistakes.wrong: この映画は私に影響を渡した。
mistakes.right: この映画は私に影響を与えた。
mistakes.why: 影響, 被害 and 印象 take 与える as a set collocation. 渡す only works for things that can literally change hands.

mistakes.wrong: 先生にプレゼントを与えました。
mistakes.right: 先生にプレゼントを渡しました。
mistakes.why: Giving upward to a superior can never be 与える. If you want to be polite, 差し上げました is the humble option.

faq.q: Can I use 与える to a teacher or a boss?
faq.a: No. 与える looks down from the giver to the receiver, so using it toward someone above you is rude. Use 渡す, or the humble 差し上げる.

faq.q: Is 与える the same as あげる?
faq.a: They overlap in meaning but not in register. あげる is the everyday spoken verb, 与える belongs to writing, news and formal announcements, and it is the only natural one with abstract nouns like 影響.

faq.q: Why is feeding animals えさを与える?
faq.a: Because the giver is clearly above the receiver and it is standard written style, which is why zoo and park signs use it. In casual speech people also say えさをあげる.

title: 集める vs 拾う
quickAnswer: 集める means bringing many things or people together into one place on purpose, and 拾う means picking something up off the ground with your hand. You 集める stamps as a collection over years; you 拾う a wallet you happen to find on the street.
summary: 集める is gathering things together deliberately; 拾う is picking something up off the ground, often by chance.

members.when: Use 集める when several things or people are brought together into one place — a collection, money for a gift, students in a classroom, information for a report.

examples.ja: レポートのために資料を集めています。
examples.reading: れぽーとのためにしりょうをあつめています。
examples.en: I'm gathering materials for my report.

examples.ja: プレゼントのお金をみんなから集めました。
examples.reading: ぷれぜんとのおかねをみんなからあつめました。
examples.en: I collected money from everyone for the present.

members.when: Use 拾う for the physical action of lifting something off the ground or floor. The thing is usually one item, and often you did not expect to find it.

examples.ja: 公園でごみを拾いました。
examples.reading: こうえんでごみをひろいました。
examples.en: I picked up litter in the park.

examples.ja: 落ちた鉛筆を拾ってくれませんか。
examples.reading: おちたえんぴつをひろってくれませんか。
examples.en: Could you pick up the pencil that fell?

contrast.ja: 道で財布を拾いました。
contrast.reading: みちでさいふをひろいました。
contrast.en: I found a wallet on the street.
contrast.note: One object, off the ground, by chance — 拾う. 財布を集める would mean you collect wallets as a hobby.

contrast.ja: 切手を集めています。
contrast.reading: きってをあつめています。
contrast.en: I collect stamps.
contrast.note: A deliberate collection built up over time, which 拾う cannot express.

contrast.ja: みんなでごみを拾って、一か所に集めました。
contrast.reading: みんなでごみをひろって、いっかしょにあつめました。
contrast.en: We picked up the litter and gathered it in one place.
contrast.note: The two verbs sit side by side: 拾う is each lifting action, 集める is bringing it all together.

contrast.ja: 駅の前でタクシーを拾った。
contrast.reading: えきのまえでたくしーをひろった。
contrast.en: I caught a taxi in front of the station.
contrast.note: An idiom: flagging down a passing taxi is 拾う, because you take what happens to come by.

mistakes.wrong: 道でごみを集めました。
mistakes.right: 道でごみを拾いました。
mistakes.why: English 'pick up litter' and 'collect litter' are both natural, but in Japanese the bending-down action is 拾う. 集める describes the pile you end up with, not the picking.

mistakes.wrong: 切手を拾っています。
mistakes.right: 切手を集めています。
mistakes.why: A hobby collection is 集める. 切手を拾う would mean you literally found stamps lying on the ground.

faq.q: Can I use both in the same sentence?
faq.a: Yes, and it is common: ごみを拾って集める — pick the pieces up one by one, then gather them together. They describe different stages, not competing choices.

faq.q: Does 拾う always mean finding something by accident?
faq.a: Not always. Volunteer litter-picking is planned, and it is still 拾う, because the verb describes lifting something from the ground. The 'by chance' feeling comes mostly with things like 財布を拾う.

faq.q: Why is catching a taxi タクシーを拾う?
faq.a: It is a set expression for hailing a taxi on the street. It is not used for taxis booked by phone or app, which take 呼ぶ.

title: 数える vs 計る
quickAnswer: 数える is counting things one by one to get a number — people, coins, pages. 計る (はかる) is measuring a quantity with an instrument, above all time and temperature: 時間を計る, 体温を計る. If you can point at each item and say one, two, three, it is 数える.
summary: 数える counts separate things one by one; 計る measures a quantity such as time or temperature with an instrument.

members.when: Use 数える when the things are separate and countable and you want to know how many. It always ends in a number of items.

examples.ja: 教室の人数を数えました。
examples.reading: きょうしつのにんずうをかぞえました。
examples.en: I counted the number of people in the classroom.

examples.ja: お金を一枚ずつ数えてください。
examples.reading: おかねをいちまいずつかぞえてください。
examples.en: Please count the money one note at a time.

members.when: Use 計る when you measure how much of something there is, using a clock, a thermometer or a similar device. It is the standard kanji for time and temperature.

examples.ja: ストップウォッチで時間を計ります。
examples.reading: すとっぷうぉっちでじかんをはかります。
examples.en: I'll time it with a stopwatch.

examples.ja: 熱があるので体温を計りました。
examples.reading: ねつがあるのでたいおんをはかりました。
examples.en: I had a fever, so I took my temperature.

contrast.ja: 本が何冊あるか数えます。
contrast.reading: ほんがなんさつあるかかぞえます。
contrast.en: I'll count how many books there are.
contrast.note: Separate items, so 数える. A number of books is not something you measure.

contrast.ja: 五十メートル走るのに何秒かかるか計った。
contrast.reading: ごじゅうめーとるはしるのになんびょうかかるかはかった。
contrast.en: I timed how many seconds it takes to run fifty metres.
contrast.note: Seconds are a continuous quantity read off a device, so 計る, even though the answer is a number.

contrast.ja: 子どもが一から十まで数えられるようになった。
contrast.reading: こどもがいちからじゅうまでかぞえられるようになった。
contrast.en: My child can now count from one to ten.
contrast.note: Reciting numbers is always 数える.

contrast.ja: 毎朝、体温を計っています。
contrast.reading: まいあさ、たいおんをはかっています。
contrast.en: I take my temperature every morning.
contrast.note: 体温 pairs with はかる, and 計 is the usual kanji for it.

mistakes.wrong: 時間を数えます。
mistakes.right: 時間を計ります。
mistakes.why: Learners map 'count the time' from English. Time is measured, not counted, so 計る is the natural verb; 時間を数える only works in the special sense of counting down the days.

mistakes.wrong: 人数を計ります。
mistakes.right: 人数を数えます。
mistakes.why: People are discrete, so they are counted. はかる with 人数 sounds like you are weighing a crowd.

faq.q: What is the difference between 計る, 測る and 量る?
faq.a: All three read はかる. 計る is used mainly for time and temperature, 測る for length, distance, area and depth, and 量る for weight and volume. The boundary is not absolute and writers differ, especially between 測る and 量る; when unsure, writing はかる in kana is safe and common.

faq.q: Which one do I use for height and weight?
faq.a: Height is normally 身長を測る and weight 体重を量る, following the length-versus-weight split. Many people write both in kana.

faq.q: Is 数える only for physical objects?
faq.a: No. You can count anything discrete — days, mistakes, reasons. 数えきれない, 'too many to count', is a common set phrase.

title: 安い vs 低い
quickAnswer: 安い means cheap — it is only about cost. 低い means low in physical height or on a scale, like a mountain, a voice or a temperature. The price itself is 値段が安い, not 値段が低い, so a cheap shop is 安い店 and a short person is 背が低い.
summary: 安い is cheap in price; 低い is low in height or level. Say 値段が安い, never 値段が低い.

members.when: Use 安い only about money: the price of goods, tickets, rent, a shop's prices. It can describe the thing being sold or the price itself.

examples.ja: この店は野菜が安いです。
examples.reading: このみせはやさいがやすいです。
examples.en: The vegetables are cheap at this shop.

examples.ja: もっと安いホテルを探しています。
examples.reading: もっとやすいほてるをさがしています。
examples.en: I'm looking for a cheaper hotel.

members.when: Use 低い for physical height — a mountain, a building, a person's stature — and for anything on a scale: temperature, a voice, a level, a percentage.

examples.ja: 今日は気温が低いです。
examples.reading: きょうはきおんがひくいです。
examples.en: The temperature is low today.

examples.ja: 弟は私より背が低いです。
examples.reading: おとうとはわたしよりせがひくいです。
examples.en: My little brother is shorter than me.

contrast.ja: この店は値段が安いです。
contrast.reading: このみせはねだんがやすいです。
contrast.en: The prices at this shop are low.
contrast.note: English says 'low prices', but Japanese pairs 値段 with 安い. 値段が低い is the classic learner error.

contrast.ja: この山は低いので、子どもでも登れます。
contrast.reading: このやまはひくいので、こどもでものぼれます。
contrast.en: This mountain is low, so even children can climb it.
contrast.note: Physical height, so only 低い works.

contrast.ja: 彼は声が低い。
contrast.reading: かれはこえがひくい。
contrast.en: He has a deep voice.
contrast.note: Pitch is a scale, so 低い; 安い has no such sense.

contrast.ja: 安いレストランですが、味はいいです。
contrast.reading: やすいれすとらんですが、あじはいいです。
contrast.en: It's a cheap restaurant, but the food is good.
contrast.note: Cost only, so 安い; 低いレストラン would describe a short building.

mistakes.wrong: 値段が低いです。
mistakes.right: 値段が安いです。
mistakes.why: 'Low price' translates word for word into 値段が低い, but the standard collocation is 値段が安い. Formal writing does use compounds like 低価格, which is why the mistake feels plausible, but 値段が低い is not natural in ordinary sentences.

mistakes.wrong: この山は安いです。
mistakes.right: この山は低いです。
mistakes.why: 安い can never mean physically low. This sentence says the mountain is inexpensive.

mistakes.wrong: 気温が安いです。
mistakes.right: 気温が低いです。
mistakes.why: Anything on a measured scale — temperature, level, rate — takes 低い. 安い is restricted to money.

faq.q: So is 値段が低い always wrong?
faq.a: In everyday sentences, yes — use 値段が安い. You will meet 低い with price-related nouns in formal economic writing, such as 価格水準が低い, but that is a different register and not a model for conversation.

faq.q: Does 安い have a negative meaning too?
faq.a: It can. 安っぽい means cheap-looking or tacky, and phrases like 安い男 suggest someone with no self-respect. Plain 安い about goods is neutral or positive.

faq.q: How do I say someone is short?
faq.a: 背が低い. Do not use 短い, which is for objects like a rope or a skirt, and never 安い.

title: 難しい vs 厳しい
quickAnswer: 難しい means hard to do or hard to understand — a task, a kanji, an exam. 厳しい means strict or severe: a person who does not let things slide, or conditions that are harsh. 厳しい先生 is a teacher who enforces the rules, not a teacher whose lessons are difficult.
summary: 難しい is hard to do or understand; 厳しい is strict or harsh. 厳しい先生 means strict, not difficult.

members.when: Use 難しい when something takes effort or skill, or cannot easily be understood or achieved: questions, books, kanji, problems, plans that are hard to carry out.

examples.ja: この漢字は読み方が難しいです。
examples.reading: このかんじはよみかたがむずかしいです。
examples.en: The reading of this kanji is difficult.

examples.ja: 今日中に終わらせるのは難しいです。
examples.reading: きょうじゅうにおわらせるのはむずかしいです。
examples.en: Finishing it today would be difficult.

members.when: Use 厳しい for people or rules that demand a lot and forgive little, and for harsh conditions such as weather, competition or a financial situation.

examples.ja: この学校は規則が厳しいです。
examples.reading: このがっこうはきそくがきびしいです。
examples.en: The rules at this school are strict.

examples.ja: 北海道の冬は寒さが厳しい。
examples.reading: ほっかいどうのふゆはさむさがきびしい。
examples.en: Winters in Hokkaido are severe.

contrast.ja: 厳しい先生ですが、教え方は分かりやすいです。
contrast.reading: きびしいせんせいですが、おしえかたはわかりやすいです。
contrast.en: He's a strict teacher, but his explanations are easy to follow.
contrast.note: Proof that 厳しい is about attitude, not difficulty — the same teacher can be strict and easy to understand.

contrast.ja: この試験は難しいです。
contrast.reading: このしけんはむずかしいです。
contrast.en: This exam is difficult.
contrast.note: The questions are hard, so 難しい. 厳しい試験 would suggest harsh marking or harsh conditions instead.

contrast.ja: 厳しく注意されました。
contrast.reading: きびしくちゅういされました。
contrast.en: I was told off sternly.
contrast.note: Only 厳しい has this sense of severity in how someone treats you.

contrast.ja: その計画は実現が難しい。
contrast.reading: そのけいかくはじつげんがむずかしい。
contrast.en: That plan is difficult to realise.
contrast.note: Hard to achieve, so 難しい.

mistakes.wrong: この問題は厳しいです。
mistakes.right: この問題は難しいです。
mistakes.why: A question cannot be strict. 厳しい with 問題 would only work in the sense of a grim situation, not a hard exercise.

mistakes.wrong: 父は難しい人です。
mistakes.right: 父は厳しい人です。
mistakes.why: 難しい人 exists but means an awkward person who is hard to deal with — not a strict parent. If you mean your father enforces rules, 厳しい is the word.

faq.q: Can 厳しい mean difficult?
faq.a: Indirectly. 厳しい状況 or 予算的に厳しい means the situation is tough or barely possible — harsh circumstances, not an intellectual challenge. For a hard task or question, use 難しい.

faq.q: Is 難しい人 the same as 厳しい人?
faq.a: No. 難しい人 is someone hard to please or hard to get along with; 厳しい人 is someone demanding who holds you to high standards. The second can be said with respect.

faq.q: How do I say a class is hard?
faq.a: 授業が難しい for the content. If the teacher demands a lot and punishes lateness, that is 授業が厳しい or 先生が厳しい.

title: 優しい vs 易しい
quickAnswer: Both are read やさしい, and only the kanji tells them apart: 優しい means kind or gentle to people, and 易しい means easy to do or understand. 優しい先生 is a kind teacher; 易しい問題 is an easy question. In speech the context decides, and in writing 易しい is often replaced by kana やさしい or by 簡単な.
summary: 優しい and 易しい are both やさしい: 優しい is kind to people, 易しい is easy to do. Only the kanji separates them.

members.when: Use 優しい about people and how they treat others — kind, gentle, considerate. It also describes gentle voices and things that are gentle on the body or the environment.

examples.ja: 彼女はだれにでも優しいです。
examples.reading: かのじょはだれにでもやさしいです。
examples.en: She is kind to everyone.

examples.ja: この洗剤は手に優しい。
examples.reading: このせんざいはてにやさしい。
examples.en: This detergent is gentle on the hands.

members.when: Use 易しい about tasks and material that take little effort to do or understand: questions, books, explanations. It is the opposite of 難しい.

examples.ja: この問題は易しいので、すぐできます。
examples.reading: このもんだいはやさしいので、すぐできます。
examples.en: This question is easy, so I can do it right away.

examples.ja: 初心者には易しい日本語の本がいいです。
examples.reading: しょしんしゃにはやさしいにほんごのほんがいいです。
examples.en: For beginners, easy Japanese books are good.

contrast.ja: 優しい先生に易しい問題を出してもらった。
contrast.reading: やさしいせんせいにやさしいもんだいをだしてもらった。
contrast.en: The kind teacher gave me an easy question.
