contrast.note: The same pronunciation twice in one sentence, and only the kanji separates the kind teacher from the easy question.

contrast.ja: お年寄りに優しい町です。
contrast.reading: おとしよりにやさしいまちです。
contrast.en: It's a town that is kind to elderly people.
contrast.note: The 〜に優しい pattern means considerate toward someone. 環境に優しい, eco-friendly, works the same way.

contrast.ja: この説明は易しくて分かりやすい。
contrast.reading: このせつめいはやさしくてわかりやすい。
contrast.en: This explanation is easy and clear.
contrast.note: Ease of understanding, so 易しい. Written with 優 it would claim the explanation is kind-hearted.

contrast.ja: 言うは易く行うは難し。
contrast.reading: いうはやすくおこなうはかたし。
contrast.en: Easier said than done.
contrast.note: A classical proverb where 易 keeps its 'easy' sense — a useful hook for remembering which kanji is which.

mistakes.wrong: 優しい問題でした。
mistakes.right: 易しい問題でした。
mistakes.why: Picking the wrong kanji when typing or writing is the real mistake here, and it makes the sentence say the question was kind-hearted. Spoken aloud it is fine, which is why learners never notice the error until they write.

mistakes.wrong: 易しい先生が好きです。
mistakes.right: 優しい先生が好きです。
mistakes.why: Reversed the other way: 易しい先生 reads as a teacher who is easy to do, which is not a meaning Japanese has for a person.

faq.q: How do I know which one someone means when they speak?
faq.a: By what the adjective describes. A person is almost always 優しい, and a question, book or explanation is 易しい. Ambiguity is rare in practice.

faq.q: Which kanji should I write for 'easy'?
faq.a: 易しい is correct, but in practice many writers use kana やさしい or switch to 簡単な to avoid confusion. 簡単 is the safest choice for beginners.

faq.q: What does 環境に優しい mean?
faq.a: Environmentally friendly. The 〜に優しい pattern extends the 'kind' sense to things that go easy on something — 体に優しい食事 is food that is gentle on your body.

title: 苦しい vs 辛い
quickAnswer: 苦しい is physical distress inside the body — you cannot breathe, your chest hurts. 辛い (read つらい) is emotional: something is hard to bear. Note that the same kanji 辛い is also read からい meaning "spicy", so the reading tells you which word it is.
summary: 苦しい is physical pain or breathlessness; 辛い (つらい) is emotionally hard. The same kanji read からい means spicy.

members.when: Use 苦しい when the body is in distress: breathing, chest, stomach. It also extends to a situation that squeezes you, especially money — 生活が苦しい means you can barely make ends meet.

examples.ja: 息が苦しいです。
examples.reading: いきがくるしいです。
examples.en: I can hardly breathe.

examples.ja: 生活が苦しいです。
examples.reading: せいかつがくるしいです。
examples.en: We are struggling to make ends meet.

members.when: Read つらい, 辛い describes something emotionally hard to endure — a painful goodbye, a gruelling job, a memory. Read からい, the very same kanji means spicy, so learners often see 辛い and say the wrong word.

examples.ja: 友だちと別れるのは辛いです。
examples.reading: ともだちとわかれるのはつらいです。
examples.en: Parting from a friend is hard.

examples.ja: このカレーは辛いです。
examples.reading: このカレーはからいです。
examples.en: This curry is spicy.

contrast.ja: 走りすぎて息が苦しいです。
contrast.reading: はしりすぎていきがくるしいです。
contrast.en: I ran too much and can hardly breathe.
contrast.note: Breathing is a body problem, so 苦しい. つらい here would sound like the running upset you emotionally.

contrast.ja: 毎日残業で辛いです。
contrast.reading: まいにちざんぎょうでつらいです。
contrast.en: Overtime every day is rough on me.
contrast.note: Nothing hurts physically; it wears you down mentally, so つらい.

contrast.ja: この料理は辛いですね。
contrast.reading: このりょうりはからいですね。
contrast.en: This dish is spicy, isn't it.
contrast.note: About food, 辛い is read からい and means spicy — 苦しい can never describe a taste.

contrast.ja: 胸が苦しくて病院へ行きました。
contrast.reading: むねがくるしくてびょういんへいきました。
contrast.en: My chest felt tight so I went to the hospital.
contrast.note: A physical symptom you can report to a doctor takes 苦しい.

mistakes.wrong: このカレーはつらいです。
mistakes.right: このカレーはからいです。
mistakes.why: The kanji is the same but food takes the からい reading. つらい about curry sounds like eating it is an emotional ordeal.

mistakes.wrong: 友だちと別れるのは苦しいです。
mistakes.right: 友だちと別れるのは辛いです。
mistakes.why: 苦しい points at the body. For heartache, Japanese uses つらい.

mistakes.wrong: お金がなくて辛い生活です。
mistakes.right: お金がなくて苦しい生活です。
mistakes.why: For a financially tight life the usual phrase is 生活が苦しい. つらい is not wrong about your feelings, but 苦しい is the word used for the situation itself.

faq.q: Is 辛い spicy or hard? How do I know?
faq.a: By the reading, and by what it describes. Food or taste means からい (spicy); a person, a job or a situation means つらい (hard to bear). Many writers put つらい in hiragana precisely to avoid the ambiguity.

faq.q: Can 苦しい ever describe feelings?
faq.a: Yes, in a heavy way — 胸が苦しい can describe an aching heart, and 苦しい立場 is a tight spot. But for ordinary "this is hard on me", つらい is the everyday word.

faq.q: Which one do I say when I'm sick?
faq.a: 苦しい. 息が苦しい, お腹が苦しい and 胸が苦しい are all symptoms. つらい is fine too if you mean the illness is wearing you down overall.

title: 怖い vs 恐ろしい
quickAnswer: 怖い describes your feeling — I am scared of it. 恐ろしい describes the thing itself as dreadful, and it belongs to a more written, dramatic register. Say 犬が怖い for your own fear; say 恐ろしい事故 about a horrific accident.
summary: 怖い is "I'm scared of it"; 恐ろしい is "it is dreadful" — more objective, more written, and much stronger.

members.when: The everyday spoken word for fear. Use it with 〜が怖い to name what frightens you, and about anything mildly scary: a dark street, a strict teacher, a horror film.

examples.ja: 犬が怖いです。
examples.reading: いぬがこわいです。
examples.en: I'm afraid of dogs.

examples.ja: 夜の道は怖いです。
examples.reading: よるのみちはこわいです。
examples.en: The road at night is scary.

members.when: Use 恐ろしい to call something dreadful in its own right — a disaster, a crime, a terrible power. It is stronger and more literary, and it is common in news and writing rather than casual chat.

examples.ja: 地震は本当に恐ろしいです。
examples.reading: じしんはほんとうにおそろしいです。
examples.en: Earthquakes are truly terrifying.

examples.ja: 恐ろしい事故が起きました。
examples.reading: おそろしいじこがおきました。
examples.en: A horrific accident happened.

contrast.ja: 私は虫が怖いです。
contrast.reading: わたしはむしがこわいです。
contrast.en: I'm scared of insects.
contrast.note: A personal fear takes 〜が怖い. 虫が恐ろしい would sound as if insects were a menace to humanity.

contrast.ja: 戦争は恐ろしいものです。
contrast.reading: せんそうはおそろしいものです。
contrast.en: War is a dreadful thing.
contrast.note: A judgement about the thing itself, not about your nerves, so 恐ろしい.

contrast.ja: 先生の顔が怖いです。
contrast.reading: せんせいのかおがこわいです。
contrast.en: The teacher's face is scary.
contrast.note: Everyday, half-joking fear — 怖い. 恐ろしい would be far too heavy here.

contrast.ja: 彼の記憶力は恐ろしいですね。
contrast.reading: かれのきおくりょくはおそろしいですね。
contrast.en: His memory is frighteningly good.
contrast.note: 恐ろしい can mean "awe-inspiring in scale", a use 怖い does not have.

mistakes.wrong: 犬が恐ろしいです。
mistakes.right: 犬が怖いです。
mistakes.why: For your own everyday fear, native speakers say 怖い. 恐ろしい makes the dog sound like a monster.

mistakes.wrong: そのニュースは怖かったですね。
mistakes.right: そのニュースは恐ろしかったですね。
mistakes.why: Not ungrammatical, but about a grave news event 恐ろしい fits the register. 怖い makes it sound like a personal jump scare.

faq.q: Is 恐ろしい just a stronger 怖い?
faq.a: Partly — it is stronger, but the real difference is direction. 怖い reports your emotion; 恐ろしい judges the thing. That is why 恐ろしい appears in writing and news far more than in conversation.

faq.q: Which one for a horror movie?
faq.a: 怖い映画 in normal speech. 恐ろしい映画 is possible but sounds like a critic writing about it.

faq.q: Can I use 恐ろしい as praise?
faq.a: Yes — 恐ろしいスピード or 恐ろしい才能, meaning "frighteningly impressive". 怖い is not used that way.

title: 静か vs 穏やか
quickAnswer: 静か is about sound: there is no noise. 穏やか is about calmness of manner or condition — gentle weather, a calm sea, a mild-tempered person. A 穏やかな人 is not a silent person; they are an even-tempered one.
summary: 静か means no noise; 穏やか means calm and gentle — weather, sea, temperament. 穏やかな人 is mild, not silent.

members.when: Use 静か when what matters is the absence of sound: a quiet library, a quiet town, telling children to be quiet. Of a person it means they do not talk much.

examples.ja: 図書館は静かです。
examples.reading: としょかんはしずかです。
examples.en: The library is quiet.

examples.ja: 静かにしてください。
examples.reading: しずかにしてください。
examples.en: Please be quiet.

members.when: Use 穏やか for something without disturbance or roughness: mild weather, a calm sea, a gentle personality, a peaceful conversation. Nothing about it requires silence.

examples.ja: 今日は海が穏やかです。
examples.reading: きょうはうみがおだやかです。
examples.en: The sea is calm today.

examples.ja: 祖母は穏やかな人です。
examples.reading: そぼはおだやかなひとです。
examples.en: My grandmother is a gentle person.

contrast.ja: この部屋は静かですね。
contrast.reading: このへやはしずかですね。
contrast.en: This room is quiet, isn't it.
contrast.note: Purely about noise level, so 静か. 穏やかな部屋 is not a normal phrase.

contrast.ja: 今日は穏やかな天気です。
contrast.reading: きょうはおだやかなてんきです。
contrast.en: The weather is mild today.
contrast.note: Weather is about wind and roughness, not sound — 穏やか only.

contrast.ja: 彼は穏やかな声で話しました。
contrast.reading: かれはおだやかなこえではなしました。
contrast.en: He spoke in a gentle voice.
contrast.note: He is speaking, so he is not silent; the point is that his manner was calm.

contrast.ja: 彼女は静かな人で、あまり話しません。
contrast.reading: かのじょはしずかなひとで、あまりはなしません。
contrast.en: She is a quiet person and doesn't talk much.
contrast.note: Of a person, 静か is specifically about talking little — a different claim from 穏やか.

mistakes.wrong: 今日は静かな天気です。
mistakes.right: 今日は穏やかな天気です。
mistakes.why: Weather has no volume. Calm, mild weather is 穏やか.

mistakes.wrong: 父は静かな性格です。
mistakes.right: 父は穏やかな性格です。
mistakes.why: If you mean he is even-tempered and does not get angry, that is 穏やか. 静かな性格 says only that he is untalkative.

faq.q: Can a person be both 静か and 穏やか?
faq.a: Yes, and many are — but they are separate claims. 静か says they are quiet; 穏やか says they are gentle and do not get worked up. A cheerful, chatty person can still be 穏やか.

faq.q: Which one do I use to ask someone to be quiet?
faq.a: 静かにしてください, always. 穏やかにして would mean "calm down", which is a different request.

faq.q: Is 穏やか too advanced for me?
faq.a: It is around N3, but it is worth knowing early because 静か simply cannot cover weather, the sea, or temperament.

title: 元気 vs 健康
quickAnswer: 元気 is about spirits and energy right now — lively, cheerful, feeling good. 健康 is medical health, the condition of your body over time. お元気ですか is a greeting like "how are you?", not a question about your medical condition.
summary: 元気 is lively spirits and energy now; 健康 is medical health. お元気ですか is a greeting, not a health question.

members.when: Use 元気 for energy and good spirits: an energetic child, feeling better after being down, greeting someone. 元気になる means you have perked up or recovered.

examples.ja: 元気な子供ですね。
examples.reading: げんきなこどもですね。
examples.en: What an energetic child.

examples.ja: お元気ですか。
examples.reading: おげんきですか。
examples.en: How are you?

members.when: Use 健康 for health as a bodily condition — check-ups, diet, a doctor's judgement. It is a noun as well as a な-adjective, so 健康のために and 健康にいい are very common.

examples.ja: 健康のために野菜を食べます。
examples.reading: けんこうのためにやさいをたべます。
examples.en: I eat vegetables for my health.

examples.ja: 祖父はとても健康です。
examples.reading: そふはとてもけんこうです。
examples.en: My grandfather is very healthy.

contrast.ja: お元気ですか。
contrast.reading: おげんきですか。
contrast.en: How are you?
contrast.note: A greeting. お健康ですか is not Japanese — you would be asking after someone's medical record.

contrast.ja: たばこは健康に悪いです。
contrast.reading: たばこはけんこうにわるいです。
contrast.en: Smoking is bad for your health.
contrast.note: A claim about the body over time, so 健康. 元気に悪い is not said.

contrast.ja: 病気が治って、また元気になりました。
contrast.reading: びょうきがなおって、またげんきになりました。
contrast.en: I got over my illness and I'm feeling myself again.
contrast.note: 元気になる is about getting your spirits and energy back.

contrast.ja: 毎年、健康診断を受けます。
contrast.reading: まいとし、けんこうしんだんをうけます。
contrast.en: I have a health check-up every year.
contrast.note: A fixed medical compound — 元気診断 does not exist.

mistakes.wrong: お健康ですか。
mistakes.right: お元気ですか。
mistakes.why: The greeting is fixed with 元気. Asking 健康 sounds like you suspect they are ill.

mistakes.wrong: 野菜は元気にいいです。
mistakes.right: 野菜は健康にいいです。
mistakes.why: "Good for your health" is 健康にいい. 元気 is a state you are in, not something food is good for.

mistakes.wrong: 元気な食事をしています。
mistakes.right: 健康的な食事をしています。
mistakes.why: A healthy diet is 健康的な食事. 元気 cannot describe food.

faq.q: If someone asks お元気ですか, am I lying if I'm on medication?
faq.a: No. The question is about how you are doing, not your medical state. はい、元気です is the normal answer even for someone with a long-term condition.

faq.q: Can 元気 and 健康 both describe a person?
faq.a: Yes, but differently. 元気なおじいさん is a sprightly grandpa; 健康なおじいさん is one whose test results are fine. Often both are true.

faq.q: Which do I use to say I recovered from a cold?
faq.a: 元気になりました. 健康になりました sounds like you fundamentally changed your constitution.

title: 危ない vs 危険
quickAnswer: The meaning is nearly the same; the register is not. 危ない is the everyday spoken word — 危ない！ is what you shout to warn someone. 危険 is the formal written word you see on signs, in news reports and in official notices.
summary: 危ない is the spoken, everyday "dangerous", and the shout of warning. 危険 is the formal word used on signs and in writing.

members.when: Use 危ない in conversation, and as an immediate shout of warning. It also covers "that was close" — 危なかった after a near miss.

examples.ja: 危ない！車が来るよ。
examples.reading: あぶない！くるまがくるよ。
examples.en: Look out! A car's coming.

examples.ja: 危ないですから、走らないでください。
examples.reading: あぶないですから、はしらないでください。
examples.en: It's dangerous, so please don't run.

members.when: Use 危険 in writing, signage and formal speech. As a noun it also names the danger itself: 危険がある, 危険を知らせる. On a sign, a single 危険 means DANGER.

examples.ja: ここで泳ぐのは危険です。
examples.reading: ここでおよぐのはきけんです。
examples.en: Swimming here is dangerous.

examples.ja: この工事現場は危険です。
examples.reading: このこうじげんばはきけんです。
examples.en: This construction site is dangerous.

contrast.ja: 危ない！
contrast.reading: あぶない！
contrast.en: Watch out!
contrast.note: A sudden warning is always 危ない. Shouting 危険 at a friend would sound like reading a sign aloud.

contrast.ja: 危険、立入禁止。
contrast.reading: きけん、たちいりきんし。
contrast.en: Danger — no entry.
contrast.note: Signs use the noun 危険. 危ない would look strangely chatty on a notice.

contrast.ja: この薬には危険があります。
contrast.reading: このくすりにはきけんがあります。
contrast.en: This medicine carries a risk.
contrast.note: Here danger is a thing you can have, and only 危険 is a noun. 危ない cannot take があります.

contrast.ja: その橋は古くて危ないよ。
contrast.reading: そのはしはふるくてあぶないよ。
contrast.en: That bridge is old and dangerous.
contrast.note: Casual speech to a friend takes 危ない.

mistakes.wrong: 危険！
mistakes.right: 危ない！
mistakes.why: As a spoken shout of warning, Japanese uses 危ない. 危険 is the label, not the cry.

mistakes.wrong: 危ないがあります。
mistakes.right: 危険があります。
mistakes.why: 危ない is an い-adjective and cannot be the subject of あります. Only the noun 危険 works there.

mistakes.wrong: 危ないな場所
mistakes.right: 危ない場所
mistakes.why: 危ない is an い-adjective, so it takes no な. The な-adjective is 危険, as in 危険な場所.

faq.q: Are they ever interchangeable?
faq.a: Often, yes. 危ない場所 and 危険な場所 both work and mean the same thing; only the tone differs. The distinction is mostly register, not meaning.

faq.q: Why do signs never say 危ない?
faq.a: Written and official Japanese prefers kanji compounds. 危険 is short, formal and instantly readable, which is exactly what signage wants.

faq.q: What does 危なかった mean on its own?
faq.a: "That was close!" — said after narrowly avoiding something. 危険でした would just be a flat statement that it was dangerous.

title: 新しい vs 新た
quickAnswer: 新しい is the everyday word for new and is what you need in almost every sentence. 新た is a written-register な-adjective used in phrases like 新たな課題 and 新たに始める; it means newly arisen or renewed rather than newly bought.
summary: 新しい is the everyday "new". 新た is written-register, takes な, and appears in phrases like 新たな課題 — learners mostly need 新しい.

members.when: Use 新しい for anything new in ordinary speech and writing: new shoes, a new car, a new friend, a new job. If you are unsure which to use, this is the right answer.

examples.ja: 新しい靴を買いました。
examples.reading: あたらしいくつをかいました。
examples.en: I bought new shoes.

examples.ja: この車は新しいです。
examples.reading: このくるまはあたらしいです。
examples.en: This car is new.

members.when: A written, formal word taking な before nouns and に as an adverb. It describes something newly arising or renewed — 新たな問題, 新たな課題, 決意を新たにする — rather than a new physical object.

examples.ja: 新たな問題が起きました。
examples.reading: あらたなもんだいがおきました。
examples.en: A new problem has come up.

examples.ja: 決意を新たにしました。
examples.reading: けついをあらたにしました。
examples.en: I renewed my resolve.

contrast.ja: 新しいかばんが欲しいです。
contrast.reading: あたらしいかばんがほしいです。
contrast.en: I want a new bag.
contrast.note: An ordinary object you buy takes 新しい. 新たなかばん would be odd and stiff.

contrast.ja: 会社は新たな計画を発表しました。
contrast.reading: かいしゃはあらたなけいかくをはっぴょうしました。
contrast.en: The company announced a new plan.
contrast.note: Formal announcement language, and the plan newly arises — 新た fits the register.

contrast.ja: 新たに三人が加わりました。
contrast.reading: あらたにさんにんがくわわりました。
contrast.en: Three more people newly joined.
contrast.note: For "newly, in addition", 新たに is the natural adverb; 新しく would not carry the "in addition" sense here.

contrast.ja: 新しい友だちができました。
contrast.reading: あたらしいともだちができました。
contrast.en: I made a new friend.
contrast.note: Everyday personal news — 新しい. 新たな友だち sounds like a press release.

mistakes.wrong: 新たい車
mistakes.right: 新しい車
mistakes.why: 新た is not an い-adjective. There is no 新たい — the two words simply have different endings.

mistakes.wrong: 新た問題
mistakes.right: 新たな問題
mistakes.why: 新た is a な-adjective, so it needs な before a noun.

mistakes.wrong: 新たなくつを買いました。
mistakes.right: 新しいくつを買いました。
mistakes.why: Grammatically fine but wrong register. For buying shoes, nobody says 新た.

faq.q: Do I really need 新た?
faq.a: Not for speaking. You need to recognise it in news, business writing and essays, where 新たな〜 is common. For producing sentences, 新しい covers almost everything.

faq.q: Is 新たに the same as 新しく?
faq.a: They overlap. 新たに leans towards "newly, afresh, in addition" and is more formal; 新しく is the everyday adverb. 新しく買った is natural speech, while 新たに追加された is written style.

faq.q: Can 新た describe an object?
faq.a: Rarely and awkwardly. It prefers abstract nouns — 課題, 問題, 局面, 展開, 決意. For a physical thing, use 新しい.

title: 若い vs 幼い
quickAnswer: 若い means young in age, and is neutral or complimentary for anyone from their teens upwards. 幼い means very young — small-child young — and applied to an adult it is a criticism meaning immature or childish.
summary: 若い is young in years, neutral or flattering. 幼い is small-child young, and about an adult it means immature.

members.when: Use 若い for anyone young relative to the context: a young teacher, young people, when I was young. Saying someone is 若い is usually a compliment.

examples.ja: 先生は若いです。
examples.reading: せんせいはわかいです。
examples.en: The teacher is young.

examples.ja: 若い時にたくさん旅行しました。
examples.reading: わかいときにたくさんりょこうしました。
examples.en: I travelled a lot when I was young.

members.when: Use 幼い for small children and early childhood — 幼い子供, 幼い頃. Applied to an adult's behaviour or thinking it means immature, and it is not a compliment.

examples.ja: 幼い頃の写真です。
examples.reading: おさないころのしゃしんです。
examples.en: This is a photo from when I was little.

examples.ja: 彼の考えは幼いです。
examples.reading: かれのかんがえはおさないです。
examples.en: His thinking is immature.

contrast.ja: この会社は若い人が多いです。
contrast.reading: このかいしゃはわかいひとがおおいです。
contrast.en: This company has a lot of young people.
contrast.note: Adults in their twenties are 若い. 幼い人 would mean toddlers at the office.

contrast.ja: 幼い子供を公園へ連れて行きます。
contrast.reading: おさないこどもをこうえんへつれていきます。
contrast.en: I take my small children to the park.
contrast.note: Pre-school age — 幼い is the natural word. 若い子供 is not used.

contrast.ja: 三十歳なのに考え方が幼いですね。
contrast.reading: さんじゅっさいなのにかんがえかたがおさないですね。
contrast.en: He's thirty but his way of thinking is childish.
contrast.note: Here 幼い is explicitly a criticism; 若い would be a neutral statement of age.

contrast.ja: 母は年より若く見えます。
contrast.reading: はははとしよりわかくみえます。
contrast.en: My mother looks younger than her age.
contrast.note: A compliment about appearance — only 若い works.

mistakes.wrong: 若い子供が公園で遊んでいます。
mistakes.right: 幼い子供が公園で遊んでいます。
mistakes.why: For little children, Japanese says 幼い子供 or 小さい子供. 若い子供 sounds contradictory.

mistakes.wrong: 先生はまだ幼いです。
mistakes.right: 先生はまだ若いです。
mistakes.why: Calling an adult 幼い says they are childish, which is an insult, not a comment on their age.

faq.q: Can I use 幼い as a compliment?
faq.a: About a child it is simply factual. About an adult, no — it means immature. If you mean someone looks youthful, say 若く見えます.

faq.q: What about 小さい for children?
faq.a: 小さい子 is the most common casual way to say "little kid". 幼い is slightly more written, and 幼い頃 for "in my childhood" is very common.

faq.q: Is 若い only for people?
faq.a: Mostly, but it extends to things with an age-like quality — 若い会社 for a young company, 若い葉 for new leaves. 幼い stays with people and their behaviour.

title: 忙しい vs 大変
quickAnswer: 忙しい means you have no time — too much to do. 大変 means something is tough, demanding or a big deal, whether or not time is the problem. When you sympathise with someone, the phrase you want is 大変ですね.
summary: 忙しい means no time; 大変 means tough or a big deal. 大変ですね is the standard way to say "that sounds rough".

members.when: Use 忙しい purely about a lack of free time: a busy week, busy with work, too busy to go. It says nothing about whether the work is hard.

examples.ja: 今週はとても忙しいです。
examples.reading: こんしゅうはとてもいそがしいです。
examples.en: I am very busy this week.

examples.ja: 忙しくて、映画を見る時間がありません。
examples.reading: いそがしくて、えいがをみるじかんがありません。
examples.en: I'm too busy to have time for a film.

members.when: Use 大変 when something is hard, demanding or serious — a tough job, a rough day, a difficult situation. 大変ですね is the standard sympathetic reply when someone tells you their troubles.

examples.ja: 子育ては大変です。
examples.reading: こそだてはたいへんです。
examples.en: Raising children is hard work.

examples.ja: それは大変ですね。
examples.reading: それはたいへんですね。
examples.en: That sounds rough.

contrast.ja: 明日は忙しいので行けません。
contrast.reading: あしたはいそがしいのでいけません。
contrast.en: I'm busy tomorrow so I can't go.
contrast.note: The issue is time, so 忙しい. 大変なので行けません would sound like something serious has happened.

contrast.ja: 毎日子供の世話で大変です。
contrast.reading: まいにちこどものせわでたいへんです。
contrast.en: Looking after the kids every day is exhausting.
contrast.note: It is demanding, not merely time-filling — 大変.

contrast.ja: お仕事、大変ですね。
contrast.reading: おしごと、たいへんですね。
contrast.en: Your job must be tough.
contrast.note: Sympathy is expressed with 大変ですね. 忙しいですね is a comment on their schedule, not a kind word.

contrast.ja: 大変！財布を忘れました。
contrast.reading: たいへん！さいふをわすれました。
contrast.en: Oh no! I forgot my wallet.
contrast.note: 大変 alone works as "oh no, this is a problem". 忙しい has no such use.

mistakes.wrong: それは忙しいですね。
mistakes.right: それは大変ですね。
mistakes.why: When someone describes a hardship, the sympathetic set phrase is 大変ですね. 忙しいですね only remarks on how packed their schedule is.

mistakes.wrong: 日本語の勉強は忙しいです。
mistakes.right: 日本語の勉強は大変です。
mistakes.why: Studying is hard, not busy. 忙しい describes a person's schedule, not the difficulty of a task.

mistakes.wrong: 大変な人ですね。
mistakes.right: 忙しい人ですね。
mistakes.why: 大変な人 sounds like a troublesome person. To say someone has a lot on, use 忙しい人.

faq.q: Can something be both?
faq.a: Often. 仕事が忙しくて大変です is completely natural — busy, and therefore tough. They stack rather than compete.

faq.q: Why do people say 大変ですね so much?
faq.a: It is the standard way to acknowledge someone's difficulty, like "that must be hard" in English. It costs nothing and is always safe with a colleague or neighbour.

faq.q: What does 大変 mean before an adjective?
faq.a: It also works as an adverb meaning "very", in formal speech: 大変おいしいです, 大変申し訳ありません. That is a separate use from "tough".

title: 面白い vs 楽しい
quickAnswer: 面白い describes the thing — it is interesting, funny or entertaining. 楽しい describes your experience — you are having a good time. So 面白い映画 is a film that grips or amuses you, while 楽しい一日 is a day you enjoyed living through. This is why 面白い人 means a funny, entertaining person and 楽しい人 means someone who is fun to be around.
summary: 面白い says the thing is interesting or funny; 楽しい says you are enjoying yourself. Compare 面白い人 with 楽しい人.

members.when: Use 面白い for a property of the thing itself: a book, film, story, idea or person that is interesting, amusing or worth paying attention to. It can be said about something you did not personally enjoy, as long as it is interesting.

examples.ja: この本はとても面白いです。
examples.reading: このほんはとてもおもしろいです。
examples.en: This book is really interesting.

examples.ja: 田中さんは面白い人ですね。
examples.reading: たなかさんはおもしろいひとですね。
examples.en: Tanaka is a funny guy, isn't he.

members.when: Use 楽しい when the point is that you, or someone, are having a good time. It fits events, activities and stretches of time you enjoy, and it is about the enjoyment, not about the thing being clever or funny.

examples.ja: きのうのパーティーは楽しかったです。
examples.reading: きのうのパーティーはたのしかったです。
examples.en: Yesterday's party was fun.

examples.ja: 友だちと話すのが楽しいです。
examples.reading: ともだちとはなすのがたのしいです。
examples.en: I enjoy talking with my friends.

contrast.ja: 彼は面白い人です。
contrast.reading: かれはおもしろいひとです。
contrast.en: He is a funny, entertaining person.
contrast.note: 面白い here says he makes people laugh. 楽しい人 would instead mean he is pleasant company.

contrast.ja: 彼といると楽しいです。
contrast.reading: かれといるとたのしいです。
contrast.en: I have a good time when I'm with him.
contrast.note: The sentence is about your enjoyment, so 楽しい. 面白い would turn it into a comment on how amusing he is.

contrast.ja: この映画は面白いですが、悲しいです。
contrast.reading: このえいがはおもしろいですが、かなしいです。
contrast.en: This film is interesting, but it's sad.
contrast.note: 面白い can mean gripping rather than cheerful, so it survives next to 悲しい. 楽しい映画 would contradict the second half.

contrast.ja: 毎日が楽しいです。
contrast.reading: まいにちがたのしいです。
contrast.en: Every day is enjoyable.
contrast.note: A stretch of lived time takes 楽しい. 毎日が面白い would sound like life keeps producing curiosities.

mistakes.wrong: パーティーは面白かったです。
mistakes.right: パーティーは楽しかったです。
mistakes.why: Saying a party was 面白い suggests something odd or amusing happened there, not that you enjoyed it. For a good time, use 楽しい.

mistakes.wrong: この本は楽しいです。
mistakes.right: この本は面白いです。
mistakes.why: Books, films and stories are normally judged by whether they are interesting, so 面白い is the standard choice. 楽しい本 sounds unusual as a plain review.

faq.q: Can both work in the same sentence?
faq.a: Often yes, with a change of meaning rather than a mistake. 日本語の勉強は面白いです says the subject itself is interesting; 日本語の勉強は楽しいです says studying it is enjoyable for you. Many learners mean both and can simply say either.

faq.q: What is the difference between 面白い人 and 楽しい人?
faq.a: 面白い人 is someone funny or unusual, the person who makes the table laugh. 楽しい人 is someone whose company is enjoyable. You can be one without being the other.

faq.q: Is 面白い always positive?
faq.a: Not always warm, but usually not an insult. It can mean interesting in a neutral or even odd way, as in 面白い考え, an interesting idea. Tone of voice decides.

title: 嬉しい vs 幸せ
quickAnswer: 嬉しい is a burst of gladness caused by something that just happened — you got a letter, you passed the test. 幸せ is a lasting state of being happy with your life. 嬉しい is normally about how you yourself feel right now, so for other people you say 嬉しそう; 幸せ can be said about others freely, as in 幸せな家族.
summary: 嬉しい is gladness at something that happened; 幸せ is the lasting state of being happy. Use 嬉しそう for other people.

members.when: Use 嬉しい for your own immediate reaction to a specific event or piece of news. It normally has a cause, often marked with 〜て or 〜から. About someone else, use 嬉しそう rather than plain 嬉しい.

examples.ja: 手紙をもらって嬉しかったです。
examples.reading: てがみをもらってうれしかったです。
examples.en: I was glad to get your letter.

examples.ja: 試験に合格して、とても嬉しいです。
examples.reading: しけんにごうかくして、とてもうれしいです。
examples.en: I passed the exam, so I'm really pleased.

members.when: Use 幸せ for a settled condition of happiness — a life, a marriage, a family, or how you feel about your situation overall. It is a な-adjective and also a noun, so 幸せな人生 and 幸せになる are both normal.

examples.ja: 家族と一緒にいて幸せです。
examples.reading: かぞくといっしょにいてしあわせです。
examples.en: I'm happy being with my family.

examples.ja: 二人は幸せな家庭を作りました。
examples.reading: ふたりはしあわせなかていをつくりました。
examples.en: The two of them built a happy home.

contrast.ja: プレゼントをもらって嬉しいです。
contrast.reading: プレゼントをもらってうれしいです。
contrast.en: I'm glad to have received a present.
contrast.note: One event, one reaction. 幸せ would overstate it, as if the present had changed your life.

contrast.ja: 今の生活はとても幸せです。
contrast.reading: いまのせいかつはとてもしあわせです。
contrast.en: I'm very happy with my life at the moment.
contrast.note: 生活 is an ongoing state, so 幸せ. 嬉しい needs a triggering event and does not sit well with 生活.

contrast.ja: 子どもが嬉しそうに笑っています。
contrast.reading: こどもがうれしそうにわらっています。
contrast.en: The child is laughing happily.
contrast.note: Someone else's gladness is reported as 嬉しそう, not plain 嬉しい, because you cannot state another person's inner feeling directly.

contrast.ja: あの二人は幸せそうですね。
contrast.reading: あのふたりはしあわせそうですね。
contrast.en: Those two look happy, don't they.
contrast.note: 幸せ can be said about others plainly too, as in 幸せな家族; here そう just softens it to an impression.

mistakes.wrong: 田中さんは嬉しいです。
mistakes.right: 田中さんは嬉しそうです。
mistakes.why: Plain 嬉しい about a third person sounds like you are reading their mind. Add そう, or report it as 嬉しいと言っていました.

mistakes.wrong: 会えて幸せです。
mistakes.right: 会えて嬉しいです。
mistakes.why: Meeting someone is a single occasion, so it calls for 嬉しい. 幸せ here sounds far heavier than intended, like a declaration about your whole life.

faq.q: Can I say 幸せ about a small nice thing?
faq.a: Yes, casually — 幸せ over a good cake is common, half-joking. But in ordinary writing, keep 幸せ for the lasting state and use 嬉しい for the moment.

faq.q: Why does 幸せ take な and 嬉しい not?
faq.a: 幸せ is a noun that also works as a な-adjective: 幸せな家族, 幸せです. 嬉しい is a plain い-adjective: 嬉しい知らせ, 嬉しいです. Their grammar never mixes.

faq.q: Which do I use to thank someone?
faq.a: 嬉しいです. For example 来てくれて嬉しいです, I'm glad you came. It reacts to what they did, which is exactly what 嬉しい is for.

title: 強い vs 丈夫
quickAnswer: 強い means strong in force or ability — a strong wind, a strong player, a strong flavour. 丈夫 means sturdy: built so it does not break or wear out. A 丈夫なかばん survives years of use, while 強いかばん is not something people say. For the body both appear, and 体が丈夫 means rarely getting ill, while 体が強い leans towards physical power.
summary: 強い is strong in force or ability; 丈夫 is sturdy and hard to break. Bags, shoes and good health take 丈夫.

members.when: Use 強い where force, power or ability is being measured: wind, rain, a team, a drink, a taste, a personality. It is an い-adjective and takes が for the thing that is strong.

examples.ja: 今日は風が強いです。
examples.reading: きょうはかぜがつよいです。
examples.en: The wind is strong today.

examples.ja: あのチームはとても強いです。
examples.reading: あのチームはとてもつよいです。
examples.en: That team is very strong.

members.when: Use 丈夫 for things that do not break, tear or wear out easily — bags, shoes, furniture, rope — and for a body that resists illness. It is a な-adjective: 丈夫な靴, この机は丈夫です.

examples.ja: この机は丈夫ですね。
examples.reading: このつくえはじょうぶですね。
examples.en: This desk is sturdy, isn't it.

examples.ja: 弟は体が丈夫で、あまり風邪をひきません。
examples.reading: おとうとはからだがじょうぶで、あまりかぜをひきません。
examples.en: My little brother is robust and rarely catches colds.

contrast.ja: 丈夫なかばんがほしいです。
contrast.reading: じょうぶなかばんがほしいです。
contrast.en: I want a bag that will last.
contrast.note: A bag is judged by durability, not by force, so 丈夫. 強いかばん is not idiomatic.

contrast.ja: このお茶は味が強いです。
contrast.reading: このおちゃはあじがつよいです。
contrast.en: This tea has a strong taste.
contrast.note: Flavour is intensity, which is 強い territory. 丈夫 never describes taste.

contrast.ja: 雨が強くなってきました。
contrast.reading: あめがつよくなってきました。
contrast.en: The rain is getting heavier.
contrast.note: Weather is force, so 強い. Note the adverb form 強く; 丈夫 would need 丈夫に and makes no sense here.

contrast.ja: 祖母は九十歳ですが、とても丈夫です。
contrast.reading: そぼはきゅうじゅっさいですが、とてもじょうぶです。
contrast.en: My grandmother is ninety but very hale.
contrast.note: About health and resilience, 丈夫 is the natural word; 強い would suggest she could win a fight.

mistakes.wrong: この靴は強いです。
mistakes.right: この靴は丈夫です。
mistakes.why: Objects that must survive wear take 丈夫. 強い靴 sounds like the shoe has power of its own.

mistakes.wrong: 強いな人
mistakes.right: 強い人
mistakes.why: 強い is an い-adjective and never takes な. The な belongs to 丈夫: 丈夫な人.

faq.q: Can I use both for the body?
faq.a: Yes, and they differ. 体が丈夫 means you rarely get ill and recover fast. 体が強い suggests physical strength or toughness. For health, 丈夫 is the usual choice.

faq.q: Is 大丈夫 related?
faq.a: It is the same 丈夫 with 大 in front, and the sense of being undamaged and all right is clearly connected, but treat 大丈夫 as its own fixed word meaning fine or no problem.

faq.q: How do I say someone holds their drink well?
faq.a: お酒に強い. That is 強い with に, and its opposite is お酒に弱い. 丈夫 is never used this way.

title: 弱い vs 苦手
quickAnswer: 弱い means weak — low in strength, force or resistance. 苦手 means you are bad at something or cannot handle it, and it covers dislike as much as inability. お酒に弱い says a little alcohol affects you; お酒が苦手 says you would rather not drink it. 苦手 is also the polite way to decline food or an invitation.
summary: 弱い is weak in strength or resistance; 苦手 is bad at or can't handle, and the polite way to say no.

members.when: Use 弱い for a measurable lack of strength: a weak body, weak wind, a weak team, low resistance to something, marked with に. It states a fact about capacity, not about preference.

examples.ja: 父は体が弱いです。
examples.reading: ちちはからだがよわいです。
examples.en: My father is in poor health.

examples.ja: 私はお酒に弱いので、一杯だけにします。
examples.reading: わたしはおさけによわいので、いっぱいだけにします。
examples.en: Alcohol goes straight to my head, so I'll stick to one glass.

members.when: Use 苦手 for things you are poor at or would rather avoid — a school subject, singing, insects, a type of food, even a person. It is a な-adjective and takes が: 数学が苦手です.

examples.ja: 歌は苦手です。
examples.reading: うたはにがてです。
examples.en: I'm no good at singing.

examples.ja: すみません、辛い物が苦手なんです。
examples.reading: すみません、からいものがにがてなんです。
examples.en: Sorry, I'm not good with spicy food.

contrast.ja: お酒に弱いです。
contrast.reading: おさけによわいです。
contrast.en: I can't hold my drink.
contrast.note: A physical fact: small amounts affect you. It says nothing about whether you like alcohol.

contrast.ja: お酒が苦手です。
contrast.reading: おさけがにがてです。
contrast.en: I'd rather not drink.
contrast.note: Preference or avoidance, and a polite refusal. You might drink perfectly well and still say this.

contrast.ja: 私は数学が苦手です。
contrast.reading: わたしはすうがくがにがてです。
contrast.en: I'm bad at maths.
contrast.note: For skills and school subjects, 苦手 is the word. 数学に弱い exists but sounds bookish next to it.

contrast.ja: 今日は風が弱いですね。
contrast.reading: きょうはかぜがよわいですね。
contrast.en: The wind is light today.
contrast.note: Only 弱い works for natural force. 苦手 describes a person's relationship to something, never the wind itself.

mistakes.wrong: 私は料理が弱いです。
mistakes.right: 私は料理が苦手です。
mistakes.why: For being bad at an activity, use 苦手. 弱い about a skill is not said outside a few fixed phrases.

mistakes.wrong: この肉が嫌いです。
mistakes.right: この肉はちょっと苦手です。
mistakes.why: Not a grammar error, but 嫌い at someone's table is blunt. 苦手 is the standard softened way to decline food.

faq.q: Is 苦手 the same as 嫌い?
faq.a: Close, but softer and vaguer. 嫌い is a clear dislike; 苦手 says the thing does not agree with you, which may be dislike, may be inability, and lets the listener not press.

faq.q: Can I say a person is 苦手?
faq.a: Yes. あの人はちょっと苦手です means you find them hard to deal with. It is much gentler than 嫌い and very common.

faq.q: What is the opposite of 苦手?
faq.a: 得意, meaning good at: 料理が得意です, I'm good at cooking. The opposite of 弱い is 強い.

title: 広い vs 大きい
quickAnswer: 広い is about area — how much floor space or surface something has. 大きい is about overall size in every direction. A room, a park or a road is 広い when there is plenty of space to spread out; a dog, a house or a box is 大きい when the object itself is large. 広い also works figuratively in 心が広い, broad-minded. For the opposites, see 狭い vs 小さい.
summary: 広い is area and floor space; 大きい is overall size. 広い部屋 has room to spare; 大きい家 is a large building.

members.when: Use 広い for two-dimensional extent: rooms, floors, land, roads, gardens, seas, and by extension a broad range or a broad mind. If you could ask how many square metres, 広い is right.

examples.ja: この部屋は広いですね。
examples.reading: このへやはひろいですね。
examples.en: This room is nice and spacious.

examples.ja: 駅前の道は広いです。
examples.reading: えきまえのみちはひろいです。
examples.en: The road in front of the station is wide.

members.when: Use 大きい for the size of an object as a whole — animals, buildings, bags, numbers — and by extension a loud voice. It answers how big, not how much floor space.

examples.ja: 公園に大きい犬がいます。
examples.reading: こうえんにおおきいいぬがいます。
examples.en: There's a big dog in the park.

examples.ja: もう少し大きい声で話してください。
examples.reading: もうすこしおおきいこえではなしてください。
examples.en: Please speak a little louder.

contrast.ja: 大きい家ですが、部屋は広くありません。
contrast.reading: おおきいいえですが、へやはひろくありません。
contrast.en: It's a big house, but the rooms aren't spacious.
contrast.note: The same building can be 大きい in outline and still have rooms that are not 広い. The sentence only works because the two words measure different things.

contrast.ja: 広い公園で子どもが遊んでいます。
contrast.reading: ひろいこうえんでこどもがあそんでいます。
contrast.en: Children are playing in a big open park.
contrast.note: A park is valued for its ground area, so 広い. 大きい公園 is possible but shifts the focus to its size on a map.

contrast.ja: 田中さんは心が広いです。
contrast.reading: たなかさんはこころがひろいです。
contrast.en: Tanaka is broad-minded.
contrast.note: A fixed figurative use of 広い. 心が大きい is not the standard phrase.

contrast.ja: 大きい声で歌いましょう。
contrast.reading: おおきいこえでうたいましょう。
contrast.en: Let's sing loudly.
contrast.note: Volume is 大きい, never 広い.

mistakes.wrong: 私のアパートは大きいです。
mistakes.right: 私のアパートは広いです。
mistakes.why: When you mean there is plenty of living space, use 広い. 大きい describes the building's bulk, which is rarely what a tenant means.

mistakes.wrong: 広い犬
mistakes.right: 大きい犬
mistakes.why: Animals and objects have size, not floor area, so 広い cannot modify them.

faq.q: Can both be used for a house?
faq.a: Yes, with different meanings. 大きい家 is a large building seen from outside; 広い家 has lots of room inside. Estate ads talk about 広い.

faq.q: Which do I use for a road?
faq.a: 広い道 for a wide road, and its opposite is 狭い道. 大きい道 is not standard; 大通り is the word for a main road.

faq.q: What are the opposites?
faq.a: 広い to 狭い, and 大きい to 小さい, and the pairs stay parallel. See the 狭い vs 小さい page for the same distinction from the other side.

title: 狭い vs 小さい
quickAnswer: 狭い means there is not enough space — a cramped room, a narrow road, a tight gap. 小さい means the thing itself is small in size. A room can be 狭い because it is packed with furniture even when it is not 小さい. 狭い also appears in 狭い意味で, in the narrow sense. This is the mirror image of 広い vs 大きい.
summary: 狭い is cramped space or narrow width; 小さい is small in size. 狭い部屋 lacks room; 小さい犬 is a small dog.

members.when: Use 狭い when area or width is insufficient: rooms, flats, roads, seats, gaps, and figuratively a narrow range or a narrow view. It is about the space, not the object that fills it.

examples.ja: 私の部屋は狭いです。
examples.reading: わたしのへやはせまいです。
examples.en: My room is cramped.

examples.ja: この道は狭いので、車は通れません。
examples.reading: このみちはせまいので、くるまはとおれません。
examples.en: This road is narrow, so cars can't get through.

members.when: Use 小さい for the size of an object or person: animals, clothes, children, boxes, numbers, and by extension a quiet voice. It is the plain opposite of 大きい.

examples.ja: うちに小さい犬がいます。
examples.reading: うちにちいさいいぬがいます。
examples.en: We have a small dog at home.

examples.ja: この靴は小さいです。
examples.reading: このくつはちいさいです。
examples.en: These shoes are too small.

contrast.ja: 部屋は小さくないですが、物が多くて狭いです。
contrast.reading: へやはちいさくないですが、ものがおおくてせまいです。
contrast.en: The room isn't small, but it's cramped because there's so much stuff.
contrast.note: The clearest proof they differ: size and available space come apart.

contrast.ja: この道は狭いです。
contrast.reading: このみちはせまいです。
contrast.en: This road is narrow.
contrast.note: The width of a passage is 狭い. 小さい道 is not said.

contrast.ja: 狭い意味では、それは正しくありません。
contrast.reading: せまいいみでは、それはただしくありません。
contrast.en: In the narrow sense, that isn't correct.
contrast.note: A set phrase where 狭い means restricted in scope; 小さい cannot replace it.

contrast.ja: もっと小さいサイズはありますか。
contrast.reading: もっとちいさいサイズはありますか。
contrast.en: Do you have a smaller size?
contrast.note: Clothes and objects are measured by size, so 小さい only.

mistakes.wrong: 私のアパートは小さいです。
mistakes.right: 私のアパートは狭いです。
mistakes.why: For living space that feels tight, Japanese uses 狭い. 小さい describes the building itself, which is not what a tenant complains about.

mistakes.wrong: 狭い箱
mistakes.right: 小さい箱
mistakes.why: A box is an object with a size, so 小さい. 狭い would only work if you meant the space inside is too tight for what you are putting in.

faq.q: Is 狭い always negative?
faq.a: Usually it carries a hint of complaint, that there is not enough room. Neutral descriptions of a small back road still use 狭い, though, so it is not always a criticism.

faq.q: How do I say my room is small without complaining?
faq.a: 部屋が狭いです is what people actually say, complaint and all. If you want compact and cosy, こぢんまりした部屋 is the friendly phrasing.

faq.q: What are the opposites?
faq.a: 狭い to 広い, and 小さい to 大きい. The distinction runs exactly parallel; see the 広い vs 大きい page.

title: 深い vs 濃い
quickAnswer: 深い is about depth — how far down or how far in something goes, literally for water and forests and figuratively for meaning, thought and relationships. 濃い is about concentration — how much of something is packed into a given amount, which is why coffee, flavour, colour and fog are 濃い. 濃いコーヒー is strong coffee; 深い意味 is a deep meaning.
summary: 深い is depth, literal or figurative; 濃い is concentration or density, as in coffee, flavour, colour and fog.

members.when: Use 深い when there is a distance downward or inward: water, holes, snow, forests. Figuratively it covers meaning, thought, sleep, and close relationships. Its opposite is 浅い.

examples.ja: この川は深いので気をつけてください。
examples.reading: このかわはふかいのできをつけてください。
examples.en: This river is deep, so please be careful.

examples.ja: その言葉には深い意味があります。
examples.reading: そのことばにはふかいいみがあります。
examples.en: Those words have a deep meaning.

members.when: Use 濃い when something is concentrated or dense: strong tea or coffee, heavy seasoning, dark colours, thick fog, thick hair. Its opposite is 薄い.

examples.ja: 濃いコーヒーが好きです。
examples.reading: こいコーヒーがすきです。
examples.en: I like strong coffee.

examples.ja: 今朝は霧が濃かったです。
examples.reading: けさはきりがこかったです。
examples.en: The fog was thick this morning.

contrast.ja: このスープは味が濃いです。
contrast.reading: このスープはあじがこいです。
contrast.en: This soup is strongly flavoured.
contrast.note: Flavour strength is concentration, so 濃い. 味が深い exists but means complex and rounded, not heavily seasoned.

contrast.ja: 深い海には光が届きません。
contrast.reading: ふかいうみにはひかりがとどきません。
contrast.en: Light doesn't reach the deep sea.
contrast.note: Physical depth, measured downward: only 深い.

contrast.ja: 濃い青のシャツを買いました。
contrast.reading: こいあおのシャツをかいました。
contrast.en: I bought a dark blue shirt.
contrast.note: Colour strength is 濃い, with 薄い for pale. 深い青 turns up in literary writing, but 濃い is the everyday word.

contrast.ja: 二人は深い関係です。
contrast.reading: ふたりはふかいかんけいです。
contrast.en: The two of them are close.
contrast.note: Relationships have depth, not concentration, so 深い.

mistakes.wrong: 深いコーヒー
mistakes.right: 濃いコーヒー
mistakes.why: The strength of a drink is concentration. 深い here sounds like the cup itself is physically deep.

mistakes.wrong: 濃い意味
mistakes.right: 深い意味
mistakes.why: Meaning is measured by depth. 濃い意味 is not a phrase Japanese speakers use.

faq.q: How do I say weak coffee?
faq.a: 薄いコーヒー. 薄い is the regular opposite of 濃い for drinks, flavour and colour. The opposite of 深い is 浅い.

faq.q: Can 濃い describe a person?
faq.a: Colloquially yes — 濃い人 means someone with a larger-than-life, intense presence. It is casual and can be teasing, so use it carefully.

faq.q: Is 味が深い wrong, then?
faq.a: No, it just means something else: a flavour with depth and complexity, the kind of praise you give a broth or a wine. 味が濃い is simply about strength of seasoning.

title: 薄い vs 細い
quickAnswer: 薄い is thin in thickness — a sheet of paper, a slice of meat — and by extension weak in flavour or pale in colour. 細い is thin in width — a narrow road, a thin line, slender legs. 薄い本 is a slim book with few pages; 細い道 is a road you can barely drive down. For a slim person you must say 細い, never 薄い.
summary: 薄い is thin in thickness or weak in flavour; 細い is narrow or slender in width. Compare 薄い本 and 細い道.

members.when: Use 薄い when something is flat and not thick: paper, books, slices, cloth, walls. It also covers weak taste, pale colour and thin hair. Its opposites are 厚い for thickness and 濃い for strength.

examples.ja: これは薄い紙です。
examples.reading: これはうすいかみです。
examples.en: This is thin paper.

examples.ja: このスープは味が薄いです。
examples.reading: このスープはあじがうすいです。
examples.en: This soup tastes bland.

members.when: Use 細い for things that are narrow across: roads, lines, string, pens, fingers, legs, a slim body. Its opposite is 太い.

examples.ja: この道は細いです。
examples.reading: このみちはほそいです。
examples.en: This road is narrow.

examples.ja: 彼女は指が細いです。
examples.reading: かのじょはゆびがほそいです。
examples.en: She has slender fingers.

contrast.ja: この本は薄いです。
contrast.reading: このほんはうすいです。
contrast.en: This book is slim.
contrast.note: A book's thinness is measured through the stack of pages, so 薄い. 細い本 would describe an unusually narrow page shape.

contrast.ja: 細い道を歩きました。
contrast.reading: ほそいみちをあるきました。
contrast.en: We walked along a narrow path.
contrast.note: Width of a path is 細い. 薄い道 makes no sense.

contrast.ja: 妹は足が細いです。
contrast.reading: いもうとはあしがほそいです。
contrast.en: My sister has slim legs.
contrast.note: Bodies and limbs take 細い. 足が薄い is not Japanese.

contrast.ja: 薄いピンクのカーテンを選びました。
contrast.reading: うすいピンクのカーテンをえらびました。
contrast.en: I chose pale pink curtains.
contrast.note: Pale colour is 薄い, matching 濃い for dark. 細い never describes colour.

mistakes.wrong: 彼女は薄いです。
mistakes.right: 彼女は細いです。
mistakes.why: For a slim person, use 細い or やせている. 薄い about a person sounds like they are flat or faint, not slender.

mistakes.wrong: 細いコーヒー
mistakes.right: 薄いコーヒー
mistakes.why: Weak drinks and weak flavour are 薄い, the opposite of 濃い. 細い only measures width.

faq.q: For a narrow road, is it 細い or 狭い?
faq.a: Both are used. 細い道 pictures the road as a thin line, often a lane or path; 狭い道 says there is not enough room to pass. For a street too tight for two cars, 狭い is the more common complaint.

faq.q: What are the opposites?
faq.a: 薄い pairs with 厚い for thickness and with 濃い for strength of taste or colour. 細い pairs with 太い.

faq.q: How do I say a thin slice of meat?
faq.a: 薄い肉 or 薄切りの肉. Slices are about thickness, so 薄い. 細切り with 細い means cut into thin strips, which is a different shape.

title: 全然 vs あまり
quickAnswer: Both 全然 and あまり are used with a negative verb or adjective, but they mark different amounts: 全然分かりません means "I don't understand at all" (zero), while あまり分かりません means "I don't understand very well" (a little, but not much). Pick 全然 for a flat zero and あまり for a softened, partial negative.
summary: 全然 with a negative means "not at all"; あまり with a negative means "not much". Both need the negative form.

members.when: Use 全然 when the amount is zero and you want to sound emphatic: 全然 + ない / ません / ~くない. In casual speech you will also hear affirmative 全然大丈夫 or 全然いい meaning "totally fine", which is common but informal, so keep it out of writing and polite situations.

examples.ja: この漢字は全然読めません。
examples.reading: このかんじはぜんぜんよめません。
examples.en: I can't read this kanji at all.

examples.ja: お金は全然ありません。
examples.reading: おかねはぜんぜんありません。
examples.en: I have no money at all.

members.when: Use あまり + negative when the level is low but not zero: あまり好きではない means you don't dislike it, you just aren't keen. It is the polite, soft way to decline or disagree, and in casual speech it often shortens to あんまり.

examples.ja: 辛い物はあまり好きではありません。
examples.reading: からいものはあまりすきではありません。
examples.en: I'm not very fond of spicy food.

examples.ja: 昨日はあまり寝ていません。
examples.reading: きのうはあまりねていません。
examples.en: I didn't sleep much last night.

contrast.ja: お酒は全然飲みません。
contrast.reading: おさけはぜんぜんのみません。
contrast.en: I don't drink alcohol at all.
contrast.note: 全然 because the amount is truly zero — this is the sentence a non-drinker says. あまり飲みません would mean you do drink, just not much.

contrast.ja: お酒はあまり飲みません。
contrast.reading: おさけはあまりのみません。
contrast.en: I don't drink much alcohol.
contrast.note: あまり because you drink a little. It is also the softer answer when you want to decline politely without shutting the topic down.

contrast.ja: 彼のことは全然知りません。
contrast.reading: かれのことはぜんぜんしりません。
contrast.en: I don't know anything about him at all.
contrast.note: Knowing someone is close to all-or-nothing here, so 全然 fits; あまり知りません would mean you know him slightly.

mistakes.wrong: 全然分かります。
mistakes.right: よく分かります。
mistakes.why: In standard, polite Japanese 全然 needs a negative. Affirmative 全然 exists in casual speech (全然大丈夫), but a bare 全然分かります in a classroom or at work sounds wrong.

mistakes.wrong: あまり嫌いです。
mistakes.right: あまり好きではありません。
mistakes.why: あまり also needs a negative predicate. Learners attach it to a positive adjective; instead, negate the opposite word.

mistakes.wrong: この本は全然難しくないです。(meaning: it is a bit difficult)
mistakes.right: この本はあまり難しくないです。
mistakes.why: 全然 says the difficulty is zero. If you mean "not that difficult", あまり is the right strength.

faq.q: Is 全然大丈夫 wrong?
faq.a: It is not wrong, it is informal. Affirmative 全然 with words like 大丈夫, いい and 平気 is normal spoken Japanese among friends and is very common. Teachers and exams still expect 全然 + negative, and you should not write it in an essay or say it to a customer.

faq.q: What is the difference between あまり and あんまり?
faq.a: None in meaning. あんまり is the casual spoken form; あまり is the neutral one you write and use in polite speech.

faq.q: Can I use 全然 to soften a refusal?
faq.a: No — it does the opposite. 全然好きではありません is a blunt "I don't like it at all". To decline gently, say あまり好きではありません, or just あまり… and trail off.

title: まず vs 初めに
quickAnswer: まず is the discourse marker for "first of all, before anything else" and is what you want when listing steps: まず手を洗って、次に野菜を切ります。初めに means "at the beginning" and points at the opening part of an event, talk or text, as in 初めに自己紹介をします。For instructions, choose まず.
summary: まず is "first of all" when listing steps; 初めに is "at the beginning" of a talk, text or event. Use まず for procedures.

members.when: Use まず to open the first step of a procedure or an argument, usually paired later with 次に and 最後に. It is about order of action, and it works in speech, recipes, manuals and explanations alike.

examples.ja: まずお湯を沸かして、次に麺を入れます。
examples.reading: まずおゆをわかして、つぎにめんをいれます。
examples.en: First boil the water, then put the noodles in.

examples.ja: まず先生に相談したほうがいいですよ。
examples.reading: まずせんせいにそうだんしたほうがいいですよ。
examples.en: You should talk to the teacher first, before anything else.

members.when: Use 初めに to mean "at the start of this thing" — the opening of a meeting, a speech, a book or a ceremony. It is slightly more formal than まず and is common in written and prepared language.

examples.ja: 初めに、本日の予定をご説明します。
examples.reading: はじめに、ほんじつのよていをごせつめいします。
examples.en: To begin with, let me explain today's schedule.

examples.ja: 初めに校長先生のお話があります。
examples.reading: はじめにこうちょうせんせいのおはなしがあります。
examples.en: At the beginning there will be a talk from the principal.

contrast.ja: まず手を洗いましょう。
contrast.reading: まずてをあらいましょう。
contrast.en: Let's wash our hands first.
contrast.note: A step in a procedure, so まず. 初めに手を洗いましょう is not wrong, but it sounds like the opening item of a formal programme rather than practical advice.

contrast.ja: 初めに自己紹介をさせていただきます。
contrast.reading: はじめにじこしょうかいをさせていただきます。
contrast.en: Let me introduce myself at the outset.
contrast.note: This is the opening of a speech, so 初めに. まず here would sound casual for the register.

contrast.ja: まず、値段が高すぎます。それに場所も遠いです。
contrast.reading: まず、ねだんがたかすぎます。それにばしょもとおいです。
contrast.en: For one thing, it's too expensive. On top of that, it's far away.
contrast.note: Listing reasons in an argument, not events in time — only まず works here; 初めに cannot introduce the first of several reasons.

contrast.ja: まず最初に名前を書いてください。
contrast.reading: まずさいしょになまえをかいてください。
contrast.en: First of all, please write your name.
contrast.note: まず最初に is a fixed, emphatic pairing you will hear constantly; 初めに最初に is not said.

mistakes.wrong: 初めに、値段が高いです。次に、遠いです。
mistakes.right: まず、値段が高いです。次に、遠いです。
mistakes.why: When you are enumerating points or reasons rather than things that happen in order, まず is the marker. 初めに locates something in time, so it does not fit a list of arguments.

mistakes.wrong: 始めに名前を書いてください。
mistakes.right: 初めに名前を書いてください。
mistakes.why: 始め belongs to beginning an action (始める); 初め is the first in a sequence or the earliest part. For "at the beginning / first of all", 初めに is the standard spelling.

faq.q: Can I always swap まず and 初めに?
faq.a: Often, but not always. When the sentence is the first step of a procedure, both can appear and まず is more natural; when you are listing reasons (まず、値段が…), only まず works; when you mean the opening section of a speech or book, 初めに is the natural choice.

faq.q: What about 最初に?
faq.a: 最初に means "first, at the very start" and overlaps with both. It emphasises being number one in a sequence, and it combines with まず as まず最初に for extra emphasis.

faq.q: Does まず have another meaning?
faq.a: Yes. まず can also mean "more or less, probably", as in まず大丈夫でしょう (it'll most likely be fine). Context separates the two easily, since that use does not start a list.

title: 急に vs 突然
quickAnswer: Both mean "suddenly" and in many sentences either is fine. The difference is that 急に focuses on a rapid change of state you notice or experience (急に寒くなった — it turned cold all of a sudden), while 突然 presents an abrupt event that breaks in with no warning (突然電話が鳴った). For things that change or speed up, use 急に; for out-of-the-blue events, 突然 is stronger.
summary: 急に is a quick change of state you experience; 突然 is an abrupt, out-of-the-blue event. The two overlap in much of their use.

members.when: Use 急に for a change that happens faster than expected — weather, mood, health, plans, speed. It pairs naturally with change verbs like なる, 変わる, 増える and 止まる, and with 急に用事ができる for plans that come up at short notice.

examples.ja: 急に寒くなりましたね。
examples.reading: きゅうにさむくなりましたね。
examples.en: It's turned cold all of a sudden, hasn't it?

examples.ja: 急に用事ができて、行けなくなりました。
examples.reading: きゅうにようじができて、いけなくなりました。
examples.en: Something came up at short notice, so I can't go any more.

members.when: Use 突然 for an event that arrives with no warning at all; it is more emphatic and a little more written-sounding than 急に. It also modifies a noun with の — 突然の雨, 突然の知らせ — which 急に cannot do (that form is 急な).

examples.ja: 突然、後ろから名前を呼ばれた。
examples.reading: とつぜん、うしろからなまえをよばれた。
examples.en: Suddenly someone called my name from behind.

examples.ja: 突然の知らせに驚きました。
examples.reading: とつぜんのしらせにおどろきました。
examples.en: I was shocked by the sudden news.

contrast.ja: 急に暑くなってきた。
contrast.reading: きゅうにあつくなってきた。
contrast.en: It's suddenly getting hot.
contrast.note: A change of state along a scale, so 急に. 突然暑くなった is possible but sounds as if the heat switched on in an instant.

contrast.ja: 突然ドアが開きました。
contrast.reading: とつぜんドアがひらきました。
contrast.en: The door suddenly flew open.
contrast.note: A one-moment event with no warning — 突然 is the natural choice and carries the surprise. 急に開いた is acceptable but weaker.

contrast.ja: 突然の雨でびしょ濡れになった。
contrast.reading: とつぜんのあめでびしょぬれになった。
contrast.en: I got soaked in a sudden downpour.
contrast.note: Modifying a noun directly needs 突然の; 急に cannot do this, and you would have to say 急な雨.

contrast.ja: 車が急に止まった。
contrast.reading: くるまがきゅうにとまった。
contrast.en: The car stopped abruptly.
contrast.note: 急に also carries the "sharply, at speed" sense that ties back to 急ぐ, which suits movement. 突然止まった shifts the focus to how unexpected it was.

mistakes.wrong: 急にの雨が降った。
mistakes.right: 突然の雨が降った。／急な雨が降った。
mistakes.why: 急に is already an adverb and cannot take の. Before a noun use 急な or 突然の.

mistakes.wrong: 突然寒くなってきました。(as small talk about the season)
mistakes.right: 急に寒くなってきました。
mistakes.why: Not ungrammatical, but for weather turning over a day or two, 急に is what people actually say; 突然 overstates it as if the temperature dropped in one instant.

faq.q: Are 急に and 突然 interchangeable?
faq.a: In a large number of sentences, yes — 急に雨が降り出した and 突然雨が降り出した are both fine and mean nearly the same thing. The reliable differences are grammatical: only 突然 takes の before a noun, and 急に is the one used for changes along a scale like temperature or speed.

faq.q: Which one is stronger?
faq.a: 突然. It implies no warning whatsoever and is the one used for shocking news or events. 急に can simply mean "sooner than expected".

faq.q: Is いきなり the same?
faq.a: いきなり is close to 突然 and more casual and spoken. It often carries a hint of complaint that something skipped the expected build-up, as in いきなり呼ばれた.

title: ほとんど vs 大体
quickAnswer: ほとんど means "almost all" and, with a negative, "hardly any" — ほとんど食べません means you eat almost none. 大体 means "roughly, approximately" and describes an amount or an understanding that is about right, as in 大体分かりました. The negative use is the key split: ほとんど + negative is standard, 大体 + negative is not.
summary: ほとんど is "almost all", or "hardly any" with a negative; 大体 is "roughly, approximately". Only ほとんど works with a negative.

members.when: Use ほとんど for a proportion close to the whole — ほとんどの人 (most people), ほとんど終わった (nearly finished). With a negative it flips to "hardly any / almost never": ほとんど見ません, ほとんどない. It can also stand before a noun with の.

examples.ja: 私はほとんどテレビを見ません。
examples.reading: わたしはほとんどテレビをみません。
examples.en: I hardly ever watch television.

examples.ja: ほとんどの学生がその本を読んでいます。
examples.reading: ほとんどのがくせいがそのほんをよんでいます。
examples.en: Almost all of the students have read that book.

members.when: Use 大体 for an approximate figure or a rough grasp of something: 大体三十分, 大体分かりました. It answers "about how much, about how well", not "what proportion is missing", and it is the everyday word for rounding a number in speech.

examples.ja: 駅まで大体十分かかります。
examples.reading: えきまでだいたいじゅっぷんかかります。
examples.en: It takes about ten minutes to the station.

examples.ja: 話は大体分かりました。
examples.reading: はなしはだいたいわかりました。
examples.en: I've got the gist of what you said.

contrast.ja: お酒はほとんど飲みません。
contrast.reading: おさけはほとんどのみません。
contrast.en: I hardly drink at all.
contrast.note: The negative forces ほとんど. 大体飲みません is not said — 大体 does not combine with a negative this way.

contrast.ja: 宿題は大体終わりました。
contrast.reading: しゅくだいはだいたいおわりました。
contrast.en: My homework is roughly finished.
contrast.note: 大体 says "broadly done, the rest is detail". ほとんど終わりました is also fine and sounds closer to "almost all of it is done", counting what remains.

contrast.ja: パーティーには大体三十人来ます。
contrast.reading: パーティーにはだいたいさんじゅうにんきます。
contrast.en: About thirty people are coming to the party.
contrast.note: An approximate number takes 大体 (or 約). ほとんど三十人 does not work, because ほとんど is about a share of a whole, not a rounded count.

contrast.ja: ほとんどの人が知っています。
contrast.reading: ほとんどのひとがしっています。
contrast.en: Almost everybody knows.
contrast.note: Quantifying a group before a noun is ほとんどの. 大体の人 exists but sounds vaguer, closer to "people in general".

mistakes.wrong: 大体テレビを見ません。
mistakes.right: ほとんどテレビを見ません。
mistakes.why: For "hardly ever", the adverb has to be ほとんど. 大体 with a negative does not produce that meaning and simply sounds broken.

mistakes.wrong: ほとんど五キロぐらいです。
mistakes.right: 大体五キロぐらいです。
mistakes.why: For a rough measurement use 大体 or 約. ほとんど would suggest "nearly all of five kilos", which is not what you mean.

faq.q: Can I use ほとんど and 大体 in the same place?
faq.a: For "mostly finished / mostly understood" both work and the difference is small. The two places they do not swap are negatives (only ほとんど) and approximate numbers (only 大体).

faq.q: Does ほとんど mean "almost" or "hardly"?
faq.a: Both — the verb decides. Affirmative ほとんど終わった is "almost finished"; negative ほとんど終わっていない is "hardly any of it is finished".

faq.q: Is 大体 the same as たいてい?
faq.a: No. たいてい is about frequency — "usually, most of the time" (たいてい七時に起きます). 大体 is about amount or degree.

title: ちょうど vs ぴったり
quickAnswer: ちょうど means "exactly, just" for times, amounts and moments — ちょうど三時です, ちょうど今出かけるところです. ぴったり means a perfect fit or a perfect match — このシャツはぴったりだ for clothes, この色は部屋にぴったりだ for something that suits. For clock time and round numbers use ちょうど; for fit and suitability use ぴったり.
summary: ちょうど is "exactly" for time, amounts and "just now"; ぴったり is a perfect fit or match, for clothes, sizes and suitability.

members.when: Use ちょうど for an exact figure (ちょうど千円), an exact time (ちょうど三時), and for "just at that moment" with ところ (ちょうど今帰ったところです). ちょうどいい is the everyday phrase for "just right" — the right size, temperature or amount.

examples.ja: 今ちょうど三時です。
examples.reading: いまちょうどさんじです。
examples.en: It's exactly three o'clock now.

examples.ja: ちょうど今、駅に着いたところです。
examples.reading: ちょうどいま、えきについたところです。
examples.en: I've just this moment arrived at the station.

members.when: Use ぴったり when two things match with no gap: clothes on a body, a lid on a pot, figures that tally, or a person or thing that suits a role (この仕事は彼女にぴったりだ). It behaves as an adverb and as a な-adjective, so ぴったりの服 and ぴったりだ are both normal.

examples.ja: このシャツは私にぴったりです。
examples.reading: このシャツはわたしにぴったりです。
examples.en: This shirt fits me perfectly.

examples.ja: その色はこの部屋にぴったりだと思います。
examples.reading: そのいろはこのへやにぴったりだとおもいます。
examples.en: I think that colour is perfect for this room.

contrast.ja: 会議はちょうど十時に始まります。
contrast.reading: かいぎはちょうどじゅうじにはじまります。
contrast.en: The meeting starts at exactly ten.
contrast.note: Clock time on the hour takes ちょうど. ぴったり十時 is heard too and sounds like "ten on the dot", but ちょうど is the neutral choice.

contrast.ja: この靴は足にぴったりです。
contrast.reading: このくつはあしにぴったりです。
contrast.en: These shoes fit my feet perfectly.
contrast.note: Fit between two objects, so ぴったり with に. ちょうどいい would say the size is acceptable; ぴったり says it matches exactly.

contrast.ja: お湯の温度はちょうどいいです。
contrast.reading: おゆのおんどはちょうどいいです。
contrast.en: The water is at just the right temperature.
contrast.note: A value landing in the right range is ちょうどいい. Temperature has no shape to match, so ぴったり does not fit.

contrast.ja: この仕事は彼にぴったりだ。
contrast.reading: このしごとはかれにぴったりだ。
contrast.en: This job is perfect for him.
contrast.note: Suitability between a person and a role is ぴったり. ちょうど cannot carry this "made for you" meaning.

mistakes.wrong: このシャツはちょうどです。
mistakes.right: このシャツはちょうどいいです。／このシャツはぴったりです。
mistakes.why: ちょうど is an adverb and cannot end the sentence as a predicate on its own. Either add いい, or use ぴったり, which can be a predicate.

mistakes.wrong: ぴったり今、出かけます。
mistakes.right: ちょうど今、出かけます。
mistakes.why: For "right now, just at this moment" the set phrase is ちょうど今. ぴったり does not mark a point in time this way.

faq.q: Can I say ぴったり三時?
faq.a: Yes. ぴったり三時 means "three on the dot" and is natural, slightly more emphatic than ちょうど三時. This is the one area where the two genuinely overlap.

faq.q: What is the difference between ちょうどいい and ぴったり for clothes?
faq.a: ちょうどいい means the size works for you — comfortable, not too big or too small. ぴったり means it matches your body exactly, which can be a compliment or, depending on the garment, mean it is tight.

faq.q: Is ぴったり too casual?
faq.a: No. It is an onomatopoeic word but perfectly normal in polite speech and in shops, for example この服はお客様にぴったりですね.

title: かなり vs なかなか
quickAnswer: かなり is a neutral "quite, considerably" that simply states a high degree: この問題はかなり難しい。なかなか adds the speaker's surprise or admiration — なかなかおいしい means "this is better than I expected". The trap is that なかなか with a negative means something else entirely: "not easily, not for ages", as in バスがなかなか来ません.
summary: かなり is a plain "quite"; なかなか is "quite" with surprise or praise — and なかなか + negative means "not easily".

members.when: Use かなり to state that the degree is high, with no attitude attached. It works with good and bad things alike (かなり高い, かなり危ない) and is safe in neutral or written contexts where you do not want to sound as if you are judging.

examples.ja: この問題はかなり難しいです。
examples.reading: このもんだいはかなりむずかしいです。
examples.en: This problem is quite difficult.

examples.ja: 駅まではかなり時間がかかります。
examples.reading: えきまではかなりじかんがかかります。
examples.en: It takes a considerable amount of time to get to the station.

members.when: In affirmative sentences, use なかなか to praise something that beat your expectations: なかなかいい, なかなか上手ですね. With a negative it has a different job entirely — it says something is slow to happen or hard to achieve, as in なかなか覚えられません.

examples.ja: この料理はなかなかおいしいですね。
examples.reading: このりょうりはなかなかおいしいですね。
examples.en: This dish is really rather good.

examples.ja: 新しい漢字がなかなか覚えられません。
examples.reading: あたらしいかんじがなかなかおぼえられません。
examples.en: I just can't seem to memorise the new kanji.

contrast.ja: バスがなかなか来ません。
contrast.reading: バスがなかなかきません。
contrast.en: The bus just won't come.
contrast.note: なかなか + negative = "not easily, not for ages", with a note of impatience. かなり来ません is not Japanese.

contrast.ja: この店はかなり高いです。
contrast.reading: このみせはかなりたかいです。
contrast.en: This shop is quite expensive.
contrast.note: A plain statement of degree about an unwelcome quality, so かなり. なかなか高い would sound oddly appreciative of the price.

contrast.ja: なかなか上手ですね。
contrast.reading: なかなかじょうずですね。
contrast.en: You're pretty good at this, you know.
contrast.note: A compliment with a flavour of pleasant surprise — exactly なかなか's job. かなり上手ですね is a flatter assessment and can sound like grading someone.

contrast.ja: 予約がなかなか取れませんでした。
contrast.reading: よやくがなかなかとれませんでした。
contrast.en: It was really hard to get a reservation.
contrast.note: Difficulty over repeated attempts, so なかなか + negative. To say it plainly you would use かなり難しかった instead.

mistakes.wrong: バスがかなり来ません。
mistakes.right: バスがなかなか来ません。
mistakes.why: かなり modifies a degree, and "not coming" has no degree. "It won't come for ages" is a fixed job of なかなか + negative.

mistakes.wrong: 先生、なかなかお上手ですね。(said to your teacher)
mistakes.right: 先生、本当にお上手ですね。
mistakes.why: なかなか carries "better than I expected", so it implies you had low expectations. It is fine to a friend or a junior, but it can be rude to a superior.

mistakes.wrong: この本はなかなか難しくないです。
mistakes.right: この本はあまり難しくないです。
mistakes.why: Learners read なかなか as "quite" and negate it. With a negative, なかなか means "not easily", so the sentence does not mean "not very difficult".

faq.q: Does なかなか mean "quite" or "not easily"?
faq.a: Both, and the verb form decides. Affirmative なかなかおいしい is "quite tasty, better than expected". Negative なかなか来ない is "doesn't come for ages, won't come easily".

faq.q: Is なかなか rude?
faq.a: Not in itself, but the praise it gives is measured against your own expectations, so aimed upward at a teacher or a boss it can sound condescending. Use 本当に or とても there.

faq.q: Can I use かなり in writing?
faq.a: Yes, かなり is neutral and fine in reports and essays. If you want something more formal still, 相当 and 非常に are the written-style alternatives.

title: ぜひ vs 必ず
quickAnswer: ぜひ expresses your own strong wish or a warm invitation — ぜひ来てください means "I'd really love you to come". 必ず expresses certainty or obligation — 必ず来てください means "be sure to come, no excuses". Swapping them changes how you sound: invite a guest with 必ず and you have given them an order.
summary: ぜひ goes with wishes and invitations (ぜひ来てください); 必ず states certainty or a requirement (必ず来てください is a demand).

members.when: Use ぜひ with requests, invitations and your own desires: ぜひ〜てください, ぜひ〜たい, ぜひお願いします. It never states a fact about the future, so it does not go with plain predictions like "it will definitely rain".

examples.ja: 今度ぜひ遊びに来てください。
examples.reading: こんどぜひあそびにきてください。
examples.en: Please do come and visit sometime.

examples.ja: いつかぜひ日本に住んでみたいです。
examples.reading: いつかぜひにほんにすんでみたいです。
examples.en: I'd really love to live in Japan one day.

members.when: Use 必ず for things that are certain or required: rules, promises, and predictions you are sure of — 必ず提出してください, 必ず連絡します. Note the separate pattern 必ずしも〜ない, meaning "not necessarily".

examples.ja: 明日までに必ず出してください。
examples.reading: あしたまでにかならずだしてください。
examples.en: Make sure you hand it in by tomorrow.

examples.ja: 着いたら必ず連絡します。
examples.reading: ついたらかならずれんらくします。
examples.en: I'll contact you without fail when I arrive.

contrast.ja: ぜひ一度お店に来てください。
contrast.reading: ぜひいちどおみせにきてください。
contrast.en: Please do drop by the shop sometime.
contrast.note: A warm invitation, so ぜひ. 必ず一度来てください would sound as if you were summoning the customer.

contrast.ja: 会議には必ず出席してください。
contrast.reading: かいぎにはかならずしゅっせきしてください。
contrast.en: You must attend the meeting without fail.
contrast.note: An obligation, so 必ず. ぜひ出席してください softens it into an invitation, which is wrong if attendance is compulsory.

contrast.ja: 練習すれば必ず上手になります。
contrast.reading: れんしゅうすればかならずじょうずになります。
contrast.en: If you practise, you'll definitely get better.
contrast.note: A confident statement about a fact. ぜひ cannot appear here at all, because there is no wish or request.

contrast.ja: ぜひご意見を聞かせてください。
contrast.reading: ぜひごいけんをきかせてください。
contrast.en: I'd really like to hear your opinion.
contrast.note: Asking a favour politely — ぜひ signals that this is your wish, not their duty.

mistakes.wrong: パーティーに必ず来てください。(inviting a friend)
mistakes.right: パーティーにぜひ来てください。
mistakes.why: 必ず makes attendance a requirement. Learners who look up "without fail" pick 必ず and unintentionally order their guests around.

mistakes.wrong: ぜひ明日は雨が降ります。
mistakes.right: 明日は必ず雨が降ります。
mistakes.why: ぜひ only attaches to wishes and requests. A statement about what will happen needs 必ず, or きっと for a confident guess.

mistakes.wrong: ぜひ行きます。
mistakes.right: 必ず行きます。／ぜひ行きたいです。
mistakes.why: Promising you will attend is a commitment, so 必ず. ぜひ has to sit with a desire form such as 〜たい.

faq.q: Is ぜひ来てください rude?
faq.a: The opposite — it is the warm, welcoming way to invite someone, and it is standard in shops, emails and everyday speech. 必ず来てください is the one that can sound harsh to a guest.

faq.q: What is the difference between 必ず and きっと?
faq.a: 必ず states objective certainty or a requirement; きっと is the speaker's confident guess (きっと来ますよ — I'm sure he'll come). If you are promising something yourself, use 必ず.

faq.q: Can I answer an invitation with ぜひ on its own?
faq.a: Yes. ぜひ or ぜひお願いします is a natural, enthusiastic "yes, I'd love to".

title: つい vs うっかり
quickAnswer: つい means you did something without meaning to because of habit or impulse — you knew better but could not resist, as in つい食べ過ぎてしまった。うっかり means you did it through carelessness or a lapse of attention, typically forgetting or mixing something up: うっかり財布を忘れた。Impulse is つい; inattention is うっかり.
summary: つい is doing something on impulse or by habit despite yourself; うっかり is doing it through carelessness or forgetting.

members.when: Use つい when temptation or habit got the better of you, usually with 〜てしまう: つい買ってしまった, つい笑ってしまった. It carries a small apology or self-reproach. Separately, つい also means "only just" in time expressions like つい先ほど and つい最近.

examples.ja: おいしくて、つい食べ過ぎてしまいました。
examples.reading: おいしくて、ついたべすぎてしまいました。
examples.en: It was so good that I ended up eating too much.

examples.ja: 彼はつい最近この町に引っ越してきました。
examples.reading: かれはついさいきんこのまちにひっこしてきました。
examples.en: He moved to this town only very recently.

members.when: Use うっかり when your attention slipped: forgetting, misreading, pressing the wrong button, saying something you should not have. It also stands alone as a verb, うっかりする, and modifies a noun in うっかりミス.

examples.ja: うっかり傘を電車に忘れてしまいました。
examples.reading: うっかりかさをでんしゃにわすれてしまいました。
examples.en: I carelessly left my umbrella on the train.

examples.ja: うっかりして、締め切りを過ぎてしまった。
examples.reading: うっかりして、しめきりをすぎてしまった。
examples.en: I wasn't paying attention and missed the deadline.

contrast.ja: つい甘い物を買ってしまう。
contrast.reading: ついあまいものをかってしまう。
contrast.en: I always end up buying sweets even though I shouldn't.
contrast.note: Impulse against your own better judgement, so つい. うっかり買った would mean you bought them by mistake, not because you wanted them.

contrast.ja: うっかり違うボタンを押してしまった。
contrast.reading: うっかりちがうボタンをおしてしまった。
contrast.en: I carelessly pressed the wrong button.
contrast.note: A slip of attention with no desire involved — うっかり. つい押した would suggest you were itching to press it.

contrast.ja: うっかり宿題を家に置いてきた。
contrast.reading: うっかりしゅくだいをいえにおいてきた。
contrast.en: I absent-mindedly left my homework at home.
contrast.note: Forgetting is the core うっかり case. There is no impulse to explain, so つい is off.

contrast.ja: つい大きな声を出してしまった。
contrast.reading: ついおおきなこえをだしてしまった。
contrast.en: I raised my voice before I could stop myself.
contrast.note: A reaction you could not hold back — つい. This is the emotional-reflex use where うっかり does not fit.

mistakes.wrong: つい財布を忘れました。
mistakes.right: うっかり財布を忘れました。
mistakes.why: Forgetting through inattention is うっかり. つい忘れる does exist, but it means you keep forgetting out of habit, which is not what you mean when you left your wallet at home once.

mistakes.wrong: うっかり食べ過ぎてしまった。
mistakes.right: つい食べ過ぎてしまった。
mistakes.why: Overeating is not a lapse of attention — you wanted to keep eating, and that impulse is つい.

mistakes.wrong: うっかり最近、引っ越しました。
mistakes.right: つい最近、引っ越しました。
mistakes.why: The "only just" time meaning belongs to つい alone: つい最近, つい先ほど, つい昨日.

faq.q: Can I use both in the same sentence?
faq.a: Yes, ついうっかり is a natural fixed pair meaning "quite without meaning to", as in ついうっかり口に出してしまった. It stacks both nuances for emphasis.

faq.q: Why is 〜てしまう so often attached?
faq.a: Both adverbs describe something you regret, and 〜てしまう (casual 〜ちゃう) is the form that carries regret. つい and うっかり sound incomplete without it in most sentences.

faq.q: What about わざと?
faq.a: わざと is the opposite — on purpose. If you want to deny intent, つい or うっかり is what you reach for, and わざとじゃない is the direct denial.

title: わざと vs わざわざ
quickAnswer: わざと means "on purpose" — the person intended the result, and it usually sounds like an accusation or a confession. わざわざ means "went out of their way" — the person took extra trouble they did not have to take, and it is normally said with thanks. Use わざと when you are talking about intent, わざわざ when you are talking about effort.
summary: わざと is on purpose (often blame); わざわざ is going to the trouble (usually thanks). Mixing them can sound like an accusation.

members.when: Use わざと when someone did something deliberately, knowing what would happen. It attaches to the intent behind an act, so with anything unwelcome it lands as blame — or, in an apology, as a denial of blame.

examples.ja: ごめん、わざとじゃないんです。
examples.reading: ごめん、わざとじゃないんです。
examples.en: Sorry, I didn't do it on purpose.

examples.ja: 父は子どもとの試合でわざと負けました。
examples.reading: ちちはこどもとのしあいでわざとまけました。
examples.en: My father lost the match to his child on purpose.

members.when: Use わざわざ when someone took trouble they could have avoided — a special trip, an extra step. It says nothing about the result being intended; it comments on the effort, and most often appears in thanks or in telling someone not to bother.

examples.ja: わざわざ来てくれてありがとう。
examples.reading: わざわざきてくれてありがとう。
examples.en: Thank you for coming all this way.

examples.ja: わざわざ買わなくてもいいですよ。
examples.reading: わざわざかわなくてもいいですよ。
examples.en: You don't need to go out of your way to buy it.

contrast.ja: わざわざ駅まで迎えに来てくださいました。
contrast.reading: わざわざえきまでむかえにきてくださいました。
contrast.en: She kindly came all the way to the station to meet me.
contrast.note: The point is the trouble she took, so わざわざ. わざと here would mean she met me deliberately, implying a hidden motive.

contrast.ja: 彼はわざと私の名前を間違えました。
contrast.reading: かれはわざとわたしのなまえをまちがえました。
contrast.en: He got my name wrong on purpose.
contrast.note: A mistake with intent behind it — only わざと. わざわざ would absurdly praise the effort he put into it.

contrast.ja: わざわざ電話をありがとうございます。
contrast.reading: わざわざでんわをありがとうございます。
contrast.en: Thank you for taking the trouble to call.
contrast.note: Fixed polite thanks. Swapping in わざと would accuse the caller of phoning with some intention.

contrast.ja: わざと遅く来たのではありません。
contrast.reading: わざとおそくきたのではありません。
contrast.en: I wasn't late on purpose.
contrast.note: Denying intent, which is わざと's job. わざわざ遅く来た would mean you made a special effort to arrive late.

mistakes.wrong: わざと来てくれてありがとう。
mistakes.right: わざわざ来てくれてありがとう。
mistakes.why: Thanking someone with わざと says thanks for coming with an ulterior motive. Thanks always takes わざわざ.

mistakes.wrong: すみません、わざわざではありません。
mistakes.right: すみません、わざとではありません。
mistakes.why: An apology denies intent, not effort. The set phrase is わざとじゃない / わざとではありません.

faq.q: Is わざわざ always polite?
faq.a: Usually, but not always. Said flatly about someone's pointless extra effort — わざわざそんなことをしなくても — it can sound like mild criticism, as in why did you bother? In thanks it is entirely warm.

faq.q: Can I use わざと about myself?
faq.a: Yes, most often in the negative: わざとじゃない, I didn't mean to. Saying わざとやりました about yourself is an outright admission that you did it deliberately.

faq.q: Are they ever interchangeable?
faq.a: No. They answer different questions — わざと answers did you mean to?, and わざわざ answers did you go out of your way? A sentence can take either word, but the meaning changes completely.

title: 場所 vs 所
quickAnswer: 場所 is a physical place or the space something occupies — a spot you can point to on a map. 所 (ところ) covers that too but is much broader: it also means an aspect or point about a person or thing, as in いい所, a good point. When you mean a concrete location, either works and 場所 is the safer choice; when you mean something abstract, only 所 will do.
summary: 場所 is a concrete spot or space; 所 is broader and also means an aspect or point about someone or something.

members.when: Use 場所 for a definite physical location — where an event is held, where you will meet — and for space in the sense of room. It is the word you want when someone asks where exactly.

examples.ja: 会議の場所を教えてください。
examples.reading: かいぎのばしょをおしえてください。
examples.en: Please tell me the location of the meeting.

examples.ja: この机は場所を取りますね。
