examples.reading: このつくえはばしょをとりますね。
examples.en: This desk takes up a lot of space, doesn't it?

members.when: Use 所 for a place in a looser sense — 静かな所, 住んでいる所 — and for a non-physical point or part: 彼のいい所 is a good quality of his, not a spot. Read ところ, it also carries a long list of grammar patterns, which is a separate topic from the noun.

examples.ja: 静かな所に住みたいです。
examples.reading: しずかなところにすみたいです。
examples.en: I want to live somewhere quiet.

examples.ja: 彼女のいい所は明るい所です。
examples.reading: かのじょのいいところはあかるいところです。
examples.en: The good thing about her is how cheerful she is.

contrast.ja: 待ち合わせの場所はどこですか。
contrast.reading: まちあわせのばしょはどこですか。
contrast.en: Where is the meeting spot?
contrast.note: A specific point to stand at, so 場所. 所 would sound vague, more like what sort of area.

contrast.ja: この計画には分からない所があります。
contrast.reading: このけいかくにはわからないところがあります。
contrast.en: There are parts of this plan I don't understand.
contrast.note: Parts of a plan are not physical, so 場所 is impossible here.

contrast.ja: 車を止める場所がありません。
contrast.reading: くるまをとめるばしょがありません。
contrast.en: There's nowhere to park the car.
contrast.note: Space for something — 場所's core use. 所 is possible but less precise about the physical room.

contrast.ja: 彼のそういう所が好きです。
contrast.reading: かれのそういうところがすきです。
contrast.en: That's the side of him I like.
contrast.note: An aspect of a person, which only 所 can express.

mistakes.wrong: 彼のいい場所は優しい場所です。
mistakes.right: 彼のいい所は優しい所です。
mistakes.why: 場所 only means a physical location, so this reads as though the man owns good real estate. A good point about someone is always 所.

mistakes.wrong: この所に名前を書いてください。
mistakes.right: この場所に名前を書いてください。
mistakes.why: Pointing at a precise spot on a form calls for 場所. この所 is not ungrammatical but is not how anyone says it.

faq.q: Is 所 always written in kanji?
faq.a: Often not. As a plain place noun the kanji 所 is common, but when it works as a grammar word — 食べたところ, 〜するところだ — it is normally written in kana as ところ.

faq.q: Can I just use 場所 for everything?
faq.a: For concrete locations, nearly always yes, and it will sound natural. But you cannot use it for aspects or points about a person or thing, and it does not appear in the ところ grammar patterns.

faq.q: Do they read the same?
faq.a: No. 場所 is ばしょ and 所 on its own is ところ. The same kanji is read しょ or じょ inside compounds like 事務所 and 近所.

title: 値段 vs 価格
quickAnswer: Both mean price and often refer to the same number. 値段 is the everyday spoken word — what you ask a shop assistant. 価格 is the formal written one, used on price tags, product pages, contracts and in business news. In conversation, default to 値段.
summary: 値段 is the everyday spoken word for price; 価格 is the formal written one used in shops, documents and business news.

members.when: Use 値段 when talking about what something costs in ordinary conversation — asking a price, saying something is expensive or cheap. It is the natural choice for daily shopping.

examples.ja: この靴の値段を聞いてもいいですか。
examples.reading: このくつのねだんをきいてもいいですか。
examples.en: May I ask the price of these shoes?

examples.ja: 思ったより値段が安かったです。
examples.reading: おもったよりねだんがやすかったです。
examples.en: It was cheaper than I expected.

members.when: Use 価格 in writing and formal speech: product listings, business reports, news about markets. It also forms compounds like 販売価格 and 価格表 where 値段 cannot be substituted.

examples.ja: 本日より販売価格を変更いたします。
examples.reading: ほんじつよりはんばいかかくをへんこういたします。
examples.en: The selling price changes as of today.

examples.ja: 原油の価格が上がっています。
examples.reading: げんゆのかかくがあがっています。
examples.en: The price of crude oil is rising.

contrast.ja: すみません、これの値段はいくらですか。
contrast.reading: すみません、これのねだんはいくらですか。
contrast.en: Excuse me, how much is this?
contrast.note: Spoken to a shop assistant, so 値段. 価格 here would sound like reading from a catalogue.

contrast.ja: 各社の価格を比較した表です。
contrast.reading: かくしゃのかかくをひかくしたひょうです。
contrast.en: This is a table comparing each company's prices.
contrast.note: A written business document — 価格 matches the register.

contrast.ja: 希望小売価格は三千円です。
contrast.reading: きぼうこうりかかくはさんぜんえんです。
contrast.en: The recommended retail price is 3,000 yen.
contrast.note: A fixed compound term; 値段 cannot replace 価格 inside it.

contrast.ja: この店は値段が高いね。
contrast.reading: このみせはねだんがたかいね。
contrast.en: This shop is pricey, isn't it?
contrast.note: Casual remark to a friend. 価格が高いね would sound oddly stiff.

mistakes.wrong: この大根の価格はいくらですか。
mistakes.right: この大根の値段はいくらですか。
mistakes.why: Asking about a vegetable at a market is everyday talk, and 価格 makes it sound like a market analysis. Not ungrammatical, just unnatural.

mistakes.wrong: 大値段
mistakes.right: 値段が高い
mistakes.why: 値段 does not form compounds the way 価格 does. Say 値段が高い in speech, and switch to 価格 when you need a compound such as 販売価格.

faq.q: Is one of them more expensive-sounding?
faq.a: No — neither implies a high or low amount. The difference is register only: 値段 casual and spoken, 価格 formal and written.

faq.q: What about 料金 and 代金?
faq.a: Those are different things: 料金 is a fee or fare for a service, and 代金 is the sum you owe for goods. 値段 and 価格 are what an item costs.

faq.q: Can I use 価格 in conversation?
faq.a: Yes, and it is normal at work or when discussing markets. Outside those contexts it sounds formal, so 値段 is the safer everyday default.

title: 仕事 vs 職業
quickAnswer: 仕事 is the work you do — your job, and also the individual tasks piled on your desk. 職業 is your occupation as a category, the word on a form next to a blank you fill in with doctor or teacher. If you can count it, finish it, or be busy with it, it is 仕事.
summary: 仕事 is the work you do or a task at hand; 職業 is occupation as a category, the formal word used on forms.

members.when: Use 仕事 for work in general, for your job, and for the concrete tasks that make it up. It goes with verbs of daily life — 仕事をする, 仕事に行く, 仕事が忙しい — where 職業 never appears.

examples.ja: 今日は仕事が多くて大変です。
examples.reading: きょうはしごとがおおくてたいへんです。
examples.en: I have a lot of work today; it's tough.

examples.ja: 七時に仕事が終わります。
examples.reading: しちじにしごとがおわります。
examples.en: I finish work at seven.

members.when: Use 職業 when naming an occupation as a type: on an application form, in a survey, in a discussion of careers. It is a classification, not an activity, so you cannot do it or go to it.

examples.ja: この用紙に職業をご記入ください。
examples.reading: このようしにしょくぎょうをごきにゅうください。
examples.en: Please write your occupation on this form.

examples.ja: 将来の職業について考えています。
examples.reading: しょうらいのしょくぎょうについてかんがえています。
examples.en: I'm thinking about what career to go into.

contrast.ja: 職業は何ですか。
contrast.reading: しょくぎょうはなんですか。
contrast.en: What is your occupation?
contrast.note: Asking for a category, typical of forms and officials. Friends ask お仕事は何ですか instead.

contrast.ja: 明日は仕事を休みます。
contrast.reading: あしたはしごとをやすみます。
contrast.en: I'm taking tomorrow off work.
contrast.note: You take a day off from the activity, so 仕事. 職業を休む is impossible.

contrast.ja: この仕事は三時までに終わらせます。
contrast.reading: このしごとはさんじまでにおわらせます。
contrast.en: I'll finish this task by three.
contrast.note: A single countable task — a meaning 職業 does not have at all.

contrast.ja: 医者という職業に興味があります。
contrast.reading: いしゃというしょくぎょうにきょうみがあります。
contrast.en: I'm interested in the profession of medicine.
contrast.note: Naming a profession as a category calls for 職業.

mistakes.wrong: 毎日職業をしています。
mistakes.right: 毎日仕事をしています。
mistakes.why: 職業 is a label, not an activity, so it cannot take をする. Daily work is always 仕事をする.

mistakes.wrong: 職業が忙しいです。
mistakes.right: 仕事が忙しいです。
mistakes.why: Being busy is about the work in front of you, not about your occupational category.

mistakes.wrong: あなたの職業は何ですか。
mistakes.right: お仕事は何ですか。
mistakes.why: Grammatically fine, but to a new acquaintance it sounds like an official interviewing you. Casual conversation uses お仕事は.

faq.q: Which one do I say when someone asks what I do?
faq.a: Answer with 仕事: 仕事は先生です, or simply 先生です. Save 職業 for written forms.

faq.q: Can 仕事 mean a single task?
faq.a: Yes, and this is a common use — この仕事 can be one report on your desk. 職業 can never be counted this way.

faq.q: What about 職 and 職場?
faq.a: 職 alone is a post or position, as in 職を探す, to look for a job. 職場 is your workplace, the physical place and the people in it.

title: 会社 vs 企業
quickAnswer: 会社 is the company you work at — a place you go to, take a day off from, and talk about with friends. 企業 is a firm as a business entity, the word used in news, analysis and job hunting. Both translate as company, but only 企業 appears in 大企業, and only 会社 in 会社に行く.
summary: 会社 is the company you go to and work at; 企業 is a firm as a business entity, used in news, analysis and job hunting.

members.when: Use 会社 for a company as an organisation you belong to or deal with, including the office itself. This is the everyday word: 会社に行く, 会社を休む, うちの会社.

examples.ja: 今日は会社を休みました。
examples.reading: きょうはかいしゃをやすみました。
examples.en: I took the day off work today.

examples.ja: うちの会社は社員が五十人です。
examples.reading: うちのかいしゃはしゃいんがごじゅうにんです。
examples.en: Our company has fifty employees.

members.when: Use 企業 when treating a company as a business entity — in news, economics, and job hunting. It is the base of compounds such as 大企業, 中小企業 and 外国企業, where 会社 does not fit.

examples.ja: 多くの企業が海外に進出しています。
examples.reading: おおくのきぎょうがかいがいにしんしゅつしています。
examples.en: Many firms are expanding overseas.

examples.ja: 中小企業を支援する制度です。
examples.reading: ちゅうしょうきぎょうをしえんするせいどです。
examples.en: It's a scheme to support small and medium-sized businesses.

contrast.ja: 兄は大企業で働いています。
contrast.reading: あにはだいきぎょうではたらいています。
contrast.en: My older brother works for a big corporation.
contrast.note: 大企業 is the fixed form; 大会社 is not used. Say 大きい会社 if you want 会社.

contrast.ja: 毎朝八時に会社に行きます。
contrast.reading: まいあさはちじにかいしゃにいきます。
contrast.en: I go to the office at eight every morning.
contrast.note: Going to a physical workplace — 企業に行く is not said.

contrast.ja: その企業の業績が悪くなりました。
contrast.reading: そのきぎょうのぎょうせきがわるくなりました。
contrast.en: That firm's results have worsened.
contrast.note: News register, the company as an economic actor, so 企業.

contrast.ja: 小さい会社ですが、働きやすいです。
contrast.reading: ちいさいかいしゃですが、はたらきやすいです。
contrast.en: It's a small company, but it's easy to work at.
contrast.note: Talking about your own workplace is 会社 territory.

mistakes.wrong: 父は大会社で働いています。
mistakes.right: 父は大企業で働いています。
mistakes.why: 大会社 is not an established word. Use 大企業, or 大きい会社 with the adjective spelled out.

mistakes.wrong: 今日は企業に行きません。
mistakes.right: 今日は会社に行きません。
mistakes.why: 企業 is an abstract entity, not a building you commute to. Going in to work is always 会社に行く.

faq.q: Is 企業 more formal than 会社?
faq.a: Yes, and it is also more abstract. 会社 is neutral and usable anywhere in daily life; 企業 belongs to news, business writing and job hunting.

faq.q: Which do I use when job hunting?
faq.a: Both come up. 企業 is standard for firms as targets — 企業研究, 大手企業 — while you still say 会社 for the specific one you join and for its office.

faq.q: Does 会社 mean the building?
faq.a: It can. 会社に忘れた means you left something at the office, so context decides between the organisation and the place. 企業 never means a building.

title: 友達 vs 友人
quickAnswer: They mean the same thing; the difference is register. 友達 is the everyday spoken word and what you should use by default. 友人 is its formal written counterpart, for essays, self-introductions at work and polite letters. Note that 友達 covers one friend or many with no change of form.
summary: 友達 is the everyday word for friend; 友人 is the same meaning in formal or written Japanese. Both cover one friend or several.

members.when: Use 友達 in conversation and casual writing — this is the default. It is also the word for making friends: 友達になる. It does not mark number, so 友達と行く can be with one friend or with several.

examples.ja: 週末に友達と映画を見ました。
examples.reading: しゅうまつにともだちとえいがをみました。
examples.en: I watched a film with a friend at the weekend.

examples.ja: 日本で友達をたくさん作りたいです。
examples.reading: にほんでともだちをたくさんつくりたいです。
examples.en: I want to make lots of friends in Japan.

members.when: Use 友人 in formal contexts: written Japanese, speeches, business settings, or when speaking politely about someone. It carries a more adult, restrained tone than 友達, but means the same relationship.

examples.ja: 大学時代の友人と再会しました。
examples.reading: だいがくじだいのゆうじんとさいかいしました。
examples.en: I met up again with a friend from my university days.

examples.ja: 友人の結婚式に出席いたします。
examples.reading: ゆうじんのけっこんしきにしゅっせきいたします。
examples.en: I will be attending a friend's wedding.

contrast.ja: ねえ、友達になろうよ。
contrast.reading: ねえ、ともだちになろうよ。
contrast.en: Hey, let's be friends.
contrast.note: Casual invitation between peers. 友人になろう would sound stiff and distant.

contrast.ja: 本日は友人を代表してご挨拶いたします。
contrast.reading: ほんじつはゆうじんをだいひょうしてごあいさついたします。
contrast.en: Today I offer a few words on behalf of the friends.
contrast.note: A formal speech, so 友人 matches the register.

contrast.ja: 子どもの友達が遊びに来ました。
contrast.reading: こどものともだちがあそびにきました。
contrast.en: My child's friend came over to play.
contrast.note: Children's friendships are normally 友達; 友人 sounds oddly adult here.

contrast.ja: 友人からいただいた本です。
contrast.reading: ゆうじんからいただいたほんです。
contrast.en: It's a book I received from a friend.
contrast.note: The humble いただく sets a polite register that 友人 fits.

mistakes.wrong: 友達たち
mistakes.right: 友達
mistakes.why: 友達 already covers the plural, so 友達たち is redundant. You hear it occasionally in casual speech, but it is not standard writing.

mistakes.wrong: 昨日、友人と遊びました。
mistakes.right: 昨日、友達と遊びました。
mistakes.why: 遊ぶ in the sense of hanging out is casual, and pairing it with the formal 友人 clashes. Match the register across the sentence.

faq.q: Is 友人 a closer friend than 友達?
faq.a: No. Neither word says how close the friendship is; the difference is only how formal the wording is. Use 親友 if you mean a close or best friend.

faq.q: How do I say my friends as a plural?
faq.a: Just 友達. If you need to make plurality explicit, add a quantity word: 友達が何人か, 友達がたくさん.

faq.q: Which should I use in a self-introduction?
faq.a: In a classroom or with peers, 友達. In a written essay or a formal introduction at work, 友人 reads better.

title: 洋服 vs 服
quickAnswer: 服 just means clothes, and it is the word to use almost all the time. 洋服 specifically means Western-style clothes as opposed to 和服 or 着物, so it only earns its keep when that contrast is actually in play — which, in modern daily life, is rarely.
summary: 服 means clothes and is the everyday default; 洋服 means Western-style clothes, and matters only when contrasted with 和服 or 着物.

members.when: Use 洋服 when the Western-versus-Japanese contrast matters — at a ceremony where some guests wear 着物, or in talk about traditional dress. It also survives in the shop name 洋服屋, and older speakers use it loosely for clothes in general.

examples.ja: 式には着物ではなく洋服で行きます。
examples.reading: しきにはきものではなくようふくでいきます。
examples.en: I'll go to the ceremony in Western dress rather than a kimono.

examples.ja: 祖母は洋服より着物のほうが好きです。
examples.reading: そぼはようふくよりきもののほうがすきです。
examples.en: My grandmother prefers kimono to Western clothes.

members.when: Use 服 for clothes in any ordinary sentence — buying them, washing them, choosing what to wear. Unless you are drawing a contrast with traditional dress, this is the word.

examples.ja: 新しい服を買いに行きます。
examples.reading: あたらしいふくをかいにいきます。
examples.en: I'm going to buy some new clothes.

examples.ja: 服が汚れてしまいました。
examples.reading: ふくがよごれてしまいました。
examples.en: My clothes got dirty.

contrast.ja: 明日はどんな服を着ますか。
contrast.reading: あしたはどんなふくをきますか。
contrast.en: What are you going to wear tomorrow?
contrast.note: Everyday question with no traditional-dress contrast, so plain 服.

contrast.ja: 成人式では着物か洋服かを選びます。
contrast.reading: せいじんしきではきものかようふくかをえらびます。
contrast.en: At the coming-of-age ceremony you choose between kimono and Western dress.
contrast.note: The contrast is explicit, which is exactly when 洋服 is needed.

contrast.ja: 服を洗濯しました。
contrast.reading: ふくをせんたくしました。
contrast.en: I did the laundry.
contrast.note: Routine household sentence; 洋服 would add a distinction nobody is making.

contrast.ja: 昔は洋服が珍しかったそうです。
contrast.reading: むかしはようふくがめずらしかったそうです。
contrast.en: Apparently Western clothes were rare in the past.
contrast.note: A historical statement about Western dress arriving in Japan — 服 would lose the point.

mistakes.wrong: 毎日洋服を着ます。
mistakes.right: 毎日服を着ます。
mistakes.why: Technically true, but pointing out that your daily outfit is Western-style is information nobody asked for. Plain 服 is what a native speaker says.

mistakes.wrong: 着物も洋服の一つです。
mistakes.right: 着物も服の一つです。
mistakes.why: 洋服 excludes 着物 by definition; the general category is 服.

faq.q: Do Japanese people still say 洋服 a lot?
faq.a: Less than they used to. It survives in 洋服屋 and in older speakers' everyday use, but younger speakers mostly say 服 unless kimono is in the picture.

faq.q: What is the opposite of 洋服?
faq.a: 和服, Japanese-style clothing, of which 着物 is the best-known form. That pairing is the whole reason 洋服 exists as a separate word.

faq.q: Is 衣服 different again?
faq.a: Yes — 衣服 is the formal written term for clothing, seen in documents and on signs. It is neutral about style, like 服, but far stiffer in tone.

title: 料理 vs 食事
quickAnswer: 料理 is cooking, or a cooked dish — the food itself and the act of making it. 食事 is a meal as an occasion, the event of eating. So 料理をする means you are at the stove, while 食事をする means you are at the table.
summary: 料理 is cooking or a dish; 食事 is a meal as an occasion. 料理をする is cooking, 食事をする is eating.

members.when: Use 料理 for the act of cooking, for a dish, and for a cuisine: 日本料理, 母の料理. If you are talking about what was made, how it tastes, or who made it, this is the word.

examples.ja: 母の料理はとてもおいしいです。
examples.reading: ははのりょうりはとてもおいしいです。
examples.en: My mother's cooking is delicious.

examples.ja: 今晩は私が料理をします。
examples.reading: こんばんはわたしがりょうりをします。
examples.en: I'll do the cooking tonight.

members.when: Use 食事 for a meal as an occasion — having one, inviting someone to one, what happens before or after it. It is also a する verb, so 食事する means to eat a meal, never to cook one.

examples.ja: 食事の前に手を洗ってください。
examples.reading: しょくじのまえにてをあらってください。
examples.en: Please wash your hands before the meal.

examples.ja: 今度一緒に食事しませんか。
examples.reading: こんどいっしょにしょくじしませんか。
examples.en: Shall we have a meal together sometime?

contrast.ja: 毎晩、夫が料理をします。
contrast.reading: まいばん、おっとがりょうりをします。
contrast.en: My husband cooks every evening.
contrast.note: Making the food, so 料理. 食事をします would mean he merely eats it.

contrast.ja: 食事はもう済ませました。
contrast.reading: しょくじはもうすませました。
contrast.en: I've already eaten.
contrast.note: The meal as an event you finish — 料理 cannot be used this way.

contrast.ja: この店の料理はおいしいです。
contrast.reading: このみせのりょうりはおいしいです。
contrast.en: The food at this restaurant is good.
contrast.note: Praising the dishes themselves, which is 料理.

contrast.ja: 食事に誘われました。
contrast.reading: しょくじにさそわれました。
contrast.en: I was invited out for a meal.
contrast.note: An occasion you invite someone to, so 食事.

mistakes.wrong: 昨日の夜、友達と料理をしました。
mistakes.right: 昨日の夜、友達と食事をしました。
mistakes.why: 料理をする is cooking. If you meant you went out to eat together, that is 食事をする — otherwise you have said you spent the evening in the kitchen.

mistakes.wrong: 母は食事が上手です。
mistakes.right: 母は料理が上手です。
mistakes.why: Being good at this means being good at cooking. 食事が上手 would oddly praise her skill at eating.

faq.q: Can 食事 mean the food itself?
faq.a: Somewhat — 食事を用意する is preparing the meal, including the food. But when you praise how something tastes, use 料理.

faq.q: What about ご飯?
faq.a: ご飯 is the casual everyday word for both cooked rice and a meal: ご飯を食べる. 食事 is the more formal way of naming the same occasion.

faq.q: Is 料理 only for Japanese-style food?
faq.a: No. 料理 takes any cuisine — イタリア料理, 中華料理 — and also just means the cooking someone does at home.

title: 道 vs 道路
quickAnswer: Default to 道 — it covers any road, street or way, including the route to somewhere and a path in the figurative sense. 道路 is the physical constructed roadway, and it belongs in traffic and civil-engineering talk: 道路工事, 高速道路, 道路が込む. Asking for directions is always 道を聞く, never 道路を聞く.
summary: 道 is any road, route or path, and the word you default to; 道路 is the built roadway used in traffic and construction contexts.

members.when: Use 道 for a road or street you walk or drive on, for the route to a place (道を聞く, 道に迷う), and for a figurative path such as a career or a way of life. It is the everyday word and is almost never wrong.

examples.ja: すみません、駅までの道を教えてください。
examples.reading: すみません、えきまでのみちをおしえてください。
examples.en: Excuse me, could you tell me the way to the station?

examples.ja: 公園の中に細い道があります。
examples.reading: こうえんのなかにほそいみちがあります。
examples.en: There is a narrow path inside the park.

members.when: Use 道路 when you mean the roadway as a piece of built infrastructure — traffic, congestion, roadworks, expressways, road signs. It is the word of news reports, road signs and official notices, and it has no figurative sense.

examples.ja: 家の前で道路工事をしています。
examples.reading: いえのまえでどうろこうじをしています。
examples.en: There are roadworks going on in front of my house.

examples.ja: 高速道路は事故で込んでいます。
examples.reading: こうそくどうろはじこでこんでいます。
examples.en: The expressway is congested because of an accident.

contrast.ja: 交番で道を聞きました。
contrast.reading: こうばんでみちをききました。
contrast.en: I asked for directions at the police box.
contrast.note: 道を聞く means to ask the way. 道路を聞く would sound like you are asking about the pavement itself, not about how to get somewhere.

contrast.ja: この道路は去年できました。
contrast.reading: このどうろはきょねんできました。
contrast.en: This road was built last year.
contrast.note: The point is the road as a constructed object, so 道路 is the natural choice. 道 here would sound oddly vague.

contrast.ja: 夢に向かって自分の道を歩きます。
contrast.reading: ゆめにむかってじぶんのみちをあるきます。
contrast.en: I walk my own path towards my dream.
contrast.note: Only 道 has the figurative sense of a path in life. 道路 cannot be used this way at all.

contrast.ja: 台風で道路が通れません。
contrast.reading: たいふうでどうろがとおれません。
contrast.en: The road is impassable because of the typhoon.
contrast.note: Traffic and road-closure reports use 道路. 道 is not wrong in speech here, but 道路 is what you will hear on the news.

mistakes.wrong: 道路を聞いてもいいですか。
mistakes.right: 道を聞いてもいいですか。
mistakes.why: Asking the way is a fixed pairing with 道. With 道路 a listener expects a question about the roadway itself, and has to work out that you are lost.

mistakes.wrong: 科学の道路に進みます。
mistakes.right: 科学の道に進みます。
mistakes.why: A career path is 道. 道路 is only ever asphalt, so this sounds like you are literally driving onto a science-themed street.

faq.q: Can I use 道 for a big highway?
faq.a: Yes. 道 covers everything from a garden path to a motorway, so 大きい道 is perfectly natural. 高速道路 is a fixed word, though, so keep 道路 in that compound.

faq.q: Is 道路 ever plain wrong?
faq.a: It is wrong for asking directions and for anything figurative. For an ordinary physical road both words work, and 道路 just sounds a little more technical.

faq.q: Which one should I use as a beginner?
faq.a: 道. It is N5, it fits nearly every sentence a beginner writes, and you only need 道路 for traffic and construction topics.

title: 店 vs 商店
quickAnswer: 店 is the everyday word for any shop, and it is the one to use in almost every sentence. 商店 is formal and now survives mostly inside compounds and names such as 商店街 and 山田商店 — a learner very rarely needs it as a standalone word.
summary: 店 is the ordinary word for any shop; 商店 is formal and mostly lives on in compounds and shop names like 商店街.

members.when: Use 店 for any shop, restaurant, café or bar, in speech and in writing. If you are talking about a place you buy things from, this is the word.

examples.ja: 駅の近くに新しい店ができました。
examples.reading: えきのちかくにあたらしいみせができました。
examples.en: A new shop has opened near the station.

examples.ja: この店は八時に閉まります。
examples.reading: このみせははちじにしまります。
examples.en: This shop closes at eight.

members.when: Use 商店 in formal or administrative writing about small retail businesses, and in the fixed compounds and shop names it lives in: 商店街, 小売商店, 田中商店. Do not reach for it to describe a shop you are standing in.

examples.ja: 駅前の商店街はいつもにぎやかです。
examples.reading: えきまえのしょうてんがいはいつもにぎやかです。
examples.en: The shopping street in front of the station is always lively.

examples.ja: 山田商店は百年続いています。
examples.reading: やまだしょうてんはひゃくねんつづいています。
examples.en: Yamada Shoten has been in business for a hundred years.

contrast.ja: どの店でご飯を食べますか。
contrast.reading: どのみせでごはんをたべますか。
contrast.en: Which place shall we eat at?
contrast.note: Everyday conversation takes 店. 商店 would sound like a line from a town-planning document.

contrast.ja: 商店街で買い物をしました。
contrast.reading: しょうてんがいでかいものをしました。
contrast.en: I did my shopping in the shopping street.
contrast.note: 商店街 is a fixed compound with no 店街 alternative, and it is by far the commonest place a learner meets 商店.

contrast.ja: 市は地域の商店を支援しています。
contrast.reading: しはちいきのしょうてんをしえんしています。
contrast.en: The city supports local retailers.
contrast.note: Formal writing about businesses as a category is where 商店 still stands alone naturally.

mistakes.wrong: この商店はおいしいです。
mistakes.right: この店はおいしいです。
mistakes.why: 商店 is a category label for a retail business, not a name for the restaurant in front of you. It sounds like reading a survey out loud.

mistakes.wrong: 商店に入りましょう。
mistakes.right: 店に入りましょう。
mistakes.why: Going into a shop is plain everyday talk and takes 店. 商店 is far too stiff for an invitation.

faq.q: Do I need to learn 商店 at all?
faq.a: Learn to recognise it, mainly in 商店街 and in shop names. You will almost never need to produce it yourself — 店 covers what you want to say.

faq.q: Is 商店 old-fashioned?
faq.a: As a standalone word it does feel dated and formal, which is why so many old family shops are called 〇〇商店. In compounds it is still completely current.

faq.q: What about お店?
faq.a: お店 is just 店 with a polite prefix, and it is very common in everyday speech. It is still the same word, so the advice above is unchanged.

title: 机 vs テーブル
quickAnswer: 机 is a desk — the thing you sit at to study or work, usually with drawers. テーブル is a table you eat at or gather around. If people are having a meal on it, it is テーブル, even though English calls both of them furniture with four legs.
summary: 机 is a desk you study or work at; テーブル is a table you eat at or sit around. Dining tables are never 机.

members.when: Use 机 for a study or office desk: the one in a classroom, a bedroom or an office, the kind with drawers where you read, write and use a computer.

examples.ja: 机で宿題をしています。
examples.reading: つくえでしゅくだいをしています。
examples.en: I am doing my homework at my desk.

examples.ja: 教室に机が三十あります。
examples.reading: きょうしつにつくえがさんじゅうあります。
examples.en: There are thirty desks in the classroom.

members.when: Use テーブル for a dining table, a café table, a low living-room table or a meeting table — anything people sit around together rather than work at alone.

examples.ja: 家族でテーブルを囲みました。
examples.reading: かぞくでテーブルをかこみました。
examples.en: The family gathered round the table.

examples.ja: テーブルにお皿を並べてください。
examples.reading: テーブルにおさらをならべてください。
examples.en: Please set the plates out on the table.

contrast.ja: 料理をテーブルに運びます。
contrast.reading: りょうりをテーブルにはこびます。
contrast.en: I carry the food to the table.
contrast.note: Food goes on a テーブル. Saying 机 here makes it sound like you are eating alone at your study desk.

contrast.ja: 机の引き出しにペンが入っています。
contrast.reading: つくえのひきだしにペンがはいっています。
contrast.en: There are pens in the desk drawer.
contrast.note: Drawers for stationery are a desk feature, so 机. A テーブル normally has no drawers.

contrast.ja: 毎晩、机に向かって勉強します。
contrast.reading: まいばん、つくえにむかってべんきょうします。
contrast.en: I sit down at my desk and study every evening.
contrast.note: 机に向かう is a set phrase for settling down to study. テーブル does not work in it.

mistakes.wrong: 毎晩、家族で机を囲んでご飯を食べます。
mistakes.right: 毎晩、家族でテーブルを囲んでご飯を食べます。
mistakes.why: This is the classic one: learners map 机 onto English "table". A family meal happens at a テーブル; 机 makes listeners picture everyone squeezed round a study desk.

mistakes.wrong: 丸い机を買いました。
mistakes.right: 丸いテーブルを買いました。
mistakes.why: If you mean a round dining table, it is テーブル. Round 机 are rare, so the sentence sounds like an unusual custom desk.

faq.q: What if I eat lunch at my desk at work?
faq.a: Then 机 is right, because you are naming the desk, not a dining table. 机でお弁当を食べます is completely natural.

faq.q: Is there a Japanese word for a dining table specifically?
faq.a: Yes, 食卓 (しょくたく), which is a little more literary. In everyday speech テーブル is what people say.

faq.q: Can a low living-room table be 机?
faq.a: You will hear both, and ローテーブル is common for the low ones. If you are unsure, テーブル is the safer default for anything in the living room.

title: 映画 vs 番組
quickAnswer: 映画 is a film — the work itself, wherever you watch it. 番組 is a programme: one unit of television or radio broadcasting, such as a news show, a drama series or a variety show. A film shown on TV can be called either, depending on whether you mean the work or the slot it fills.
summary: 映画 is a film; 番組 is a TV or radio programme. Choose by whether you mean the work itself or the broadcast slot.

members.when: Use 映画 for a film, whether you see it at the cinema, stream it or catch it on television. It names the work, so it never depends on how it reaches you.

examples.ja: 週末に映画を見に行きます。
examples.reading: しゅうまつにえいがをみにいきます。
examples.en: I am going to see a film at the weekend.

examples.ja: この映画は三時間もあります。
examples.reading: このえいがはさんじかんもあります。
examples.en: This film is a full three hours long.

members.when: Use 番組 for anything that fills a slot on TV or radio: news, dramas, quiz shows, sports coverage. It is the unit of broadcasting, so it only makes sense when something is being broadcast or streamed as a show.

examples.ja: 七時のニュース番組を見ます。
examples.reading: しちじのニュースばんぐみをみます。
examples.en: I watch the seven o'clock news programme.

examples.ja: ラジオ番組に手紙を送りました。
examples.reading: ラジオばんぐみにてがみをおくりました。
examples.en: I sent a letter to a radio programme.

contrast.ja: 映画館で映画を見ました。
contrast.reading: えいがかんでえいがをみました。
contrast.en: I saw a film at the cinema.
contrast.note: Nothing is being broadcast, so 番組 is impossible here.

contrast.ja: 今日の番組は何ですか。
contrast.reading: きょうのばんぐみはなんですか。
contrast.en: What is on today?
contrast.note: You are asking about the schedule, not about a particular work, so only 番組 fits.

contrast.ja: 今夜テレビで映画をやります。
contrast.reading: こんやテレビでえいがをやります。
contrast.en: There is a film on TV tonight.
contrast.note: Here both are possible: 映画 names the work, and 番組 would be right if you meant the slot in the evening's schedule.

contrast.ja: その番組は毎週水曜日にやっています。
contrast.reading: そのばんぐみはまいしゅうすいようびにやっています。
contrast.en: That show is on every Wednesday.
contrast.note: A weekly series is a 番組. A 映画 is a single finished work and does not run weekly.

mistakes.wrong: 映画館で番組を見ました。
mistakes.right: 映画館で映画を見ました。
mistakes.why: 番組 implies broadcasting. In a cinema there is no broadcast, so the sentence sounds like the cinema was showing live TV.

mistakes.wrong: 好きな映画は毎週金曜日にあります。
mistakes.right: 好きな番組は毎週金曜日にあります。
mistakes.why: Learners use 映画 for anything on a screen. A recurring weekly show is a 番組; 映画 makes it sound like the same film is screened every Friday.

faq.q: If a film is showing on TV, is it 映画 or 番組?
faq.a: Either, depending on what you mean. 映画 if you are talking about the film; 番組 if you mean the item in tonight's schedule. Both are heard.

faq.q: Is a drama series a 映画?
faq.a: No. A TV drama is a 番組, or more specifically ドラマ. 映画 is reserved for films.

faq.q: Does 番組 work for something on the internet?
faq.a: Yes, when it is show-shaped — a scheduled or serialised programme. People say ネット番組 and 配信番組 quite naturally.

title: 先生 vs 教師
quickAnswer: 先生 is a title and a way of addressing someone — teachers, but also doctors, lawyers and other experts. 教師 is the name of the occupation, the word you write on a form or use to describe what someone does. Never call your teacher 教師さん; you address them as 先生, or as 名前 plus 先生.
summary: 先生 is the respectful title you call someone by; 教師 is the occupation word you write on a form and never use to address anyone.

members.when: Use 先生 to address or refer to someone with respect, on its own or after their family name. It covers teachers, doctors, lawyers, writers and others, and it already carries respect, so no さん is added.

examples.ja: 田中先生、質問があります。
examples.reading: たなかせんせい、しつもんがあります。
examples.en: Tanaka-sensei, I have a question.

examples.ja: 病院で山田先生に診てもらいました。
examples.reading: びょういんでやまだせんせいにみてもらいました。
examples.en: Dr Yamada examined me at the hospital.

members.when: Use 教師 as a neutral job label: on forms, in job listings, and when stating someone's profession. It is never used to address a person and never takes さん.

examples.ja: 職業の欄に教師と書きました。
examples.reading: しょくぎょうのらんにきょうしとかきました。
examples.en: I wrote "teacher" in the occupation box.

examples.ja: 姉は中学校の教師です。
examples.reading: あねはちゅうがっこうのきょうしです。
examples.en: My older sister is a junior-high teacher.

contrast.ja: 先生、おはようございます。
contrast.reading: せんせい、おはようございます。
contrast.en: Good morning, sensei.
contrast.note: Addressing someone is the one job 教師 can never do. Only 先生 works here.

contrast.ja: 兄は高校の教師をしています。
contrast.reading: あにはこうこうのきょうしをしています。
contrast.en: My older brother works as a high-school teacher.
contrast.note: Talking about your own family to an outsider calls for the neutral 教師; 先生 would put respectful language on your own relative.

contrast.ja: 教師になるために大学で勉強しています。
contrast.reading: きょうしになるためにだいがくでべんきょうしています。
contrast.en: I am studying at university to become a teacher.
contrast.note: This is about the profession, so 教師 is the standard choice. 先生になる is also said, and sounds slightly more everyday.

contrast.ja: 日本語の先生はとても優しいです。
contrast.reading: にほんごのせんせいはとてもやさしいです。
contrast.en: My Japanese teacher is very kind.
contrast.note: Referring to your own teacher takes 先生. 教師 would sound like you were describing a stranger in a report.

mistakes.wrong: 教師さん、ありがとうございました。
mistakes.right: 先生、ありがとうございました。
mistakes.why: 教師 is a job label, not a form of address, and it never takes さん. To a Japanese ear this is like calling someone "Mr Occupation" — clearly wrong, and slightly comic.

mistakes.wrong: 私の父は先生です。
mistakes.right: 私の父は教師です。
mistakes.why: When you tell an outsider what your own family member does, you use plain, humble language. 先生 puts a respectful title on your father, which sounds boastful.

mistakes.wrong: 先生さんに聞いてください。
mistakes.right: 先生に聞いてください。
mistakes.why: 先生 is itself an honorific title, so adding さん doubles it up. The title alone is already polite.

faq.q: Can I call my teacher 教師?
faq.a: No. Use 先生, either alone or after their family name. 教師 describes the job from the outside and sounds cold when aimed at a person.

faq.q: Why are doctors called 先生?
faq.a: 先生 is a title for anyone whose expertise you are relying on — doctors, lawyers, politicians, writers, instructors. Teaching is only one of its uses.

faq.q: Which do I write on a form?
faq.a: 教師. Forms and job listings want the neutral occupation word, and 先生 would look out of place there.
